sources_md.2b. Grid carbon is an average, attributi:
## 2b. Grid carbon is an average, attributional, life-cycle figure

**Average, not marginal.** Every grid import is charged the half-hour's
*average* life-cycle intensity of the region's generation mix, never the
marginal plant's. That is the attributional reading, and it matches every
other coefficient in the study: an asset is charged its own inventory, not the
change it causes elsewhere. A marginal (consequential) factor answers a
different question — what the system emits *because* the data centre draws one
more kWh — and would change what avoiding an import is worth: Hawkes puts GB's
long-run marginal at 0.26–0.53 kg CO₂/kWh now against a 0.69 short-run, both
well above today's average. Using it would need a consequential treatment of
every asset as well, so it is out of scope, and the Overview lists it as an
extension. Which way it would move the answer is not one-signed — a marginal
factor values an avoided import differently and swings differently across the
day — so this is recorded as a limitation, not a bias of known direction.

**Delivered at the connection voltage.** A kWh imported carries the losses and
the network's embodied carbon down to the voltage the site connects at
(`optimiser_lca.grid.DELIVERY`, ecoinvent's GB voltage chain). Every site this
study prices connects at high voltage — transmission, or an EHV distribution
band — so imports pay ×1.0338 on generation plus 1.93 g/kWh. A bought-hydrogen
seller's grid electricity is delivered on the same constants
(`h2_prices.GREEN_H2_SELLER_VOLTAGE`), so the two grid users share one basis.

**Imports follow the flows that reach the region.** The API reports a region's
imports as one figure. It is split across exporting countries each half-hour by
Elexon's interconnector flows, weighted by a per-region attribution fitted to
NESO's own regional import share (`optimiser_lca.grid.IMPORT_ATTRIBUTION`). The
fit is a calibration to NESO's regional model, not a physical flow trace;
every exporter is scored on its own country's average HV market, not on the
plant at its margin.

sources_md.8. Cut-off rule:
## 8. Cut-off rule

A flow that is in a held source and inside the boundary is always in; the
boundary excludes only end-of-life, delivery to site and the standby generator
(§6–7). The cut-off test below applies to flows no held source itemises: each
may stay out only if its upper estimate is under 1% of its technology's
carbon (rule 1), all of a technology's together under 5% (rule 2), and
adding them all back must not change the best design (rule 3, the `cutoff`
sensitivity knob). Criteria after PAS 2050 and Vestas V162 §3.3, applied per
technology; rule 3 is this study's addition under ISO 14044's sensitivity
requirement for comparative assertions. Not ecoinvent's "cut-off" system model.
Battery power-side flows are tested at a 1 h floor; energy-side flows at their
ceiling. A flow that fails is included (status below). Register:
`optimiser_lca/exclusions.py`; this section is generated by
`python optimisation/cutoff.py --write`.

sources_md.1. Data centre runs flat at 100 %:
## 1. Data centre runs flat at 100 %

Continuous draw of **7,306 kW**. This is not an added assumption: the Zhang et
al. foreground's own operation exchange is 1.60e9 kWh over a 25-year life,
which is 7,306 kW continuous. It is where the old `dashboard_config.SYS_DC_DEMAND_MW
= 7.31` came from.

That figure is the **whole facility**, at Zhang's own PUE of 1.4, so the IT load
behind it is **5,219 kW**. The two must not be confused: `size_mw_it` is an IT
load and is multiplied by the caller's PUE to get demand, so passing 7.31 with a
PUE above 1.0 models a facility larger than Zhang's. `DC_REFERENCE_PUE` exists to
make the conversion explicit and is the only place Zhang's PUE is used — the
facility's embodied burden is anchored on IT capacity, not on facility draw, so
improving PUE no longer shrinks the building.

*Consequence*: no load-shifting option, and no diurnal or seasonal demand
shape. Storage is therefore sized purely against supply variability, never
against demand variability — which makes renewables+storage look somewhat
harder than it would with a flexible AI training load.

children.name: 2. Geography is GB, via the electricity exchange

sources_md.2. Geography is GB, via the electricity:
## 2. Geography is GB, via the electricity exchange

The data centre foreground is authored in Virginia against `market for
electricity, medium voltage [US-SERC]`. Rather than re-authoring the
inventory, that electricity is swapped for the half-hourly GB grid mix from the
Carbon Intensity API (`optimisation/grid_build.py`, originally notebook 3.1),
by the exact `fixed + Σ kWh×EF` decomposition in `baseline_grid.py`.

The inventory has **exactly one** electricity exchange — IT + cooling/aux,
1.60e9 kWh over 25 years — and it is the only US-*grid* input in the activity
(the concrete is RNA, i.e. North American, as the audit noted).
The swap is applied two ways, which agree to 1e-4 %: the full Brightway
substitution above, and the `fixed + Σ kWh×EF` decomposition
`baseline_grid.py` uses so the optimiser can treat the facility as linear
coefficients.

*Residual*: the remaining twelve exchanges are **global-market** datasets —
`GLO` for reinforcing and structural steel, copper, aluminium, tap water, the
diesel genset, the UPS battery and R134a; `RoW` for PUR foam and sodium
hypochlorite. So they are not US-specific, but they are not GB-specific either,
and no transport leg is modelled at all. Together with the materials they are
about 963 t CO2e/y charged at the reference facility (14 Oct 2026, after the
refrigerant leakage was added), plus the 32.5 t genset the LP excludes.
Sourcing them to GB/European supply chains is a known, unmodelled refinement.
The R134a top-up is also emitted as HFC-134a: Zhang derive it as leakage
replacement (see SOURCES.md).

*Scope*: the activity is **Material Production + Construction + Operation**
(construction energy and water in since 21 Oct 2026: they are in the source
and inside the boundary). Transportation (delivery to site), disposal and
recycling are outside the boundary — so the facility carries no
decommissioning or demolition burden. See §6. Zhang's own figures put the
facility at 7.53 MW with 5.38 MW of IT; the 7,306 / 5,219 kW read out of the
1.60e9 kWh they print sit 3 % under those (7.53 MW × 8,760 h × 25 y is 1.649e9,
printed rounded down). The energy-driven part is charged per MWh of that printed
electricity, so it is unaffected. The IT-driven part (servers, UPS, building,
construction) was sized on 5.38 MW of IT, so since 26 Oct 2026 it is normalised
by 5.38 MW, not by the 5.219 MW read back (`data_centre.ZHANG_IT_MW`; it was 3.1 %
high per MW of IT before). Zhang's §2.2b names chillers, cooling towers, pumps and
piping as in scope but S1 does not disaggregate them, and the 2,000 kg initial
R134a charge is a sizing note, not an inventory row: both are taken as inside
Zhang's own rows and not added (user, 26 Oct 2026).

children.name: 3. Hydrogen the study *makes* is co-located with its use; hydrogen it *buys* is compressed but not hauled

sources_md.3. Hydrogen the study *makes* is co-loca:
## 3. Hydrogen the study *makes* is co-located with its use; hydrogen it *buys* is compressed but not hauled

No hydrogen transport, distribution or liquefaction is modelled, for any
hydrogen pathway — green, grey, blue or turquoise. Self-production assumes a
plant adjacent to the data centre, feeding the fuel cell (or the storage tank)
directly at the plant gate.

**Delivery compression is no longer excluded.** It used to be, on the same
co-location argument — but that argument covers hydrogen this study produces and
not hydrogen it purchases, which by definition comes from somebody else's plant.
Meanwhile self-produced hydrogen was charged a compression parasitic to enter
the tank and bought hydrogen was not, so the exclusion was also an asymmetry
that favoured buying. Every bought colour now carries the work of compressing it
to 200 bar tube-trailer pressure at the seller's gate, in both objectives —
`h2_prices.bought_h2_compression_*`, detailed in `SOURCES.md`. Road haulage
itself is still excluded, and is registered in `DATA_GAPS.md` rather than
justified here.

*Verified*: no H2 distribution exchange exists in `hydrogen foreground`,
`fuel cell foreground` or `hydrogen storage foreground`, so nothing is being
double-counted. The two transport exchanges that do exist are unrelated —
CO2-to-storage pipeline inside the CCS chain, and the negative passenger-car
term that removes ecoinvent's domestic-micro-CHP service-visit artefact.

*Consequence*: the SMR / SMR-CCS / MP-E options implicitly site a reformer or
pyrolysis unit on the data centre campus, fed from the gas grid. Plausible at
this scale, but it is an assumption, not a finding. The "off-site green
hydrogen" option is now "green hydrogen bought at a price, with its production
burden and its compression, but no haulage".

Storage compression is still counted where it applies, via
`h2_storage.compression_kwh_per_kg` from the electrolyser's delivery pressure
to the tank's — zero for the 28 bar design, since the electrolyser already
delivers at ~30 bar.

**Bought green hydrogen is green by definition, and that rests on certificates.**
Decided 2–3 Sep. The grid-connected share of bought green
(`h2_prices.GREEN_H2_GRID_SHARE`, 0.5) is scored on a *renewable* electricity
basis plus the grid's high-voltage delivery terms — 1.107 kg CO₂e/kg against
0.976 behind the meter — not on the grid mix the electrolyser physically draws from. That is a
market-based reading, and it holds only if the seller's grid electricity is
backed by matched renewable certificates (REGOs, or an RFNBO-style hourly match).
Two things follow that the numbers do not show on their own:

- The price carries **no certificate premium**. NESO's and EHO's grid-connected
  LCOH are priced on wholesale power, so the bought-green price is the cost of
  the electricity, not of the claim to it.
- The LP's **own** grid electrolyser (`grid_h2`) is scored on the real
  location-based grid mix instead. Same physical setup, two bases: about
  **8.8 kg CO₂e/kg** made on site at London's 2025 annual mean against **1.06**
  bought. The asymmetry favours
  buying, and it is deliberate — the study assumes a buyer can contract for
  certified green hydrogen but does not assume the data centre certifies its own
  imports. Anyone comparing `grid_h2` with bought green should read the gap as
  partly an accounting convention, not only physics. Audit §3.6.

children.name: 3a. The site is a coordinate, and everything follows from it

sources_md.3a. The site is a coordinate, and everyt:
## 3a. The site is a coordinate, and everything follows from it

`sites.resolve(lat, lon)` derives the Carbon Intensity region and the TNUoS
demand zone from the coordinate, so the weather, the grid mix and the network
bill cannot drift apart from one another. Two real lookups
(postcodes.io → Carbon Intensity API) plus a fixed GSP-group correspondence for
the TNUoS zone, checked against presets set independently from published
sources.

*Consequence, and it is a correction*: the old `dashboard_config.WIND_LAT / WIND_LON`
(51.7320, -0.3711) is a field near **St Albans** — Carbon Intensity region 10,
TNUoS zone 9. Every cached grid series in this repo is **region 13, London**,
TNUoS zone 12. So the study as it previously stood paired London's grid carbon
intensity and London's £7.41/kW demand tariff with a Hertfordshire wind site.

Carbon-wise the two regions are similar and the error is small. The network
charge is not: zone 12 is £7.41/kW against zone 9's £1.11/kW. Nothing warned
about it because nothing connected the wind coordinate to the grid region.
`require_grid_region()` now refuses the combination outright, and the matrix is
run at a coordinate genuinely inside region 13.

children.name: 3b. Every half-hourly series is on UTC

sources_md.3b. Every half-hourly series is on UTC:
## 3b. Every half-hourly series is on UTC

Grid carbon, wholesale price and wind/solar are joined on naive UTC timestamps,
and a requested window is read as UTC. Until 12 Oct 2026 the grid series was
London local time while price and weather were UTC, so from late March to late
October intraday grid carbon sat an hour late against everything else (Audit
§3.5). Every saved grid file was rebuilt on UTC that day and carries a
`clock = UTC` column; `profiles.py` ignores grid files without it.

Rules published on the UK clock convert from UTC where they are applied: the
DUoS red/amber/green bands (`network_charges.duos_band`) and Elexon settlement
periods (`grid_build.normalise_elexon`). The DUoS red band is November-February
only, so it never moved; amber did, by an hour, all summer.

children.name: 3c. Generation is onshore wind and ground-mount solar only

sources_md.3c. Generation is onshore wind and groun:
## 3c. Generation is onshore wind and ground-mount solar only

Every site is on land (decided 3 Sep), so offshore wind is out of scope and
`dc_architectures.OFFSHORE_IN_SCOPE` holds it off for every architecture and
every caller. It used to be unlocked wherever `sites.Site.offshore_wind` flagged
a coastal region, and the LP has no offshore profile — `cap_offshore` ran on the
*onshore* capacity-factor series, so in the high cost case it built offshore on
onshore yield. The offshore coefficients are still built and reported; turning
the switch back on needs an offshore series first.

sources_md.4. Cost basis:
## 4. Cost basis

DESNZ/Arup 2024 Cost of Electricity reports, **2023 real prices**, with each
technology's own pre-tax real hurdle rate (onshore wind 5.8 %, offshore wind
6.2 %, solar PV 5.0 %) rather than a single project WACC. Set
`optimisation.tech_costs.DISCOUNT_RATE_OVERRIDE` to impose one rate instead.

*One asymmetry, deliberate*: generation step-up transformers
(`transformers.py`) are charged in **carbon and not in cost**. The DESNZ/Arup
capex is plant-plus-connection-to-the-point-of-connection, so it already
contains the electrical balance of plant; a separate £/MW transformer charge
would double count, while the carbon side has no such term anywhere — none of
the generation inventories contains a transformer, and ecoinvent has no power
transformer at any rating to supply one. See SOURCES.md.

Electricity is priced at the Elexon APXMIDP half-hourly wholesale price plus
the demand-side network charges `network_charges.py` builds (TNUoS, BSUoS,
DUoS). Levies (RO/FiT/CfD/CM/AAHEDC, CCL) and supplier margin are not
included, so absolute £/MWh still understates a real import bill (TODO). The
connection and UoS figures in the DESNZ tables are *generator*-side and are
not a substitute.

sources_md.5. Emissions are IPCC 2021 GWP100, attri:
## 5. Emissions are IPCC 2021 GWP100, attributional

Grid electricity uses the **average** attributional intensity of the regional
mix, not short-run marginal intensity. This is the right basis for reporting
the facility's footprint; it is the wrong basis for claiming that shifting a
load reduces real-world emissions. Any timing-based result should be reported
against both.

**No credits anywhere; co-products carry no burden away.** Decided 21 Oct
2026. The study takes no avoided-burden credits: not for recycling (§6), and
not for co-products. Two cases in the inventories: methane pyrolysis, where
Hermesmann & Müller credit the 3 kg of solid carbon per kg H₂ against carbon
black, and SMR / SMR-CCS, where they credit the excess electricity (1.10 and
0.05 kWh per kg) as an avoided burden — the second was carried "as the source
does" until 22 Oct 2026 and is now dropped too (+1.4 % on grey). Here the whole
burden sits on the hydrogen. Electrolysis oxygen is likewise an unallocated
co-product. This keeps the study attributional throughout, at the cost of
making turquoise hydrogen look worse than its source reports.

sources_md.6. No end-of-life, anywhere:
## 6. No end-of-life, anywhere

The study is **cradle-to-gate on every input**, with the functional unit being
the data centre powered at a given size, year and location. Nothing is followed
past the site gate on the way out: no demolition, decommissioning, disposal or
recycling, and no recycling credit, for the facility or for any energy asset.

**Transport to site is outside the boundary, and nothing else is.** No capital
good, cable or hydrogen is carried to the site, for any technology, because
where the site will be is not known. Transport further up the supply chain does
not depend on the site and is kept: ecoinvent's market transport, legs between
manufacturing stages, materials to a factory.

Every foreground already meets this without modification:

| Foreground | Position |
|---|---|
| Data centre | Material production, construction and operation; transportation (delivery to site), disposal and recycling outside the boundary |
| H2 storage tank | Shell, its forming, frame and pad; valves and compressor hardware on the cut-off register; end-of-life out |
| Grid connection | Transformer materials (Leng 2026's 100 MVA, 110 kV main transformer, per MVA, × 2 for N-1) and the switchyard's civils per MW of connection (Leng's outdoor venue, D2), plus a line term reported but not charged per MW; switchgear, protection and manufacturing energy carried as cut-off estimates (§8); losses in the LP; no end-of-life |
| Generation step-up transformers | Transformer capital (wind materials-only; solar with IEA PVPS process energy); no switchgear, protection or civils. Losses are charged as energy in the LP (`conversion_losses.py`), not as a coefficient |
| Battery and fuel-cell step-ups (15 Oct) | Jasper 2026's container transformer mass on the IEA PVPS composition (with its process energy), a stated substitution for Jasper's own Hunziker-derived recipe on representativeness (SOURCES.md, 22 Oct), per MW of inverter rating, over the asset's own life; no switchgear, protection or civils. Losses in the LP at ASSUMED loadings (0.5 battery, 1.0 fuel cell), the fuel cell's unit energised on standby |
| Grid battery | Jasper/Voß cradle-to-gate manufacture including the cell factory's energy and upstream transport; Jasper's EOL sheet not taken, his delivery-to-site rows left out (Voß's legs to a German factory not taken, and subtracted where folded into a factor), no foundation |
| Electrolysers | Capital good plus consumables; no end-of-life exchange |
| Fuel cell stack | Babatunde et al. cradle-to-gate manufacture, no use or end-of-life phase |
| Fuel cell BoP / maintenance | Usai et al. 2021 process loops + inverter + container, cradle-to-gate; service consumables only. No end-of-life, no delivery transport |

The SMR-CCS chain's "CCS waste treatment" activity is **not** an exception: it
is the capture and storage leg of a production route, inside the gate.

*Residual, and it cannot be declared away*: coefficients scored on **ecoinvent
3.9.1 apos** carry end-of-life inside their background datasets, because the
APOS system model allocates waste-treatment burdens back into the product
system. This affects the wind, offshore, battery pack, inverter, transformer
and tank-steel terms, and cannot be stripped exchange-by-exchange from outside.
The cut-off system model is the one that corresponds to a strict cradle-to-gate
rule; moving to it would break the "3.9.1 apos throughout" consistency claim and
every pinned constant, so the embedded share is declared here rather than
removed.

children.name: 7. The facility's standby generator is excluded

sources_md.7. The facility's standby generator is e:
## 7. The facility's standby generator is excluded

Zhang's inventory carries a diesel standby generator — 8.6e6 MJ over the life,
**32.5 t CO2e/yr** at his facility size. It is scored, reported by
`dc_inputs.data_centre_coefficients()` as
`backup_kgco2e_per_year_excluded`, and **left out of every objective**.

Backup is a *decision variable* in this study: the optimiser sizes a fuel cell,
a battery, a grid connection and an unserved-energy allowance to provide exactly
the resilience the genset provides. Charging Zhang's genset on top would bill
every architecture for a second backup system, and would bill the islanded ones
twice over for a function they were built to supply.

*Consequence*: the grid-connected baselines lose an asset a real site would
probably have. The number is preserved rather than deleted so it can be added
back for a like-for-like comparison against a conventional facility.

The UPS battery is **not** treated this way and stays in. Ride-through over
seconds is a different function from bulk storage, so it is not a double count.

The two reference cases re-solved at both anchors with every still-excluded flow added at its
upper estimate (`dc_inputs.build_tech(cutoff="upper")`, sensitivity knob `cutoff`), against the
central model. Q4's test: the same technologies are built and no built capacity moves by more than
5 %. Solved 23 Oct 2026; `optimisation_outputs/sensitivity_cutoff_*.csv`.

sources_md.Renewable generation \u2014 embodied car:
## Renewable generation — embodied carbon per MW
`renewables.py`

ecoinvent supplies renewables as **per-kWh** activities with capital already
amortised over a lifetime output ecoinvent chose. This module strips that back
out to **kg CO₂e per MW installed**, so the burden of building capacity does
not depend on how much it happens to generate.

| Technology | Capital | ecoinvent implied LF | Restated at DESNZ LF | Grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Onshore wind | 658 t CO₂e/MW | 26.2 % over 20 y | 5.6 g CO₂e/kWh (was 14.5) | transcribed / derived |
| Offshore wind | 890 t CO₂e/MW | 30.0 % over 20 y | 5.7 g CO₂e/kWh (was 17.1) | transcribed / derived |
| Solar PV | **1,048 t CO₂e/MWp** (IEA PVPS) | — | **25.8 g CO₂e/kWh** | transcribed / derived |
| Solar PV, ecoinvent basis | 2,303 t CO₂e/MWp | 11.0 % over 30 y | 56.7 g CO₂e/kWh (was 79.8) | transcribed / derived |

Wind capital scores are **transcribed** from ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos (`market for
wind turbine, 2MW, onshore` + its network connection). The restatement is
**derived**, using DESNZ/Arup load factors and lifetimes from `tech_costs.py`.

**Verification built in.** `check_reconstruction()` re-amortises the per-MW
figure back over ecoinvent's own implied lifetime output and fails unless it
reproduces ecoinvent's published per-kWh score exactly. All three pass — it is
anchored on `ecoinvent_capital_kgco2e_per_MW`, which every row keeps whatever
basis is in force, so substituting solar's basis does not retire the check.

sources_md.Generation step-up transformers \u2014 e:
## Generation step-up transformers — embodied carbon per MW connected
`transformers.py`, inventory built by `optimiser_lca/stepup_transformers.py`

A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage — below the 1 kV
boundary ecoinvent itself draws. The data centre draws at *medium* voltage,
1–24 kV, because that is what `market for electricity, medium voltage` describes
and what the Zhang foreground is authored against. Something must bridge them,
and it is **not optional**:

| | at 690 V | at 20 kV |
|---|---|---|
| one 2 MW turbine | 1,673 A | 58 A |
| a 100 MW farm | **83,674 A** | 2,887 A |

So every turbine carries its own transformer at the foot of its tower — **one
per turbine, not one per farm**, and a 100 MW farm has fifty.

**No inventory in this study contains them.** Checked exchange by exchange:
`wind turbine construction, 2MW, onshore` lists its own parts in its comment
("Rotor, Nacelle, Electronics, Tower, Foundation") with no transformer among
them; its only electrical item is **438.7 kg** of `electronics, for control
units`, against the 3–5 t a 2 MW turbine transformer weighs; its stated
component masses (rotor 37 t, nacelle 61 t, tower 165 t) account for the
materials without leaving room for one; and it says outright that it excludes
the grid connection, which is a separate dataset of cable and trench (253.8 kg
copper, 1,375.7 kg HDPE, 1,398.7 m³ excavation).

**And ecoinvent cannot supply the asset.** It has **four** transformer
activities, which are two products with a market and a production each, and both
are electronics — by ecoinvent's own comments, *"a typical high voltage use
transformer **in electronic modules** has an average weight of **280 g** … used
in the information and communication technology"*, and **30 g** for the
low-voltage one. Their compositions match: 0.50 kg ferrite, 0.31 kg epoxy and
0.51 kg injection moulding per kg, against **5 g of steel**. There is no
`substation` activity, no `switchgear` activity, and no power transformer at any
rating. Until this rewrite wind scaled that 280 g component up by a factor of
**205,000**; rebuilding a real transformer's bill of materials gives 177.3 t
CO₂e against 306.2 t on that dataset, with the manufacturer declaring 147.4 t,
so the old basis ran about **2×** high. Nobody who has looked at this used
ecoinvent's transformer — Leng built theirs from materials, Teffera built theirs
from materials, and Vestas scaled a real ABB EPD.

So the transformer is assembled from a published bill of materials, exactly as
the hydrogen tank is, and for the same reason.

children.module_doc:
Renewable generation — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

ecoinvent supplies renewable electricity as a **per-kWh** activity, with the
plant's capital burden already amortised over a lifetime output that ecoinvent
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape here, for two reasons:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW should not be a function of how much they happen to
   generate in the modelled year.
2. **ecoinvent's implied yield is not this study's yield.** Generation comes
   from Renewables.ninja at a chosen site, and the cost side uses DESNZ/Arup's
   load factors and lifetimes. Neither matches ecoinvent's own assumption, and
   for onshore wind the gap is a factor of 2.5.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the plant/turbine unit
exchange from the per-kWh activity, scores that unit, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. Per-kWh burden is then recomputed at whatever load factor and
lifetime the study actually uses. Nothing is invented - the reconstruction is
checked against ecoinvent's own per-kWh score, which it reproduces exactly.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Solar is not scored on ecoinvent, and why
-----------------------------------------
ecoinvent 3.9.1's GB open-ground PV activity is the 570 kWp Solarpark El
Tesoro in Andalusia, **installed in 2008**, carrying 4,401.7 m2 of panel for
570 kWp - a 129.5 W/m2, **12.95 %** module. It restates to 57 g CO2e/kWh,
about ten times onshore wind, which is not a defensible basis for a plant that
has not been built yet. 95.5 % of that burden is in the two exchanges that
scale with panel area, so the vintage is the whole story.

The obvious fixes are both closed. Upgrading the database does nothing: the
plant inventory is byte-identical in ecoinvent 3.10.1, so only the background
would move. And no other GB PV activity exists at utility scale - the only
alternatives are 3 kWp slanted-roof systems of the same vintage.

So the default basis for solar is **IEA PVPS Task 12**, the standard reference
for PV LCA, whose 2023 data update uses the same IPCC 2021 GWP100 method this
study uses throughout: 35.8 g CO2e/kWh for mono-Si at 976 kWh/kWp/year over 30
years, which is 1,048 kg CO2e/kWp of embodied carbon against ecoinvent's
2,303. Their reference yield sits within 10 % of the DESNZ GB solar load
factor, so the figure transfers with no irradiance correction - unusual, and
the reason this substitution is clean rather than a fudge.

Mono-Si, and not the like-for-like multi-Si IEA PVPS also publish, because
``cap_solar`` is a *decision variable* for a plant that does not exist yet, so
the question is what would actually be built. IEA PVPS record multi-Si market
share falling below 3 % in 2022 and to ~1 % in 2023 - they could not update
its parameters for want of current data. That is the same argument this module
already makes about not inheriting ecoinvent's yield for a sized asset, and it
is why multi-Si is not offered as a basis: it would fail the test on exactly
the ground ecoinvent fails it. Its number is kept in SOURCES.md as evidence,
where it answers the reviewer who suspects the technology was switched to
flatter the result.

So there are two bases, and the second exists only to reproduce older runs.
Pass ``solar_basis="ecoinvent"`` for that; both live in
``SOLAR_EMBODIED_BASES``. Wind and offshore wind are mostly steel and concrete
and ageing far more slowly than a PV module, so their capital dominates - but
the boundary still has to match solar's. IEA PVPS's per-kWh figure is a
**full-scope** footprint (module, BOS, inverter, install, EOL); a capital-only
wind figure restated on top of it would be comparing different things. So
``restate()`` adds ecoinvent's own non-capital consumables (lubricating oil,
water - the ~1 % ``residual_per_kWh`` from ``decompose()``) back on top of
wind and offshore's restated capital by default, making both technologies
full-scope. It is skipped only where the capital figure is already full-scope
itself (solar under its default IEA basis); it still applies under
``solar_basis="ecoinvent"``, since that basis is capital-only too.

Sources
-------
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100. Activities are the
wind, offshore    GB per-kWh generation datasets and the capital "unit"
                  exchanges they draw on.
embodied carbon   IEA PVPS Task 12, "Environmental Life Cycle Assessment of
solar             Electricity from PV systems - 2023 data update", Stucki M.,
                  Goetz M., de Wild-Scholten M. & Frischknecht R., May 2024.
load factor,      DESNZ/Arup 2024 Cost of Electricity reports, via
lifetime          ``tech_costs.py``. See SOURCES.md.

Run:  python optimisation/renewables.py

One unit per TURBINE, not one per farm. Not optional: 100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A. ecoinvent 3.9.1 has no power transformer at any rating - its four transformer activities are two electronic components of 280 g and 30 g average weight, by its own comments - and its wind turbine dataset lists its parts as Rotor/Nacelle/Electronics/Tower/Foundation with no transformer among them, its only electrical item being 438.7 kg of control electronics. So this is assembled from Leng et al. (2026), Processes 14(7) 1045, Supplementary Table S1: the 50 x 2.2 MVA S11-2200/35 box transformers on their 100 MW Gaoyou farm, 282,343 kg in total, divided by the farm. Cross-checked against Teffera et al. (2021) Int J LCA 26:76-96 Table 5, which lands within the same band by a different route. Functional unit is 1 MW of wind CONNECTED - amortise over TX_ASSET_LIFE_YEARS (dc_config). INCLUDES Leng Table S3's box-transformer foundations (since 21 Oct 2026) and electrical installation - section steel, terminal blocks, welding rod, lead seals (since 22 Oct 2026), per MW of the same farm. EXCLUDES: the grid-export transformer (this study is behind the meter, there is nothing to export into, and the grid intake is charged by grid_connection.py); any step between the collection network and the data centre (both sit in the medium-voltage band); switchgear and protection; losses; end-of-life. Leng publish no factory energy for the unit, so none is charged.

Why this inventory exists

A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage (<1 kV, the band

sources_md.Solar is not scored on ecoinvent \u2014:
### Solar is not scored on ecoinvent — `renewables.SOLAR_EMBODIED_BASES`

ecoinvent 3.9.1's GB open-ground PV activity is the 570 kWp **Solarpark El
Tesoro**, Alcolea del Río, Andalusia, **installed 2008** — the dataset's own
comment says so; the "2012" this register carried previously was the citation's
URL access date. It holds 4,401.7 m² of panel for 570 kWp, i.e. 129.5 W/m² or a
**12.95 % module**, against 21–23 % for a module built today. 95.5 % of its
burden is in the two exchanges that scale with panel area (panel 72.0 %,
mounting 23.5 %), so the vintage is essentially the whole number.

Neither obvious fix works. The plant inventory is **byte-identical in ecoinvent
3.10.1** — verified exchange by exchange against the copy in the `hypt`
Brightway project — so upgrading moves only the background. And GB has just
three PV activities in either version, of which the other two are 3 kWp
slanted-roof systems of the same vintage.

So solar's default basis is **IEA PVPS Task 12**, the standard reference for PV
LCA, on the same IPCC 2021 GWP100 method used throughout this study.

| Basis | Source | g CO₂e/kWh at this study's yield | t CO₂e/MWp | Grade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `smith_2024_upv_fixed_tilt` *(default)* | Smith et al. 2024 (NREL/TP-7A40-87372) utility-scale inventory, fixed tilt, **rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos** | **22.0** | **895** | derived |
| `iea_pvps_2023_mono_si` | IEA PVPS T12 2023 update, mono-Si, 20.9 % module — a **3 kWp ROOFTOP** system | 25.8 | 1,048 | transcribed |
| `ecoinvent` | ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, as above | 56.7 | 2,303 | transcribed |

Three bases. `ecoinvent` exists only to reproduce runs from before the rooftop
default arrived; `iea_pvps_2023_mono_si` only to reproduce runs from before the
utility-scale rebuild.
sources_md.Why the default is now a rebuild rather:
### Why the default is now a rebuild rather than a citation

`cap_solar` is a utility-scale MWp. The basis it replaces is quoted, in IEA
PVPS's own words, against *"1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop
mounted"* — so a solar farm was priced with roof rails, a domestic string
inverter, and **no** perimeter fence, **no** plant-scale site cabling and **no**
land. It was also the one coefficient in the study not on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos:
IEA PVPS use UVEK in SimaPro under **recycled-content** allocation, a different
system model, which `SOURCES.md` had not previously recorded.

Smith publishes on ecoinvent **cut-off**, so his results cannot simply be
relabelled — APOS and cut-off differ precisely where recycled content matters,
which for a PV plant is the aluminium, steel and copper. His **inventory** is
therefore taken and rescored in this project, which makes the answer apos by
construction, exactly as the wind transformer and the data centre are. His
process names are ecoinvent-native, so 93 % resolve with no decision at all.

**Verification.** 290 of 290 scientific-notation values in Appendix A appear in
the transcription; 251 rows were association-checked against the PDF text and
249 are clean, the two flagged being zero-GWP flows. Of 79 biosphere rows,
exactly **four** carry a non-zero GWP100 factor — the silicon-smelting CO₂ and
the two fluorinated cell gases, CF₄ at 7,380 and C₂F₆ at 12,400 — and all four
are included. The module lands at **684 kg CO₂e/kWdc**, and Smith states his
average-import module sits *above* the 630 kg CO₂e/kW EPEAT low-carbon
threshold: his own published result, reproduced from his inventory, on a
different system model.

| per MWp | t CO₂e |
|---|---|
| module (A1–A8) | 683.8 |
| fixed-tilt mounting (IEA PVPS T12-33:2026), incl. its upstream transport, packaging waste and land rows since 21 Oct 2026 | 161.4 (was 148.6) |
| electrical balance of system | 30.8 |
| inverters | 11.7 |
| fence | 1.3 |
| installation energy | 1.3 |
| O&M, 30 y prorated to 38 y | 17.8 |
| **total** | **908.1** (was 895.3) |

**Four substitutions, each stated.** Smith's system is single-axis **tracked**;
GB utility-scale is fixed tilt, so Table A9 is replaced by IEA PVPS T12-33:2026
`Z-PV-239`, a pile-driven steel table at 20°. That makes the mounting *heavier*,
not lighter — 9.730 against 9.618 kg/m² of structure — because a fixed table
needs more clamps and fasteners per m² than a torque tube; the module frame is
untouched, being 1.51 kg/m² of AlMg3 inside the module. The **transformer** is
excluded because `transformers.py` already charges the step-up, and Smith's A11
is unusable regardless at 19,796 kg/MVA, ~9× the measured specific mass at that
rating. The **inverter count** comes from Smith's stated DC/AC of 1.34, not from
his Table A14 count, which implies 1.75 — the two are inconsistent in the
source. **O&M** keeps his replacement *fraction* (30 % of the installed count
over 30 years, Mason's 10 %/decade) rather than his absolute count, since our
inverter count differs.

**Excluded, with direction.** End-of-life, as everywhere in this study.
Construction transport — the sea leg alone is 201 t·km/m² for this import
chain, so the figure **understates by roughly 1.5 %**. Supply chain is the SE
Asia import case: China's national grid for the silicon chain, Thailand for cell
fabrication and module assembly.

**The O&M prorating cancels in the objective.** Since `restate()` gives
`annual = capital_total / life` and `capital_total = capital + om30 × life/30`,
the annual charge is `capital/life + om30/30`. The O&M term is life-independent
once annualised, so the 30 → 38 year scaling moves only the reported per-kWh
columns, never the LP.

Issues knowingly parked are listed in `data/UPV-DEFERRED-ISSUES.md`. Every
Smith table this study uses (A1–A8, A10, A12, A13) is written out in
`optimiser_lca/upv.py`, one activity per table with the rows as printed,
checked against the transcription in `data/smith-nrel-2024-life-cycle-inventory.md`;
the parsing heuristics that first read the PDF ran once and are not shipped.
IEA PVPS's multi-Si figure is **not** offered as a basis — see
below for why it is evidence rather than a scenario.

Source: Stucki M., Götz M., de Wild-Scholten M. & Frischknecht R. (2024),
*Environmental Life Cycle Assessment of Electricity from PV systems — 2023 data
update*, IEA PVPS Task 12, May 2024. Reference system: 1 kWh AC from a 3 kWp
rooftop array, in-plane irradiation 1,331 kWh/m², **annual yield 976 kWh/kWp**
including 0.7 %/a degradation, 30 y panel / 15 y inverter.

**Why the transfer is clean.** A published per-kWh figure carries its author's
yield and lifetime, so it is turned back into t CO₂e/MWp before `restate()` puts
it on this study's own yield — the **derived** half. That works here because IEA
PVPS's 976 kWh/kWp sits within 10 % of the DESNZ GB solar load factor (12.2 % =
1,069 kWh/kWp), so no irradiance correction is needed. Most PV harmonisations
normalise to 1,700 kWh/m²/yr and would need a large one.

**Why mono-Si, and why multi-Si is evidence rather than an option.** `cap_solar`
is a decision variable for a plant that does not exist yet, so the question is
what would actually be built. IEA PVPS record multi-Si market share below 3 % in
2022 and ~1 % in 2023 — they could not even update its parameters for want of
current data. Offering it as a basis would let the study be run on a technology
nobody deploys, failing the test on exactly the ground ecoinvent fails it, so it
is deliberately absent from `SOLAR_EMBODIED_BASES`.

Its **number** is kept here, because it is what shows this correction is not
merely an efficiency story. Hold the technology fixed at multi-Si and update
only the manufacturing — thinner wafers, lower kerf loss, less electricity and
heat per m² — and IEA PVPS's 2023 figure is **43.6 g CO₂e/kWh = 1,277 t
CO₂e/MWp**, still 0.55× ecoinvent's 2,303. Most of the gap is manufacturing
vintage, not module efficiency. That is the answer to a reviewer who suspects
the technology was switched in order to flatter the result: switching
technology accounts for 1,277 → 1,048, and the vintage for 2,303 → 1,277.

**Corroboration.** IEA PVPS track the same Swiss mono-Si rooftop system across
editions: 121 (1996) → 76 (2007, 14.0 % module) → 43 (2020) → 36 g CO₂e/kWh
(2023, 20.9 %). ecoinvent's 2008 / 12.95 % plant restating to 57 g/kWh sits
exactly where its vintage predicts once ground-mount and this study's longer
life are allowed for — so the ecoinvent figure is *correct for its vintage*,
which is both its defence and the case against using it. Independently,
NREL/TP-7A40-87372 (Smith et al., March 2024) puts US utility-scale PV at 10–36
g CO₂e/kWh across six supply-chain and end-of-life cases, built on ecoinvent 3.9
with 20.3 % PERC modules.

**Caveats, stated.** IEA PVPS's reference is a **3 kWp rooftop** array, so
ground-mount swaps roof rails for heavier steel; NREL's utility-scale range
brackets the figure, so the error is real but small and points upward. And this
is the one coefficient in the study not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos — IEA
PVPS use the UVEK LCI database in SimaPro. Both are IPCC 2021 GWP100, but the
backgrounds differ.

**No UK source exists for this.** POSTnote 383 *Carbon Footprint of Electricity
Generation* is from June 2011; the DESNZ GHG Conversion Factors cover
operational emissions only, with no capital goods for generation assets; the
DESNZ/Arup cost reports carry no inventories; and the UK Solar Roadmap (June
2025) is deployment and planning policy. This is the same pattern as the
hydrogen chain — the UK publishes costs and tariffs, not inventories.

**Why it matters.** ecoinvent's GB onshore wind assumes 45,918 kWh/kW over
its life; DESNZ/Arup give 116,815 kWh/kW — **2.5× more**. Charging embodied
carbon per kWh at ecoinvent's rate overstates it by that factor. Notebooks 4.1
and 4.3 charge wind per kWh generated and so carry ecoinvent's assumption:
fine for a fixed plant, wrong once capacity is a decision variable.

**Wind is unaffected by the PV vintage problem** above: ecoinvent's turbine is
mostly steel and concrete and ages far more slowly than a PV module. Its
datasets stay the basis for both onshore and offshore.

sources_md.Solar's inverter-station step-ups \u2014:
### Solar's inverter-station step-ups — IEA PVPS Task 12 (2026)

`solar_pv` used to keep an *invented* plant-rated unit on the electronics
dataset, with **no per-inverter-station transformers at all**. That is now
closed, from a source that did not exist when the wind side was written:

> Götz, M., Deuber, R., Gazbour, N., Brailovsky, P.H., Nold, S.,
> Marchand-Lasserre, M., Frischknecht, R., Khan, A.A., Bovo, G. & Stucki, M.
> (2026), *Life Cycle Inventories of Photovoltaic Systems*, IEA PVPS Task 12,
> Report **T12-33:2026**, July 2026. DOI 10.69766/WJTE1771. **Table 49**
> (the unit) and **Table 50** (four per 10 MWp plant).

The workbook is shipped at
`optimisation/data/IEA-PVPS-T12-33-2026-LCI-PV-SupplyChains.xlsx`.

| material, per 2.5 MVA unit | kg | note |
|---|---|---|
| steel, converter, unalloyed | 2,079.8 | GOES core base metal |
| MG-silicon | 73.2 | the core's alloying input |
| lubricating oil | 1,060.0 | |
| aluminium, wrought | 618.0 | windings — **aluminium**, not copper |
| steel, low-alloyed | 1,734.5 | tank, frame, fittings |
| kraft paper | 34.1 | ASSUMED proxy: ecoinvent has no *unbleached* kraft |
| epoxy, copper, chromium steel, rubber, paint | 33.4 | |
| hardboard pressboard | 36.96 | **unit correction, below** |
| **total** | **5,670.0** | the bill's own sum; the report says "approximately 5,680" (0.2 % high) |

**Two things make this better than the wind side, not merely equal to it.**

*The voltage is exact.* The unit is wound **20 / 0.4 kV** — that is
`TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV` and the inverter's LV terminals, the same two numbers.
Leng's wind units are wound for 35 kV, so their mass has to be taken as erring
high (above); here no adjustment is applied at all.

*The count is read off, not derived.* Table 50 is titled *"10 MW utility-scale
electrical BoS including 4 units 2.5 MW transformers"* → 0.4 units/MWp. This
retires both ASSUMED constants the old solar path needed, `SOLAR_DC_AC_RATIO`
and `POWER_FACTOR`.

It also resolves the *"Iron"* judgement that is wind's one soft spot. The core
is grain-oriented electrical steel; no LCI database carries a GOES dataset, so
the report disaggregates it into converter-route steel + MG-silicon + hot and
cold rolling + annealing, and states why converter rather than EAF steel (GOES
composition limits cannot be met from scrap).

**A unit error in the source workbook, corrected.** The hardboard cell reads
**36.96 m³**. At ~1,270 kg/m³ that is ~47 **tonnes** — eight times the whole
transformer, and it would have dominated the score. The cell is kg mislabelled
as m³: its own comment reads "Al × 0.115 × 0.52 = 36.96 kg", the printed Table 49
gives the row in kg, and the end-of-life sheet's paper row is 71.07 kg = 34.11
kraft + 36.96 pressboard. The bill then sums to **5,670.0 kg**; the report's
"approximately 5,680" is 0.2 % high (its paint row, "Total × 0.0024 = 13.61 kg",
reproduces only from 5,670). Until 21 Oct 2026 the row was back-solved to
46.9 kg to hit 5,680 exactly, which reconciled on the wrong lever.
`stepup_transformers.check()` holds the bill within 0.5 % of the report's
figure.

**Two sources, two technologies, one answer.** Solar's **296.0** against wind's
**278.7** kg CO₂e per unit of capacity per year, for step-ups of comparable
rating (2.5 and 2.2 MVA) transcribed by different teams from different
countries (transformers only; both carry their civils on top since 21 Oct
2026). The one asymmetry is stated: **solar carries factory electricity and
heat and wind does not**, because IEA PVPS publish theirs and Leng publish
none (corrected 21 Oct 2026: there is no Leng figure to take). Process energy
is ~6 % of the solar unit, so materials-only
the two land within ~1 % of each other — which is what makes the agreement a
corroboration rather than a coincidence. It also means **wind now errs low
relative to solar**, and that is the direction to fix next.

The legacy basis gave 184.2, i.e. **1.61× off**. It carried two errors that
partly cancelled: the electronics dataset runs high for a given mass, while a
40 MVA specific mass under-counts a 2.5 MVA unit by ~1.6×. It survives only as
`transformers.SOLAR_BASIS = "legacy"`, to reproduce pre-2026 runs.

children.module_doc:
Renewable generation — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

ecoinvent supplies renewable electricity as a **per-kWh** activity, with the
plant's capital burden already amortised over a lifetime output that ecoinvent
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape here, for two reasons:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW should not be a function of how much they happen to
   generate in the modelled year.
2. **ecoinvent's implied yield is not this study's yield.** Generation comes
   from Renewables.ninja at a chosen site, and the cost side uses DESNZ/Arup's
   load factors and lifetimes. Neither matches ecoinvent's own assumption, and
   for onshore wind the gap is a factor of 2.5.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the plant/turbine unit
exchange from the per-kWh activity, scores that unit, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. Per-kWh burden is then recomputed at whatever load factor and
lifetime the study actually uses. Nothing is invented - the reconstruction is
checked against ecoinvent's own per-kWh score, which it reproduces exactly.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Solar is not scored on ecoinvent, and why
-----------------------------------------
ecoinvent 3.9.1's GB open-ground PV activity is the 570 kWp Solarpark El
Tesoro in Andalusia, **installed in 2008**, carrying 4,401.7 m2 of panel for
570 kWp - a 129.5 W/m2, **12.95 %** module. It restates to 57 g CO2e/kWh,
about ten times onshore wind, which is not a defensible basis for a plant that
has not been built yet. 95.5 % of that burden is in the two exchanges that
scale with panel area, so the vintage is the whole story.

The obvious fixes are both closed. Upgrading the database does nothing: the
plant inventory is byte-identical in ecoinvent 3.10.1, so only the background
would move. And no other GB PV activity exists at utility scale - the only
alternatives are 3 kWp slanted-roof systems of the same vintage.

So the default basis for solar is **IEA PVPS Task 12**, the standard reference
for PV LCA, whose 2023 data update uses the same IPCC 2021 GWP100 method this
study uses throughout: 35.8 g CO2e/kWh for mono-Si at 976 kWh/kWp/year over 30
years, which is 1,048 kg CO2e/kWp of embodied carbon against ecoinvent's
2,303. Their reference yield sits within 10 % of the DESNZ GB solar load
factor, so the figure transfers with no irradiance correction - unusual, and
the reason this substitution is clean rather than a fudge.

Mono-Si, and not the like-for-like multi-Si IEA PVPS also publish, because
``cap_solar`` is a *decision variable* for a plant that does not exist yet, so
the question is what would actually be built. IEA PVPS record multi-Si market
share falling below 3 % in 2022 and to ~1 % in 2023 - they could not update
its parameters for want of current data. That is the same argument this module
already makes about not inheriting ecoinvent's yield for a sized asset, and it
is why multi-Si is not offered as a basis: it would fail the test on exactly
the ground ecoinvent fails it. Its number is kept in SOURCES.md as evidence,
where it answers the reviewer who suspects the technology was switched to
flatter the result.

So there are two bases, and the second exists only to reproduce older runs.
Pass ``solar_basis="ecoinvent"`` for that; both live in
``SOLAR_EMBODIED_BASES``. Wind and offshore wind are mostly steel and concrete
and ageing far more slowly than a PV module, so their capital dominates - but
the boundary still has to match solar's. IEA PVPS's per-kWh figure is a
**full-scope** footprint (module, BOS, inverter, install, EOL); a capital-only
wind figure restated on top of it would be comparing different things. So
``restate()`` adds ecoinvent's own non-capital consumables (lubricating oil,
water - the ~1 % ``residual_per_kWh`` from ``decompose()``) back on top of
wind and offshore's restated capital by default, making both technologies
full-scope. It is skipped only where the capital figure is already full-scope
itself (solar under its default IEA basis); it still applies under
``solar_basis="ecoinvent"``, since that basis is capital-only too.

Sources
-------
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100. Activities are the
wind, offshore    GB per-kWh generation datasets and the capital "unit"
                  exchanges they draw on.
embodied carbon   IEA PVPS Task 12, "Environmental Life Cycle Assessment of
solar             Electricity from PV systems - 2023 data update", Stucki M.,
                  Goetz M., de Wild-Scholten M. & Frischknecht R., May 2024.
load factor,      DESNZ/Arup 2024 Cost of Electricity reports, via
lifetime          ``tech_costs.py``. See SOURCES.md.

Run:  python optimisation/renewables.py

children.name: Step-up transformer, 0.4 → 20 kV, at the inverter station (2.5 MVA, 4 per 10 MWp)
children.comment: The oil-immersed transformers in a utility PV plant's inverter stations, stepping the inverters' 400 V (LOW, <1 kV) up to the site collection voltage so the data centre can draw at MEDIUM voltage (1-24 kV). The source unit is wound 20/0.4 kV, which is TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV (20 kV) exactly, so no voltage adjustment is applied - unlike the wind units, which are wound for 35 kV and whose mass therefore errs high. ecoinvent 3.9.1 has no power transformer at any rating, so this is assembled from a published bill of materials: IEA PVPS Task 12, Report T12-33:2026 (July 2026), Tables 49 and 50. Table 49 gives one 2.5 MVA unit at 5,680 kg; Table 50 puts 4 of them on the 10 MWp reference plant, so the count is READ OFF at 0.4 units/MWp rather than derived - which retires the ASSUMED SOLAR_DC_AC_RATIO and POWER_FACTOR the old path needed. The magnetic core is grain-oriented electrical steel, disaggregated by the source into converter-route steel + MG-silicon + hot and cold rolling because no LCI database carries a GOES dataset. The workbook's '36.96 m3' hardboard cell is 36.96 kg mislabelled (its own comment says kg), carried as 0.0291 m3; the bill then sums to 5,670 kg against the report's 'approximately 5,680' (stepup_transformers.check). Functional unit is 1 MWp of PV CONNECTED - amortise over TX_ASSET_LIFE_YEARS (dc_config). INCLUDES factory electricity and heat, which the wind bill does not - process energy is ~6% here, so materials-only the two land within 1% of each other; the asymmetry is stated in SOURCES.md. INCLUDES (since 21 Oct 2026) the transformer station building from Z-PV-238, 10 m2 per unit. EXCLUDES: the grid-export transformer (behind the meter); any step between collection and the data centre (both medium voltage); switchgear and protection; losses; end-of-life.

Power transformers — Leng et al. 2026 (wind step-ups and the grid intake),
IEA PVPS 2026 (solar step-ups).
=============================================================================

Why this inventory exists
-------------------------
A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage (<1 kV, the band
ecoinvent itself draws). A PV inverter's terminals are 400 V. The data centre
draws at *medium* voltage, 1–24 kV, because that is the level ``market for
electricity, medium voltage`` describes and the level the Zhang foreground is
authored against. Something has to bridge those, and it is not optional:
100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A, which is not a cable. So every turbine carries its
own transformer at the foot of its tower — one per turbine, not one per farm —
and every PV inverter station carries one.

Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.name: UPV, trimethylaluminum, purified
children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A1, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

todo.name: The import price carries no levies.
todo.body: RO/FiT/CfD/CM/AAHEDC ≈ £54/MWh plus CCL — about +50 % on the grid-only bill, and it flatters import against every on-site asset. `ELECTRICITY_DELIVERED_UPLIFT` cannot reach the LP (`profiles.py` never reads `price_timeslices`). Audit §3.5.

todo.name: Connection tier and band follow the cap, not the connection built
todo.body: (19 Oct, supervisor point 4). Replace the assumed 100 MW threshold with GB's voltage rule (ENWL ES216, 240 MVA in England and Wales; 132 kV in Scotland), and bound `cap_grid` below by its band's floor. Moves the London headline. Sequenced in `docs/CONNECTION_TIER_PLAN.md`.

todo.name: Report the two big assumed scalars as bands, not points.
todo.body: `green_h2_grid_share` and `transmission_connected` both already have override hooks on `build_tech()`. No sourcing — just run the sweep and publish the range. The T/D threshold alone swings TDR £270k–£4.67m/year.

todo.name: Network charge shape.
todo.body: DUoS uses the "No Residual" class (a data centre is Band 1–4) and an unverified Nov–Feb red band (historic LPN is all-year 11–14 and 16–19: £6.96 vs £2.05/MWh); TDR is banded on the connection ceiling while DUoS bills `cap_grid`; TNUoS HH is a Triad charge, not a capacity one. Audit §3.5.

todo.name: Docs: reconcile 118 vs ~250 gCO₂/kWh
todo.body: (reviewer, 30 Sep). 250 is the grid-only *total per MWh of load*, not a grid intensity: 118 (FES, national, direct, 2024) → 139 (API London 2025, direct) → 159 (life-cycle, delivered) → 174 (+ facility embodied). The drafted line in plan §4 carries these numbers (13 Oct, after the gas, import, delivery and grid-solar fixes); what is left is putting it in the Overview and the brief, which wait on the figure regeneration below.

todo.name: Regenerate every doc figure
todo.body: — `validate.py` was re-run on 12 Oct after the FC fixes, but the Overview and brief still quote 2026-08-24 numbers (16,014 t baseline, 6,605 t optimised). The grid-only baseline is now 11,114 t/yr at 174 g/kWh after the 13 Oct grid fixes (gas, imports, delivery, solar). `validate.py` and `myopic.py` already size Zhang's 7.31 MW as facility draw at `DC_REFERENCE_PUE` (audit §7 A4 is done).

todo.name: "Flexible" with a grid is identical to "free"
todo.body: (`dc_model.py:448-449`), so three matrix scenarios are duplicates. Drop it or define it. Audit §3.3.

todo.name: Transmission connection capital cost.
todo.body: A grid connection in a floored TNUoS zone currently costs £0/MW/year — right as a tariff, wrong as a cost, and it flatters exactly the Scottish sites the locational headline turns on. Needs a module reading the Connection Charging Methodology, and would remove `dc_pareto`'s lexicographic second stage.

| Silicon dioxide | 228.6 | 2.3 | transcribed (printed in kg); silica-sand proxy |
| **total** | **71,458.6** | **714.6** | `check()` holds the sum |

Scored materials-only on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos: **2,753 kg CO₂e per MVA**
(3.85 kg CO₂e/kg — above the box units' 3.46 because copper is 23.5 % of the
mass rather than 16.6 %, and half the carbon). × 2 MVA/MW (N-1 ÷ power factor
1.0) ÷ 40 years = **137.7 kg CO₂e/MW/year**, −59 % on the old basis. Leng's own
342 t CO₂e for this unit against the 275 t here is a scoring difference
(ecoinvent 3.11 with RoW steel proxies against 3.9.1 apos); Leng publish no
factory energy for it (corrected 21 Oct 2026).

*The voltage judgement.* The unit is wound for **110 kV**, which fits a GB
**132 kV** EHV/DNO connection — the common case for a ~100 MW data centre. For a
site connected at **275/400 kV** it errs **low**, supergrid transformers being
heavier per MVA. It is used for every site as the default and registered in
DATA_GAPS.md. Switchgear, protection, the bay, civils, losses and end-of-life
are excluded, as for the step-ups.

**Sources.** Leng et al. (2026), *Processes* 14(7) 1045 —
<https://doi.org/10.3390/pr14071045>. Teffera et al. (2021), *Int J LCA* 26:76–96
— <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11367-020-01834-5>. Vestas, *LCA of Electricity
Production from an onshore V136-4.2MW Wind Plant* (2018), critically reviewed to
ISO/TS 14071. Götz et al. (2026), *Life Cycle Inventories of Photovoltaic
Systems*, IEA PVPS Task 12 Report T12-33:2026 — DOI 10.69766/WJTE1771, Tables 49
and 50 (solar step-ups). Legacy solar basis:
Hitachi Energy S.p.A., *Environmental Product Declaration*, 40 MVA power
transformers (Monselice), EPDItaly rev. 3, 2022 —
<https://www.epditaly.it/wp-content/uploads/2016/12/EPD_40MVA_Hitachi_rev3-11.03.2022-29.04.2022bis.pdf>.
ABB, *Environmental Product Declaration, Power transformer TrafoStar 500 MVA*,
S-P 00020 —
<https://library.e.abb.com/public/566748ad75116903c1256d630042f1af/ProductdeclarationStarTrafo500.pdf>.

children.module_doc:
Grid and price series for a region and window — built in Python, on demand.
=============================================================================

The optimiser needs two half-hourly series for every run: grid carbon for the
site's Carbon Intensity region, and the GB wholesale price. ``profiles.py``
reads them from ``custom_grid_lca_outputs/`` and ``price_outputs/``; when a
window is missing, ``sites.ensure_grid_series`` calls this module to make it.

This replaces the notebook route (``1.dashboard_lca_adaptive`` → ``3.1`` →
``5.prices``, run through nbconvert after patching the config file on disk).
The science is unchanged — it is the same API calls, the same fuel-to-ecoinvent
mapping and the same closed-form score — but it now takes the region and dates
as arguments, so nothing on disk is edited to ask for a build.

Grid carbon, per half-hour
--------------------------
1. The Carbon Intensity API's regional endpoint gives the generation mix
   (% gas, wind, nuclear, imports, ...) for each half-hour. Its own
   ``intensity`` figure is kept as ``carbon_intensity`` for reference only:
   it counts direct combustion, not life cycle.
2. Elexon's FUELHH gives every interconnector's flow for the same half-hours.
   The region's imports are split across exporting countries from those flows,
   weighted by how much of each link reaches the region
   (``optimiser_lca.grid.IMPORT_ATTRIBUTION``, fitted by
   ``fit_import_attribution``). Recorded per row as ``imp_<CC>``.
3. Each fuel maps to one activity, named by its exact identity in
   ``optimiser_lca.grid.SOURCES`` and resolved by exact match — never by search
   ranking — then scored once per process for GWP100. Those per-kWh scores are
   life cycle: plant construction, fuel supply chain and combustion.
   Everything LCA about the series is in that one module.
4. ``generation_kgco2e_per_kwh`` = Σ share × score, per kWh generated, and
   ``custom_electricity_score`` = that delivered at high voltage (losses plus
   network). The LP reads the generation column and delivers it at the site's
   own voltage (``dc_inputs.build_series``).

Every file records what scored it
---------------------------------
``grid_sources_id()`` is a short hash of ``optimiser_lca.grid.basis()`` —
sources, method, weights, import attribution and delivery terms. Each grid CSV
carries it in a ``grid_sources`` column, with the basis and the scored sources
in a ``.sources.json`` beside it, and ``profiles`` ignores a series scored on
any other basis. Changing any of it therefore makes every series stale rather
than silently mixing bases; ``rescore()`` (``--rescore`` on the command line)
re-scores the files already on disk from the fuel mix each one recorded. The
first rescore of a file written before the import split fetches its window's
interconnector flows; after that it needs no API calls.

Output file names match what notebook 3.1 wrote, so every series already on
disk still reads.

Every series is UTC
--------------------
Grid, price (Elexon ``startTime``) and weather (Renewables.ninja) are all
stored as naive UTC timestamps, and a requested window is read as UTC. The
grid series used to be London local time, which put intraday carbon an hour
out of step with price and weather for seven months of the year. Files are
marked with a ``clock`` column; ``profiles.py`` ignores grid files without it,
so a series in the old basis is rebuilt rather than silently used. Anything
defined on the UK clock (DUoS time bands) converts from UTC itself.

Run:  python -m optimisation.grid_build 13 2025-06-02 2025-06-09
      python -m optimisation.grid_build --rescore
      python -m optimisation.grid_build --fit-imports

London 2025 is shown because this map is built for the London reference case; a run at Inverness reads region 1's series, and the region id is recorded in every series file.

children.name: Intake transformers, 110/132 → 20 kV, N-1 (2 MVA per MW of connection)
children.comment: The power transformer that steps the network's high voltage down onto the site, sized by cap_grid. Functional unit is 1 MVA of rating; grid_connection.py turns it into a per-MW figure with N-1 redundancy and the power factor, and amortises it over its own ASSET_LIFE_YEARS. ecoinvent 3.9.1 has no power transformer at any rating - its four transformer activities are two electronic components of 280 g and 30 g average weight, 'used in the information and communication technology' by its own comments - and no substation or switchgear dataset either. So this is assembled from Leng et al. (2026), Processes 14(7) 1045, Supplementary Table S1: the Gaoyou farm's grid-end main transformer, XZ11-100000/110, one 100 MVA unit wound for 110 kV, 71,458.6 kg in total = 714.6 kg/MVA, divided by its rating. Materials mapped exactly as the wind step-ups are, Iron read as core steel. VOLTAGE: a 110 kV unit fits a GB 132 kV EHV/DNO connection, the common case for a ~100 MW data centre; for a 275/400 kV transmission-connected site it errs LOW, supergrid transformers being heavier per MVA. Used for every site as the default. EXCLUDES: switchgear and protection (cut-off register); the line to the site (grid_connection.py reports it separately); losses; end-of-life. The switchyard's civils are their own activity, grid_intake_substation_civils_per_mw (Leng Table S3's outdoor venue, decision D2, 22 Oct 2026). Leng publish no factory energy for this unit; their 342 t CO2e against ~275 t here is a scoring difference (ecoinvent 3.11 v 3.9.1), not a dropped flow.
children.source:
Power transformers — Leng et al. 2026 (wind step-ups and the grid intake),
IEA PVPS 2026 (solar step-ups).
=============================================================================

Why this inventory exists
-------------------------
A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage (<1 kV, the band
ecoinvent itself draws). A PV inverter's terminals are 400 V. The data centre
draws at *medium* voltage, 1–24 kV, because that is the level ``market for
electricity, medium voltage`` describes and the level the Zhang foreground is
authored against. Something has to bridge those, and it is not optional:
100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A, which is not a cable. So every turbine carries its
own transformer at the foot of its tower — one per turbine, not one per farm —
and every PV inverter station carries one.

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.name: UPV, trimethylaluminum, purified
children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.
