sources_md.The grid battery's energy term \u2014 Ja:
### The grid battery's energy term — Jasper et al. 2026, Voß et al. 2025

> F.B. Jasper, Y. Zhou, H. Ersoy, M. Baumann et al. (2026), "Life Cycle
> Assessment of Grid-Scale Battery Storage", *Energy Advances* **5**, 550–570,
> doi:10.1039/D5YA00341E. SI workbook on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.17651912,
> **CC-BY-NC**.
>
> P. Voß, B. Gruber, M. Mitterfellner, J.-D. Plöpst, F. Degen, R. Schmuch,
> S. Lux (2025), "Benchmarking state-of-the-art sodium-ion battery cells",
> *Energy Environ. Sci.* **18**, 8104–8129, doi:10.1039/D5EE00415B. Table 3
> and ESI Tables S5, S31, S32, S35, S36.

**Why it replaced the EV pack.** ecoinvent's pack is an electric-vehicle
traction pack (Dai et al. / GREET, 2016-era) with no container, racking, HVAC
or fire suppression. The "25–35 % high" finding in the review plan (§6.1–6.2)
compared it with *newer EV packs* (BatPaC, EverBatt), which is right pack for
pack and wrong for a grid battery: every stationary system source — Jasper's
inventory, and the Trina (140.7, DC block), Sungrow (152–160 with PCS) and
Huawei (106–114, on 3.9.1) EPDs — lands **above** 98.2, because the enclosure
is 18–23 % of a DC block's carbon and a whole container is no lighter per kWh
than an EV pack.

**What is built.** Jasper's liquid-cooled LFP design, 1,600 kW / 3,008 kWh, 8
racks × 8 modules × 47 kWh, 306 Ah cells — liquid cooling being what current
containers ship with. The cell is Voß's, which Jasper link and do not
reproduce; Voß is on ecoinvent 3.9.1, so it rebuilds here without a version
mismatch.

| Part | kg CO₂e/kWh nameplate | Jasper Fig. 4, LC LFP (3.11, EF 3.1) |
|---|---|---|
| Cells (made in China) | **80.58** | 95.44 |
| Modules without cells | 6.59 | 6.57 |
| Racks | 6.91 | 6.59 |
| Container, incl. the 43.9 t concrete block since 21 Oct | 3.37 (1.22 container + 2.15 block) | 3.50 + 2.06 foundation |
| Liquid cooling | 2.58 | 2.64 |
| Fire suppression | 0.76 | 0.76 |
| Others (BESS controller) | 0.32 | 0.25 |
| **DC block** | **101.11** | 117.81 (140.11 less PCS and transformer) |

**Transport (20 Oct 2026).** Only delivery to site is excluded, because the site
is not known; upstream transport is in. Jasper's SI has two patterns of row:
1,000 km lorry + 8,000 km sea + 1,000 km European rail per tonne on the
container, cooling, fire suppression, PCS and transformer, which ships finished
parts from his Chinese factory to his German site (left out); and ecoinvent's
default 100 km lorry + 600 km rail per tonne on the modules, racks and rack
housing, which brings materials to those factories (kept since 20 Oct, +0.10 kg
CO₂e/kWh). Voß's China-to-Berlin legs serve their German factory, so the
China-made cell does not take them; from the natural-graphite factor only the
sea and European legs are subtracted, and the 1,000 km in-China lorry leg
stays (+0.05 kg/kWh on the cell). Together +0.15 % on the DC block.

Every non-cell part reproduces Jasper's to within 5 % except the container,
where ecoinvent 3.9.1's 20 ft intermodal container (2.9 t CO₂e) is about a
third of whatever 3.11 carries; this is built as the inventory says, on the
study's database, and the gap is stated rather than patched. The cell gap is
the graphite route (3.11's Acheson dataset against Voß's own Table S5) and the
blend (65:35 against 75:25).

**The cell, validated.** Voß Table 3's LFP/graphite cell — 383.4 Wh,
2,170.8 g, 176.6 Wh/kg — with each material from its ESI table:

| Check | Rebuilt | Voß |
|---|---|---|
| Synthetic graphite, Acheson powder route (Table S5) | 24.51 kg/kg, +0.51 of Voß's transport = 25.02 | 25.1 |
| Natural graphite (Engels 2022) | 5.19 kg/kg before transport (Voß §3.1.1.2), + the 1,000 km China leg = ~5.38 built; Voß's in-cell figure with all three legs is 5.7 (main text Fig. 6, §4.2.2). Until 22 Oct 2026 the module read 5.19 as including the legs and subtracted two, landing at 4.87 | 5.7 |
| Cell, German factory, 75:25 | 72.50 kg/kWh | 71.2 |

The German cell lands 1.8 % high *despite* leaving out the transport and
processing materials Voß include, so like for like it is ~6 % high. The
likeliest cause is the factory energy, which Voß do not tabulate: 18 kWh
electricity + 19 kWh gas per kWh is Degen et al. (2023) as restated by Jasper
§2.4.1. It errs high, the conservative direction.

**Choices this study makes, not the sources.**
- *Cells made in China* — where most stationary LFP cells are made, and what
  Jasper assume. +7.0 kg/kWh over Voß's German factory. The German cell is
  built too (`bess_lfp_cell_1kwh_de`) so Voß's figure stays reproducible.
- *Graphite 75:25 synthetic:natural* — Voß's benchmark, given as current market
  share. All-synthetic would be +5.0 kg/kWh, all-natural −15.0 (Voß's own
  figures move by +4.9 and −14.7).
- *The 330 g housing is charged wholly on Voß Table S36* — Voß put fixing and
  isolation materials (S37, all PET) inside it without a split; S36 already
  carries PET, and the Al-heavy table errs high.
- *Ellingsen's busbars*, which Jasper do not reproduce, are mapped to their
  metals, the bimetallic set 50:50 copper:aluminium (~1.8 kg/kWh in all).
- *The BESS controller* (30 kg), which has no inventory in the SI, is
  ecoinvent's electronics for control units, as Jasper's HV control box is.

**Pinned footprints, not inventories.** Five source figures are carbon
footprints: natural graphite 5.19, PVDF 60.6 (Hu et al.), separator 5.06
(ecoinvent 3.8, which Voß chose over 3.9.1's 39.6 as "unrealistically high";
3.9.1 scores 34.4–39.5 here), and Carrère's crucible (7.346) and packaging
(0.432) per kg of synthetic graphite. Each enters as fossil CO₂ of its own
size: right for GWP100 and *only* for GWP100.

**Boundary — the same as every other inventory here.** No end-of-life
(Jasper's EOL sheet and `treatment of used CSS` are not taken). No delivery
transport: every rail, lorry and sea row in both sources is left out, as
`upv.py` leaves out Smith's, and where Voß folded their China-to-Berlin legs
into one factor (natural graphite) they are subtracted back out with negative
exchanges. Factory energy is *in*, as it is for solar. Jasper's PCS (charged on
the power term), transformer (battery step-up closed as negligible, 4 Sep) and
concrete foundation (civils are outside every capital inventory) are excluded.
Voß's processing materials — NMP, argon, nitrogen, compressed air — are not
tabulated by them and are left out; this errs low.

**What is still not in it.** Current 20 ft products pack ~5 MWh against
Jasper's 3 MWh; spreading the per-container items over 5 MWh would take ~3
kg/kWh off. End-of-life, as everywhere. And the cell is the soft spot: Jasper's
3.11 cell is 20 % above this one on the same bill.

**Why Modo rather than NREL.** The FES 2025 Economics Methodology report
states NESO's Li-ion CAPEX is *"a combination of Modo survey data with CAPEX
data from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory"*. Modo's assumptions are
published openly and already in real 2025 GBP, so they need neither FX nor
deflation — unlike NREL, which is USD and US-market.

**Verification built in.** `check_against_ecoinvent()` re-scores the battery
foreground and both ecoinvent factors, and fails if any has moved by more than
0.1 %.

**Life.** The battery's 15-year life against the data centre's 25 means **1.67
builds** over the study horizon, which both cost and carbon must carry.

---

children.module_doc:
Lithium-ion battery storage — cost and embodied carbon.
=============================================================================

Costs come from **Modo Energy**, which is the source NESO itself uses: the FES
2025 Economics Methodology report states its Li-ion CAPEX is "a combination of
Modo survey data with CAPEX data from the National Renewable Energy
Laboratory". Modo's model assumptions are published openly at
docs.modoenergy.com, already in **real 2025 GBP** — the same basis as every
other cost in this study, so no deflation or FX is needed.

Embodied carbon comes from ecoinvent 3.9.1. Cost and carbon are deliberately
kept on the same two-part structure — a **power** term (£/kW, kg CO2e/kW) and
an **energy** term (£/kWh, kg CO2e/kWh) — so the optimiser can size power and
duration independently instead of being locked to a 4-hour product.

Sources
-------
cost, technical   Modo Energy, "BESS Cost and Technical Assumptions",
                  docs.modoenergy.com/pages/jan-2026/uk-europe/model-assumptions/
                  (July 2026). ~£400/kW for a 1-hour system today falling to
                  ~£200/kW by 2040; each additional hour of duration adds
                  £100/kW in 2025. 15-year asset life, ~67 % capacity
                  remaining after 10,000 cycles (~12-15 years), 1-2 cycles per
                  day, WACC 5.0 % real. Real 2025 GBP.

cost spread       Modo Energy BESS CapEx Survey 2024 (30 market participants,
                  2.8 GW at 1.9 h average): average £580k/MW, two-hour median
                  £650k/MW, 68 % of projects between £400k/MW and £700k/MW.

round-trip eff.   88 %, Modo's standard assumption. Not stated on the model
                  assumptions page itself, so it is the least firmly sourced
                  number here.

embodied carbon   energy term: the ``battery foreground`` built by
                  ``optimiser_lca/bess.py`` — Jasper et al. (2026) Energy
                  Advances 5:550, liquid-cooled LFP container, around the Voß
                  et al. (2025) Energy Environ. Sci. 18:8104 LFP cell, on
                  ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos. Power term: ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos
                  500 kW inverter. IPCC 2021 GWP100.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/battery.py

children.name: Step-up transformer, 0.4 → 20 kV, one per container (1.6 MVA per 1.6 MW of PCS)
children.comment: The transformer that steps a battery container's PCS output, or a fuel-cell container's inverter output, from LOW voltage (400 V) up to the site collection voltage (20 kV). Functional unit is 1 MW of inverter rating: transformers.py charges it per MW of cap_batt_p and per MW of cap_fc, each amortised over the asset's own life (the battery's 15 y; the fuel cell's BoP calendar life). MASS from Jasper et al. 2026, CSS (liquid cooled) bill, 'transformer, for grid connection': 5,500 kg per 1,600 kW container = 3,437.5 kg/MW, on the measured curve (2,566 kg/MVA at 2.2 MVA, 2,272 at 2.5). COMPOSITION, forming and factory energy per kg from the IEA PVPS T12-33:2026 Table 49 20/0.4 kV oil-immersed unit, a STATED SUBSTITUTION for Jasper's own recipe on technological representativeness (decided 22 Oct 2026). Jasper give a per-kg split (air-cooled sheet rows 225-236), but their §2.4.3 says it is derived from Hunziker et al. (2020): a 630 kVA line-frequency transformer with an ON-LOAD TAP CHANGER, scaled by mass to 1,800 kVA. The IEA unit is a current 2,500 kVA distribution transformer built from product documentation at exactly the 20/0.4 kV step the container needs. Jasper's recipe scores 7.85 kg CO2e/kg against 4.57 here (+72 %, mostly its 0.09 kg/kg of control electronics, likely the tap changer's); it is the sensitivity case. Closed as negligible on 4 Sep 2026 and modelled on 15 Oct: the inventory and loss machinery existed by then, and leaving it out favoured the storage chains against the generation chains, which pay for theirs. EXCLUDES: switchgear, protection and civils (as every transformer here); losses, which conversion_losses.py charges as energy; end-of-life.
children.source:
Power transformers — Leng et al. 2026 (wind step-ups and the grid intake),
IEA PVPS 2026 (solar step-ups).
=============================================================================

Why this inventory exists
-------------------------
A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage (<1 kV, the band
ecoinvent itself draws). A PV inverter's terminals are 400 V. The data centre
draws at *medium* voltage, 1–24 kV, because that is the level ``market for
electricity, medium voltage`` describes and the level the Zhang foreground is
authored against. Something has to bridge those, and it is not optional:
100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A, which is not a cable. So every turbine carries its
own transformer at the foot of its tower — one per turbine, not one per farm —
and every PV inverter station carries one.

Why this inventory exists
-------------------------
The battery used to be ecoinvent's ``market for battery, Li-ion, LFP,
rechargeable, prismatic`` [GLO]: an **electric-vehicle traction pack**
(Dai et al. / GREET lineage, 2016-era, 116 Wh/kg) with no container, racking,
HVAC or fire suppression — ``battery.CONTAINER_UPLIFT_FRACTION`` was 0.0 and
said so. A grid battery is neither of those things. It is large-format
prismatic cells in racks, in a 20 ft container, with its own thermal
management and fire suppression, and those non-cell parts are 18-23 % of the
DC block's carbon in every source that itemises them.

Why this inventory exists
-------------------------
The battery used to be ecoinvent's ``market for battery, Li-ion, LFP,
rechargeable, prismatic`` [GLO]: an **electric-vehicle traction pack**
(Dai et al. / GREET lineage, 2016-era, 116 Wh/kg) with no container, racking,
HVAC or fire suppression — ``battery.CONTAINER_UPLIFT_FRACTION`` was 0.0 and
said so. A grid battery is neither of those things. It is large-format
prismatic cells in racks, in a 20 ft container, with its own thermal
management and fire suppression, and those non-cell parts are 18-23 % of the
DC block's carbon in every source that itemises them.

Materials only - the factory energy is added per kWh in bess_lfp_cell_1kwh_cn / bess_lfp_cell_1kwh_de. Graphite 75% synthetic / 25% natural, Voß's market-share benchmark.

children.comment: Voß ESI Table S32, every input at the printed amount, per 1.00 kg of FePO4. S32 prints its output as 0.91 kg, but that is S31's consumption copied across: ESI p. 23 says the precursors are stoichiometric (Eq. S25), and on the 'without water' datasets 1.00 kg FeSO4, 0.65 kg H3PO4 and 0.11 kg H2O2 are each ~6.6 mol, i.e. 1.00 kg of FePO4. It matters more for the non-GWP categories, where Gerloff blames that coal-heavy proxy for SOEC's particulate, ionising-radiation and carcinogen results. children.module_doc:
Electrolysers — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

The Gerloff 2021 foreground (``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py``; called Hermesmann's
here until 22 Oct 2026) supplies electrolysis as a **per-kg-H2** activity
with the capital good already amortised over a lifetime output that Gerloff
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape for an optimiser, for exactly the reasons set out in
``renewables.py``:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW must not depend on how much hydrogen they happen to make.
2. **Gerloff's implied utilisation is not this study's.** All three
   technologies amortise their capital over **160 GWh of lifetime electricity
   throughput at 1 MW** — 160,000 full-load hours. Spread over a 25-year plant
   life that is a **73 % capacity factor**. An optimiser that builds an
   electrolyser to chase surplus wind at 20 % CF and charges its capital per kg
   produced would understate that machine's embodied carbon **by a factor of
   3.5**.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the ``unit``-denominated
capital exchange from the per-kg activity, scores it, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. What remains — water, heat, electrolyte — stays per kg, because
those genuinely do scale with output.

Nothing is invented. ``check_reconstruction()`` asserts that capital-per-MW
re-amortised at Gerloff's own throughput, plus the per-kg remainder,
reproduces ``lca_helpers.run_non_electricity_lca()`` exactly.

The 1 MW rating
---------------
Only PEM states its rating in the foreground ("1 unit (1 MW)"). AE and SOEC do
not, so the rating is **derived and cross-checked** rather than assumed: each
technology's lifetime hydrogen output times its own specific energy comes to
160 GWh to within 0.2 %, despite specific energies ranging from 42.3 to
54.0 kWh/kg. Three independent inventories agreeing to 0.2 % on a quantity none
of them states is not a coincidence — it is one shared 1 MW / 160 GWh capital
basis. ``check_rating()`` enforces the agreement, so if the foreground is ever
rebuilt on a different basis this module fails loudly instead of scaling
everything by a silent factor.

Stacks
------
Gerloff's unit carries **three stacks** over its 20-year life (§2.1.3; the
module carries the stack's rows x3 since 22 Oct 2026, as the SI's stack
manufacturing energy always was). The capital good is still one activity per
unit, amortised here on calendar life: a duty-driven stack count, as
``fuel_cell.py`` does for the fuel cell, would need the stack rows split out
as their own activity — possible from the SI's Stack/BoP labels, not done.
For an electrolyser run harder than Gerloff's 160,000 full-load hours this
understates the stack burden. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Sources
-------
inventories       Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage 43, 102759: alkaline / PEM / SOEC.
                  Built into ``hydrogen foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.
plant lifetime    25 years — NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal, the same figure
                  ``price_outputs/electrolyser_costs_clean.csv`` carries.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/electrolysers.py

Gerloff 2021 (Table 3) carried the 5.24 kWh but modelled it on "heat, district or industrial, other than natural gas" (52 % coal and peat, his §2.2.3), and Hermesmann copied Gerloff. That swap is why this row used to sit on `market group … other than natural gas` [RER]. The two datasets score 0.0749 and 0.0751 kg/MJ, so the switch fixes the provenance and moves GWP by +0.004 kg/kg. It matters more for the non-GWP categories, where Gerloff blames that coal-heavy proxy for SOEC's particulate, ionising-radiation and carcinogen results. Cross-check: Mehmeti's own heat line is 1.294 kg CO₂e/kg H₂ (0.0686/MJ, supplementary Table A1), against 1.417 here. Heat is still 87 % of SOEC's 1.632 kg/kg. A data centre's waste heat cannot supply it at these temperatures. A boiler cannot literally reach 750 °C either, but it is the source's own basis. Not costed: see `DATA_GAPS.md`, *Electrolyser consumables cost*. Audit §3.3 |
| SOEC heat, electric-boiler scenario | 5.24 kWh ÷ 0.99 = **5.29 kWh/kg H₂** of site electricity, replacing the gas row | assumed | `soec_heat="electric_boiler"` on a `Scenario` (matrix rows 22–25, and a toggle on the optimiser page). `electrolysers.with_heat_source` drops the gas row's 1.417 kg/kg, leaving 0.215 kg/kg of water, and adds the boiler's kWh to `kwh_per_kg`, so the heat costs and emits whatever the LP's electricity does in that hour. children.module_doc:
Electrolysers — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

The Gerloff 2021 foreground (``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py``; called Hermesmann's
here until 22 Oct 2026) supplies electrolysis as a **per-kg-H2** activity
with the capital good already amortised over a lifetime output that Gerloff
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape for an optimiser, for exactly the reasons set out in
``renewables.py``:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW must not depend on how much hydrogen they happen to make.
2. **Gerloff's implied utilisation is not this study's.** All three
   technologies amortise their capital over **160 GWh of lifetime electricity
   throughput at 1 MW** — 160,000 full-load hours. Spread over a 25-year plant
   life that is a **73 % capacity factor**. An optimiser that builds an
   electrolyser to chase surplus wind at 20 % CF and charges its capital per kg
   produced would understate that machine's embodied carbon **by a factor of
   3.5**.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the ``unit``-denominated
capital exchange from the per-kg activity, scores it, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. What remains — water, heat, electrolyte — stays per kg, because
those genuinely do scale with output.

Nothing is invented. ``check_reconstruction()`` asserts that capital-per-MW
re-amortised at Gerloff's own throughput, plus the per-kg remainder,
reproduces ``lca_helpers.run_non_electricity_lca()`` exactly.

The 1 MW rating
---------------
Only PEM states its rating in the foreground ("1 unit (1 MW)"). AE and SOEC do
not, so the rating is **derived and cross-checked** rather than assumed: each
technology's lifetime hydrogen output times its own specific energy comes to
160 GWh to within 0.2 %, despite specific energies ranging from 42.3 to
54.0 kWh/kg. Three independent inventories agreeing to 0.2 % on a quantity none
of them states is not a coincidence — it is one shared 1 MW / 160 GWh capital
basis. ``check_rating()`` enforces the agreement, so if the foreground is ever
rebuilt on a different basis this module fails loudly instead of scaling
everything by a silent factor.

Stacks
------
Gerloff's unit carries **three stacks** over its 20-year life (§2.1.3; the
module carries the stack's rows x3 since 22 Oct 2026, as the SI's stack
manufacturing energy always was). The capital good is still one activity per
unit, amortised here on calendar life: a duty-driven stack count, as
``fuel_cell.py`` does for the fuel cell, would need the stack rows split out
as their own activity — possible from the SI's Stack/BoP labels, not done.
For an electrolyser run harder than Gerloff's 160,000 full-load hours this
understates the stack burden. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Sources
-------
inventories       Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage 43, 102759: alkaline / PEM / SOEC.
                  Built into ``hydrogen foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.
plant lifetime    25 years — NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal, the same figure
                  ``price_outputs/electrolyser_costs_clean.csv`` carries.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/electrolysers.py

That swap is why this row used to sit on `market group … other than natural gas` [RER]. The two datasets score 0.0749 and 0.0751 kg/MJ, so the switch fixes the provenance and moves GWP by +0.004 kg/kg. It matters more for the non-GWP categories, where Gerloff blames that coal-heavy proxy for SOEC's particulate, ionising-radiation and carcinogen results. Cross-check: Mehmeti's own heat line is 1.294 kg CO₂e/kg H₂ (0.0686/MJ, supplementary Table A1), against 1.417 here. Heat is still 87 % of SOEC's 1.632 kg/kg. The audit's comparison on renewable power (SOEC 2.27 against PEM 0.89, or 0.22 on zero-burden heat) moves by that same +0.004, so the dataset choice no longer swings the ranking; the heat itself still does. A data centre's waste heat cannot supply it at these temperatures. A boiler cannot literally reach 750 °C either, but it is the source's own basis. Not costed: see `DATA_GAPS.md`, *Electrolyser consumables cost*. Audit §3.3 |

children.module_doc:
Electrolysers — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

The Gerloff 2021 foreground (``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py``; called Hermesmann's
here until 22 Oct 2026) supplies electrolysis as a **per-kg-H2** activity
with the capital good already amortised over a lifetime output that Gerloff
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape for an optimiser, for exactly the reasons set out in
``renewables.py``:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW must not depend on how much hydrogen they happen to make.
2. **Gerloff's implied utilisation is not this study's.** All three
   technologies amortise their capital over **160 GWh of lifetime electricity
   throughput at 1 MW** — 160,000 full-load hours. Spread over a 25-year plant
   life that is a **73 % capacity factor**. An optimiser that builds an
   electrolyser to chase surplus wind at 20 % CF and charges its capital per kg
   produced would understate that machine's embodied carbon **by a factor of
   3.5**.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the ``unit``-denominated
capital exchange from the per-kg activity, scores it, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. What remains — water, heat, electrolyte — stays per kg, because
those genuinely do scale with output.

Nothing is invented. ``check_reconstruction()`` asserts that capital-per-MW
re-amortised at Gerloff's own throughput, plus the per-kg remainder,
reproduces ``lca_helpers.run_non_electricity_lca()`` exactly.

The 1 MW rating
---------------
Only PEM states its rating in the foreground ("1 unit (1 MW)"). AE and SOEC do
not, so the rating is **derived and cross-checked** rather than assumed: each
technology's lifetime hydrogen output times its own specific energy comes to
160 GWh to within 0.2 %, despite specific energies ranging from 42.3 to
54.0 kWh/kg. Three independent inventories agreeing to 0.2 % on a quantity none
of them states is not a coincidence — it is one shared 1 MW / 160 GWh capital
basis. ``check_rating()`` enforces the agreement, so if the foreground is ever
rebuilt on a different basis this module fails loudly instead of scaling
everything by a silent factor.

Stacks
------
Gerloff's unit carries **three stacks** over its 20-year life (§2.1.3; the
module carries the stack's rows x3 since 22 Oct 2026, as the SI's stack
manufacturing energy always was). The capital good is still one activity per
unit, amortised here on calendar life: a duty-driven stack count, as
``fuel_cell.py`` does for the fuel cell, would need the stack rows split out
as their own activity — possible from the SI's Stack/BoP labels, not done.
For an electrolyser run harder than Gerloff's 160,000 full-load hours this
understates the stack burden. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Sources
-------
inventories       Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage 43, 102759: alkaline / PEM / SOEC.
                  Built into ``hydrogen foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.
plant lifetime    25 years — NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal, the same figure
                  ``price_outputs/electrolyser_costs_clean.csv`` carries.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/electrolysers.py

children.module_doc:
Hydrogen storage — embodied carbon per kg of capacity.
=============================================================================

The one asset in the hydrogen chain that was already the right shape. ecoinvent
3.9.1 has no hydrogen vessel, so ``optimiser_lca/h2_tank.py`` builds one the
way Gandiglio et al. (2022) do — as a mass of steel and nothing else — with a
reference product of **one kilogram of storage capacity**. That is already a
capacity basis, so unlike the electrolyser and the fuel cell there is nothing to
decompose: this module reads it, amortises it, and offers the second design the
config defines but does not build.

What it adds over reading the activity directly:

1. **Both tank designs**, not just the one ``h2_tank.TANK_DESIGN``
   currently selects, so the optimiser can run 28 bar against 200 bar as a
   sensitivity without a foreground rebuild. The as-built design is
   cross-checked against Brightway; the other is scored from its own steel
   process at its own steel intensity.
2. **The charging parasitic**, which belongs to storage and not to the
   electrolyser: compression from the electrolyser's delivery pressure to the
   tank's. Zero for the 28 bar design, because the electrolyser already leaves
   at ~30 bar.
3. **Standing loss**, which is *not* in the inventory and is not modelled here
   either — see below.

Why steel mass alone is defensible, and where it is not
------------------------------------------------------
Gandiglio's inventory is one line: 15,652 kg of chromium steel 18/8 for a
21.6 m3, 28 bar vessel. Missing are foundations, the enclosure, valves and
instrumentation, and end-of-life. The notebook says so, and so does this module.
Against that, steel is the overwhelming majority of a pressure vessel's embodied
carbon, so the figure is a defensible lower bound rather than a guess.

Standing loss is deliberately zero and needs a source
-----------------------------------------------------
There is **no boil-off** from compressed gas at ambient temperature — that is a
liquid-hydrogen phenomenon, and this is a steel bottle at 28 bar. The real
losses are permeation through the wall, which is negligible for steel at this
pressure, and fitting and valve leakage, which is a maintenance-quality
question rather than a physical constant. ``LEAKAGE_FRAC_PER_HOUR`` is exposed
for the optimiser and **defaults to zero with no source**, which is the honest
position but not a verified one. It was thought to decide the seasonal
hydrogen-versus-battery contest; swept over 0-0.1 %/day on 14 Oct (an ASSUMED
range, through ``build_tech(tank_leakage_per_hour=...)``) it moves cost and
carbon by under 0.1 % and does not change which store dominates. Registered,
with the band, in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

If it is ever set non-zero, the leaked hydrogen should also be charged as a
greenhouse gas in its own right — H2 is an indirect GHG — from DESNZ / Warwick
et al. 2022, *Atmospheric implications of increased hydrogen use*.

Sources
-------
inventory         Gandiglio, M., Marocco, P., Bianco, I., Lovera, D.,
                  Blengini, G.A., Santarelli, M. (2022), "Life cycle assessment
                  of a renewable energy system with hydrogen-battery storage
                  for a remote off-grid community", Int. J. Hydrogen Energy 47.
                  Table 3 — the as-built 21.6 m3 vessel at Ginostra.
type I cylinder   ~1 wt% gravimetric capacity, a typical industrial stationary
                  bottle. DERIVED, not transcribed — see optimiser_lca/h2_tank.py.
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.
vessel lifetime   25 years, the paper's own plant life. The tank is never
                  replaced within it.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/h2_storage.py

### PEM fuel cell — `fuel_cell.py`

| Input | Value | Grade | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stack | 97.4 t CO₂e per MW, **30,000 h** duty life | derived | Babatunde et al. 2024 Table S1. Duty life: stationary H₂ stacks are refurbished at 24–30k running hours (Nedstack datasheets, as reported); Bionaz et al. 2022 use 40k. Babatunde's 32k was ecoinvent's own figure, so never an independent check |
| Balance of plant | **44.3 t CO₂e per MW**, **80,000 h** duty life | derived | Rebuilt 14 Oct, below. Duty life: DOE's 100 kW–3 MW stationary class, and ecoinvent's own system life (60,000 h was the 1–25 kW residential target) |
| BoP **calendar** life | **20 y** | **assumed** (indicative) | Nedstack: 20 y for the BoP of their 120 kW CHP unit, 10 y for their mobile unit; DOE backup-power target, 15-y system life. Sweep 15–25. Was 25 y, matched to the electrolyser. Also sets the cost-side annuity: +8.3 % on the fuel-cell cost line |
| Stack **calendar** life | **10 y** | **assumed** (indicative) | Clean Hydrogen Partnership stationary PEMFC KPIs are set on a 10-y system life; Nedstack mobile unit 10 y; Gandiglio et al. 2022 replace their 50 kW Engie-EPS unit every 5 y. Binds for an idle backup stack (membranes age at open circuit). Sweep 5 / 10 / 15. Was a 25-y placeholder |
| Maintenance | **0.003** kg CO₂e per MWh delivered | derived | An air filter and a coolant change per 8,000 h (interval ASSUMED; Battelle 2016 gives one year for backup units), Usai's amounts. Was 3.11, ecoinvent's reformer-catalyst service event |
| Hydrogen consumption | 63.16 kg H₂ per MWh | derived | 1/(η 0.475 × LHV 33.33 kWh/kg) |

Both replaceable components are charged at
`max(1/calendar_years, full_load_hours_per_year/duty_hours)` — a maximum of two
linear functions, exact in an LP. This matters at both ends: charged on duty
alone a **backup** fuel cell at 100 h/yr is under-counted **~31×**; charged on
calendar alone a **baseload** one is under-counted ~2.8×. `check_full_duty()`
asserts the rule collapses onto the foreground's own per-kWh figure at 8,760 h/yr.

#### The balance of plant — a hydrogen-fed stationary unit, not a micro-CHP

Until 14 Oct it was ecoinvent's `fuel cell production, polymer electrolyte
membrane, 2kW electrical, future` net of its stack: a **natural-gas domestic
micro-CHP** ("operation with connection to low pressure gas network"), with
fuel-processor items, a hot-water kit and 400 km of installer driving, scaled
linearly from 2 kW to MW — 469 t CO₂e/MW, and reformer-catalyst replacement as
its maintenance. Audit §3.4.

**No MW-class hydrogen PEM inventory exists.** Checked: Stropnik et al. 2018
(*Energy* 165:824, 3 kW H₂ UPS — the only stationary H₂ unit with a component
bill), Gandiglio et al. 2022 (a 50 kW unit, but inventoried as ecoinvent's 2 kW
stack alone), Gramc, Stropnik et al. 2025 (*IJHE* 104:623, a 48 kW stack only),
Belmonte 2016/2017 (3 kW, on ecoinvent's 2 kW dataset), Gentilucci et al. 2024
(SAE 2024-24-0020, 200 kW truck, BoP from Miotti 2017), Syré et al. 2024 (*WEVJ*
15:114, trucks and buses, Usai's data). A 2026 review (*Energies* 19:3808) finds
fuel-cell BoP inventories still "simplified using obsolete" bills. So the BoP is
assembled, per kW, in `optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.py`:

| Part | kg CO₂e/kW | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Process loops — air, water, heat, fuel, controller, wiring, frame | 8.81 | **Usai et al. 2021**, *J Cleaner Prod* 280:125086, SI Table 1 (`sources/usai supplementary materials/`): an 80 kW H₂ system per kW net, every line on the ecoinvent process Usai name |
| Power conversion to AC | 31.86 | ecoinvent `market for inverter, 500kW` [GLO], the battery's power-term dataset. A vehicle's DC/DC boost sits in its drivetrain, so nothing is counted twice |
| Enclosure | 3.66 | the battery's fire-lined 20 ft container (Jasper 2026, `bess.py`), one per MW — **assumed**, no source gives MW per container for fuel cells; sweep 0.5–2 MW |
| **Balance of plant** | **44.3** | |
| Stack (Babatunde) | 97.4 | unchanged |
| **System** | **141.8** | |

*Two lines of Usai's Table 1 are per system, not per kW.* The 3 coolant pumps
and 16 m of wiring (Miotti's per-system figure) are printed as per kW net;
taken literally they rebuild Usai's own heat and "other" results 17× and 35×
over. Divided by 80 kW they rebuild them. *The rest is as printed*, and rounded
to two decimals, so the loops land at **0.82×** Usai's own 854 kg CO₂e per 80 kW
(their results workbook, ecoinvent 3.6): water 0.99, fuel 0.91, air 1.11, the
radiator and controller lost to rounding. Where Usai's 3.6 GLO market is
regional in 3.9.1 (sulfur trioxide, rigid PU, nylon 6), RoW stands in.

*What is a vehicle part and stays.* The compression-expansion motor stands in
for a stationary air blower (errs high, small); the belly pan for the module
frame.

**Benchmarks**, whole systems cradle-to-gate per kW: Miotti 29, Usai 37.3 (no
tank), Gentilucci 30.5–51.4 (200 kW truck), Ballard 73 (70 kW module, its own
note), Stropnik/Bionaz 405 (3 kW UPS). This system's 142 sits above the vehicle
band because it carries an inverter and an enclosure and because Babatunde's
2 kW graphite-plate stack (97 kg/kW) is ~3–4× an automotive stack. **The stack
is now the soft spot**: Gramc 2025's 48 kW stack inventory is the obvious
sensitivity, rebuilt on this study's boundary.

**Effect**, t CO₂e per MW per year: backup (200 h/yr) 23.3 → **12.0**; baseload
(8,760 h/yr) 122.4 → **33.3**. At backup duty the stack's 10-y calendar life now
carries 81 % of it.

Hydrogen is excluded from every coefficient — the LP supplies it explicitly.

children.module_doc:
PEM fuel cell — embodied carbon split into capital, wear and maintenance.
=============================================================================

``pemfc_op_1kwh_h2`` charges **everything per kWh delivered**: the stack over
30,000 operating hours, the balance of plant over 80,000, and a service every
8,000. For an attributional study of a fuel cell
that runs continuously, that is correct and elegant.

For an optimiser it is a trap, and a worse one than the electrolyser's. The
configuration ``grid_h2`` most wants to build is a fuel cell **installed at full
data-centre rating and run a few hundred hours a year** — backup, not baseload.
Charged per kWh delivered, that machine arrives with almost **no** embodied
burden at all, because it delivers almost no kWh. The steel, the platinum and
the graphite are real whether or not the thing ever runs.

So this module splits the inventory three ways:

| term | scales with | why |
|---|---|---|
| **balance of plant** | whichever runs out first: 20 calendar years, or 80,000 operating hours | a physical system that both ages and wears |
| **stack** | whichever runs out first: 10 calendar years, or 30,000 operating hours | you must buy one to have a fuel cell; you buy another every 30,000 hours of running |
| **maintenance** | MWh delivered | a service (air filter, coolant) every 8,000 operating hours |

Neither replaceable component is simply "capital" or "throughput". Each is

    replacements per MW per year = max( 1 / calendar_life_years ,
                                        full_load_hours_per_year / duty_life_hours )

which looks non-linear but is a maximum of two linear functions, so an LP
expresses it exactly: put ``units ≥ cap_fc / calendar_life`` and
``units ≥ throughput_MWh / duty_life`` on a free variable and let the objective
push it down onto whichever binds. ``REPLACEMENT_LP_NOTE`` carries the
formulation to the model layer so it cannot be lost in translation.

This matters at **both** ends. Charge the balance of plant on calendar life
alone and a fuel cell run flat out gets 20 years out of an 80,000-hour machine —
under-charged by 2.2x. Charge it on duty alone and a backup machine gets 400
years out of it. ``check_full_duty()`` asserts that at 8,760 h/yr the rule
reproduces the foreground's own per-kWh figure exactly, which is the case where
the two conventions must agree.

Hydrogen is deliberately **excluded** from every coefficient here. In the
optimiser the LP supplies hydrogen explicitly, from an electrolyser or a
purchase, each with its own burden; leaving the inventory's own hydrogen input
in would count the fuel twice. ``h2_kg_per_MWh`` is reported separately as the
consumption rate the LP needs.

Sources
-------
stack             Babatunde, S. et al. (2024), "Environmental Impact Assessment
                  of a 1 kW Proton-Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell", Table S1.
                  Built into ``fuel cell foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
balance of plant  Usai et al. 2021 SI Table 1 process loops (80 kW H2 PEM
                  system, per kW net) + ecoinvent 500 kW inverter + the
                  battery's 20 ft container at one per MW. Built as
                  ``pemfc_bop_stationary_1kw`` by optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.py.
                  Replaced ecoinvent's 2 kW natural-gas micro-CHP on 14 Oct.
maintenance       an air filter and a coolant change every 8,000 h (ASSUMED
                  interval), Usai's amounts. Replaced ecoinvent's reformer-
                  catalyst service event.
stack duty life   30,000 h — stationary H2 stacks refurbished at 24-30k h
                  (Nedstack); Bionaz et al. 2022 use 40k.
system duty life  80,000 h — DOE's 100 kW-3 MW stationary class, and
                  ecoinvent's own system life. Was 60,000, the residential class.
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.

**BoP calendar life: 20 years.** Nedstack give 20 y for the balance of plant
of their 120 kW CHP unit (10 y for their mobile unit); DOE's backup-power target
is a 15-year system life. Sweep 15-25. Was 25 y, ASSUMED to match the
electrolyser.

**Stack calendar life: 10 years.** The Clean Hydrogen Partnership's stationary
PEMFC KPIs are set on a 10-year system life, and Nedstack's mobile unit is
10 y; Gandiglio et al. 2022 replace their 50 kW Engie-EPS unit every 5. PEM
membranes age at open circuit, so this is the life that binds for a backup
stack that sits idle. Sweep 5 / 10 / 15. It was a 25-year placeholder.

Neither calendar life is a manufacturer warranty on a MW-class H2 unit, and
none was found; both stay flagged ``*_IS_ASSUMED`` for that reason.

Both calendar lives are read from the constants below on every call, never from
the decomposition cache, so editing one takes effect without a Brightway rerun.

Run:  python optimisation/fuel_cell.py

children.name: Step-up transformer, 0.4 → 20 kV, one per container (1 MVA per 1 MW)
children.comment: The transformer that steps a battery container's PCS output, or a fuel-cell container's inverter output, from LOW voltage (400 V) up to the site collection voltage (20 kV). Functional unit is 1 MW of inverter rating: transformers.py charges it per MW of cap_batt_p and per MW of cap_fc, each amortised over the asset's own life (the battery's 15 y; the fuel cell's BoP calendar life). MASS from Jasper et al. 2026, CSS (liquid cooled) bill, 'transformer, for grid connection': 5,500 kg per 1,600 kW container = 3,437.5 kg/MW, on the measured curve (2,566 kg/MVA at 2.2 MVA, 2,272 at 2.5). COMPOSITION, forming and factory energy per kg from the IEA PVPS T12-33:2026 Table 49 20/0.4 kV oil-immersed unit, a STATED SUBSTITUTION for Jasper's own recipe on technological representativeness (decided 22 Oct 2026). Jasper give a per-kg split (air-cooled sheet rows 225-236), but their §2.4.3 says it is derived from Hunziker et al. (2020): a 630 kVA line-frequency transformer with an ON-LOAD TAP CHANGER, scaled by mass to 1,800 kVA. The IEA unit is a current 2,500 kVA distribution transformer built from product documentation at exactly the 20/0.4 kV step the container needs. Jasper's recipe scores 7.85 kg CO2e/kg against 4.57 here (+72 %, mostly its 0.09 kg/kg of control electronics, likely the tap changer's); it is the sensitivity case. Closed as negligible on 4 Sep 2026 and modelled on 15 Oct: the inventory and loss machinery existed by then, and leaving it out favoured the storage chains against the generation chains, which pay for theirs. EXCLUDES: switchgear, protection and civils (as every transformer here); losses, which conversion_losses.py charges as energy; end-of-life.
children.source:
Power transformers — Leng et al. 2026 (wind step-ups and the grid intake),
IEA PVPS 2026 (solar step-ups).
=============================================================================

Why this inventory exists
-------------------------
A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage (<1 kV, the band
ecoinvent itself draws). A PV inverter's terminals are 400 V. The data centre
draws at *medium* voltage, 1–24 kV, because that is the level ``market for
electricity, medium voltage`` describes and the level the Zhang foreground is
authored against. Something has to bridge those, and it is not optional:
100 MW at 690 V is 83,674 A, which is not a cable. So every turbine carries its
own transformer at the foot of its tower — one per turbine, not one per farm —
and every PV inverter station carries one.

Why this inventory exists
-------------------------
The battery used to be ecoinvent's ``market for battery, Li-ion, LFP,
rechargeable, prismatic`` [GLO]: an **electric-vehicle traction pack**
(Dai et al. / GREET lineage, 2016-era, 116 Wh/kg) with no container, racking,
HVAC or fire suppression — ``battery.CONTAINER_UPLIFT_FRACTION`` was 0.0 and
said so. A grid battery is neither of those things. It is large-format
prismatic cells in racks, in a 20 ft container, with its own thermal
management and fire suppression, and those non-cell parts are 18-23 % of the
DC block's carbon in every source that itemises them.

children.module_doc:
Hydrogen purchase price by colour.
=============================================================================

Hydrogen is **bought**, not self-produced: every colour is a delivered £/kg
that the data centre pays. These are plant-gate prices plus one leg of
delivery: the compression that puts the hydrogen on a road trailer, which the
seller pays for and the buyer therefore does too. Road *haulage* itself remains
out of scope — ``ASSUMPTIONS.md`` excludes it on the grounds that production is
co-located with use, which is true of the hydrogen this study makes and not of
the hydrogen it buys. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Each colour is tied to the Brightway activity that supplies its *emissions*,
so a price and its LCA can never drift apart.

Sources, and how solid each one is
----------------------------------
green (PEM / Alkaline)  TRANSCRIBED. NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal,
                        "Levelised cost of green hydrogen modelling, 2025 to
                        2050" (resource cc2dad0c). A full sensitivity cube:
                        tech x scenario x build year x capacity factor x
                        electricity price x discount rate.

blue (ATR + CCS)        TRANSCRIBED. Same NESO dataset family, "Levelised
                        cost of blue hydrogen modelling, 2025 to 2050"
                        (resource 3f3b1bf0). Includes its own fuel, CO2 T&S
                        and emissions cost components.

grey (SMR unabated)     DERIVED. NESO and FES model green, blue and pink
                        only — neither publishes a grey price. So grey is
                        built from this study's own SMR inventory (4.85 m3
                        natural gas per kg H2) priced at the FES 2025 NBP gas
                        projection, plus a non-fuel cost scaled off NESO's
                        own blue cost stack, plus UK ETS carbon on the 9 kg
                        CO2/kg H2 the inventory emits directly.

turquoise (pyrolysis)   ASSUMED. Methane pyrolysis is pre-commercial and
                        appears in no UK official dataset. Built the same way
                        as grey from the MP-E inventory (5.72 m3 gas +
                        10.29 kWh per kg), with a non-fuel cost premium for
                        first-of-a-kind plant and an optional carbon-black
                        co-product credit. Treat as a scenario, not a price.

Deriving grey and turquoise from the project's *own* inventories is
deliberate: it means the gas consumption behind the price is the same number
the LCA charges emissions on.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/h2_prices.py

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.name: UPV, trimethylaluminum, purified
children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

Source and scope
----------------

solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's

("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.name: UPV, trimethylaluminum, purified
children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's

("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's

land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.name: UPV, trimethylaluminum, purified
children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.name: UPV, trimethylaluminum, purified
children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.module_doc:
Hydrogen purchase price by colour.
=============================================================================

Hydrogen is **bought**, not self-produced: every colour is a delivered £/kg
that the data centre pays. These are plant-gate prices plus one leg of
delivery: the compression that puts the hydrogen on a road trailer, which the
seller pays for and the buyer therefore does too. Road *haulage* itself remains
out of scope — ``ASSUMPTIONS.md`` excludes it on the grounds that production is
co-located with use, which is true of the hydrogen this study makes and not of
the hydrogen it buys. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Each colour is tied to the Brightway activity that supplies its *emissions*,
so a price and its LCA can never drift apart.

Sources, and how solid each one is
----------------------------------
green (PEM / Alkaline)  TRANSCRIBED. NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal,
                        "Levelised cost of green hydrogen modelling, 2025 to
                        2050" (resource cc2dad0c). A full sensitivity cube:
                        tech x scenario x build year x capacity factor x
                        electricity price x discount rate.

blue (ATR + CCS)        TRANSCRIBED. Same NESO dataset family, "Levelised
                        cost of blue hydrogen modelling, 2025 to 2050"
                        (resource 3f3b1bf0). Includes its own fuel, CO2 T&S
                        and emissions cost components.

grey (SMR unabated)     DERIVED. NESO and FES model green, blue and pink
                        only — neither publishes a grey price. So grey is
                        built from this study's own SMR inventory (4.85 m3
                        natural gas per kg H2) priced at the FES 2025 NBP gas
                        projection, plus a non-fuel cost scaled off NESO's
                        own blue cost stack, plus UK ETS carbon on the 9 kg
                        CO2/kg H2 the inventory emits directly.

turquoise (pyrolysis)   ASSUMED. Methane pyrolysis is pre-commercial and
                        appears in no UK official dataset. Built the same way
                        as grey from the MP-E inventory (5.72 m3 gas +
                        10.29 kWh per kg), with a non-fuel cost premium for
                        first-of-a-kind plant and an optional carbon-black
                        co-product credit. Treat as a scenario, not a price.

Deriving grey and turquoise from the project's *own* inventories is
deliberate: it means the gas consumption behind the price is the same number
the LCA charges emissions on.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/h2_prices.py

children.name: Hydrogen production, methane pyrolysis MP-E (Hermesmann & Müller 2022)
children.comment: Electrically heated methane pyrolysis, 1 kg H2 at the plant: Hermesmann & Müller 2022 Table 3, every row at the printed amount, gas and electricity on GB datasets. The 3.00 kg of solid carbon per kg H2 (Table 3 'Output flows: Carbon') is not credited against carbon black as §3.2.4 do: the whole burden sits on the hydrogen (ASSUMPTIONS §5; user decision 21 Oct 2026). No direct CO2.

Source and scope
----------------

  Turquoise, Blue, or Grey? Environmentally friendly Hydrogen Production in
  Transforming Energy Systems", Prog. Energy Combust. Sci. 90, 100996 —
  Tables 2–3 (inventories per kg H2) and §3.2.3 (CCS). Transcribed through the

* AE, PEM and SOEC units and operation: Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage

children.name: UPV, trimethylaluminum, purified
children.comment: Smith 2024 Table A6, every row at the printed amount. Smith et al. (2024), NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A (inventory rescored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos). Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off; his inventory is rescored here on 3.9.1 apos and his results are never transcribed. Boundary and substitutions: UPV_PV_SCOPE (end-of-life and delivery to site out; the tracker and the transformer substituted). SE Asia import supply chain.
children.source:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

children.module_doc:
Hydrogen purchase price by colour.
=============================================================================

Hydrogen is **bought**, not self-produced: every colour is a delivered £/kg
that the data centre pays. These are plant-gate prices plus one leg of
delivery: the compression that puts the hydrogen on a road trailer, which the
seller pays for and the buyer therefore does too. Road *haulage* itself remains
out of scope — ``ASSUMPTIONS.md`` excludes it on the grounds that production is
co-located with use, which is true of the hydrogen this study makes and not of
the hydrogen it buys. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Each colour is tied to the Brightway activity that supplies its *emissions*,
so a price and its LCA can never drift apart.

Sources, and how solid each one is
----------------------------------
green (PEM / Alkaline)  TRANSCRIBED. NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal,
                        "Levelised cost of green hydrogen modelling, 2025 to
                        2050" (resource cc2dad0c). A full sensitivity cube:
                        tech x scenario x build year x capacity factor x
                        electricity price x discount rate.

blue (ATR + CCS)        TRANSCRIBED. Same NESO dataset family, "Levelised
                        cost of blue hydrogen modelling, 2025 to 2050"
                        (resource 3f3b1bf0). Includes its own fuel, CO2 T&S
                        and emissions cost components.

grey (SMR unabated)     DERIVED. NESO and FES model green, blue and pink
                        only — neither publishes a grey price. So grey is
                        built from this study's own SMR inventory (4.85 m3
                        natural gas per kg H2) priced at the FES 2025 NBP gas
                        projection, plus a non-fuel cost scaled off NESO's
                        own blue cost stack, plus UK ETS carbon on the 9 kg
                        CO2/kg H2 the inventory emits directly.

turquoise (pyrolysis)   ASSUMED. Methane pyrolysis is pre-commercial and
                        appears in no UK official dataset. Built the same way
                        as grey from the MP-E inventory (5.72 m3 gas +
                        10.29 kWh per kg), with a non-fuel cost premium for
                        first-of-a-kind plant and an optional carbon-black
                        co-product credit. Treat as a scenario, not a price.

Deriving grey and turquoise from the project's *own* inventories is
deliberate: it means the gas consumption behind the price is the same number
the LCA charges emissions on.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/h2_prices.py

children.module_doc:
Baseline 1 — data centre on the GB grid.
=============================================================================

The Zhang et al. data centre is authored against ``market for electricity,
medium voltage [US-SERC]``. This replaces that with the half-hourly GB grid
mix built by ``grid_build.py`` from the Carbon Intensity API, and prices the
same electricity at the Elexon half-hourly wholesale price it also fetches.

The data centre is assumed to run flat at 100%. That is not a new assumption:
the foreground's own 1.60e9 kWh over 25 years is 7,306 kW continuous, which is
where the old ``dashboard_config.SYS_DC_DEMAND_MW = 7.31`` came from.

Emissions are computed as ``fixed + sum_t(kWh_t * EF_t)`` rather than by
re-solving the LCI per slice. That decomposition is exact — validated against
a full Brightway swap to within 1e-4 % — and it is what lets an optimiser
treat the LCA as linear coefficients instead of calling Brightway in its
inner loop.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run from the project root with the ``brightway`` environment:

    python optimisation/baseline_grid.py

children.name: How the LP organises it — the carbon objective (dc_model.objective_terms)
children.module_doc:
The data centre powering LP — size and dispatch, solved together.
=============================================================================

Give it a data centre size, a site, a window and a power option; it returns the
cheapest or the cleanest set of kit that keeps that data centre running every
half-hour of the window, and the dispatch that goes with it.

Why a linear program
--------------------
``sizing.py`` searches four dimensions with differential evolution over a
merit-order dispatch. That works for its question — cheapest build for a *fixed*
electrolyser. This problem has **nine** sizing dimensions and an inter-seasonal
hydrogen store, and at ~17,000 half-hourly steps per evaluation a population
search would take hours per configuration and still not find the global optimum.

Both objectives are linear in the same decision variables. That is not luck: it
is what ``baseline_grid.py``'s ``fixed + Σ kWh × EF`` decomposition established,
and what the capacity-shaped coefficients in ``electrolysers.py``,
``fuel_cell.py`` and ``h2_storage.py`` preserve. So the sizing and the dispatch
can be solved *jointly and exactly*, and the Pareto front between cost and
carbon is exact rather than sampled.

Solving them jointly is the point. A tank's value comes from filling in March
and draining in November, so its size cannot be chosen before its dispatch is
known. A merit-order rule — like the one in ``4.3.wind_h2_storage_system.ipynb``
— has no foresight and systematically mis-sizes the store.

One node, and what that means
-----------------------------
Constraint (1) is a copper plate at the campus. There is deliberately no
"route renewables to the data centre" variable separate from "route renewables
to the electrolyser": the allocation is what the LP *solves for* when it picks
``p_ely[t]`` against ``demand[t]``, and generation not consumed is curtailed
because (2) is an inequality. Adding routing variables would double the model
and change nothing. It does mean no internal network, no transmission limits and
no curtailment priority within the site.

Perfect foresight is an optimistic bound
----------------------------------------
The LP sees every half-hour at once, so it will electrolyse in March surplus
*because* it knows a November lull is coming. No operator has that forecast.
This is a legitimate way to answer **"what should I build?"** and an illegitimate
way to answer **"what will I achieve?"**. Every result carries
``perfect_foresight=True`` so the distinction survives into the write-up.

Linearisations, stated
----------------------
* **No unit commitment.** Minimum load on the electrolyser and the fuel cell is
  genuinely a binary constraint. The LP will run an electrolyser at 1 % of
  rating, which is physically wrong and economically near-irrelevant since full
  capital is charged either way. Revisit only if a result looks wrong.
* **Replacement counts** for the fuel cell stack and BoP use the convex
  ``max(calendar, duty)`` rule from ``fuel_cell.REPLACEMENT_LP_NOTE``, expressed
  exactly as two ``>=`` constraints on a free variable the objective minimises.
* **Storage is cyclic.** ``soc.roll(t=1)`` wraps the last step into the first, so
  the store cannot free-ride on ending the year empty.
* **Surplus-only is a window constraint**, not a per-step one — the per-step form
  is infeasible rather than binding whenever generation falls short. See
  ``apply_strategy``. One consequence, expected rather than a bug: in the
  islanded rows ``flexible`` and ``free`` land close together, because with no
  grid and no battery the only alternatives to serving demand from renewables
  are unserved load or a lossy round trip through the tank. The real contrast
  there is ``baseload`` against the rest.

Run:  python optimisation/dc_model.py

Every term here points at the chain its numbers come from. The sum over a solved year is the carbon objective.

children.module_doc:
Renewable generation — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

ecoinvent supplies renewable electricity as a **per-kWh** activity, with the
plant's capital burden already amortised over a lifetime output that ecoinvent
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape here, for two reasons:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW should not be a function of how much they happen to
   generate in the modelled year.
2. **ecoinvent's implied yield is not this study's yield.** Generation comes
   from Renewables.ninja at a chosen site, and the cost side uses DESNZ/Arup's
   load factors and lifetimes. Neither matches ecoinvent's own assumption, and
   for onshore wind the gap is a factor of 2.5.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the plant/turbine unit
exchange from the per-kWh activity, scores that unit, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. Per-kWh burden is then recomputed at whatever load factor and
lifetime the study actually uses. Nothing is invented - the reconstruction is
checked against ecoinvent's own per-kWh score, which it reproduces exactly.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Solar is not scored on ecoinvent, and why
-----------------------------------------
ecoinvent 3.9.1's GB open-ground PV activity is the 570 kWp Solarpark El
Tesoro in Andalusia, **installed in 2008**, carrying 4,401.7 m2 of panel for
570 kWp - a 129.5 W/m2, **12.95 %** module. It restates to 57 g CO2e/kWh,
about ten times onshore wind, which is not a defensible basis for a plant that
has not been built yet. 95.5 % of that burden is in the two exchanges that
scale with panel area, so the vintage is the whole story.

The obvious fixes are both closed. Upgrading the database does nothing: the
plant inventory is byte-identical in ecoinvent 3.10.1, so only the background
would move. And no other GB PV activity exists at utility scale - the only
alternatives are 3 kWp slanted-roof systems of the same vintage.

So the default basis for solar is **IEA PVPS Task 12**, the standard reference
for PV LCA, whose 2023 data update uses the same IPCC 2021 GWP100 method this
study uses throughout: 35.8 g CO2e/kWh for mono-Si at 976 kWh/kWp/year over 30
years, which is 1,048 kg CO2e/kWp of embodied carbon against ecoinvent's
2,303. Their reference yield sits within 10 % of the DESNZ GB solar load
factor, so the figure transfers with no irradiance correction - unusual, and
the reason this substitution is clean rather than a fudge.

Mono-Si, and not the like-for-like multi-Si IEA PVPS also publish, because
``cap_solar`` is a *decision variable* for a plant that does not exist yet, so
the question is what would actually be built. IEA PVPS record multi-Si market
share falling below 3 % in 2022 and to ~1 % in 2023 - they could not update
its parameters for want of current data. That is the same argument this module
already makes about not inheriting ecoinvent's yield for a sized asset, and it
is why multi-Si is not offered as a basis: it would fail the test on exactly
the ground ecoinvent fails it. Its number is kept in SOURCES.md as evidence,
where it answers the reviewer who suspects the technology was switched to
flatter the result.

So there are two bases, and the second exists only to reproduce older runs.
Pass ``solar_basis="ecoinvent"`` for that; both live in
``SOLAR_EMBODIED_BASES``. Wind and offshore wind are mostly steel and concrete
and ageing far more slowly than a PV module, so their capital dominates - but
the boundary still has to match solar's. IEA PVPS's per-kWh figure is a
**full-scope** footprint (module, BOS, inverter, install, EOL); a capital-only
wind figure restated on top of it would be comparing different things. So
``restate()`` adds ecoinvent's own non-capital consumables (lubricating oil,
water - the ~1 % ``residual_per_kWh`` from ``decompose()``) back on top of
wind and offshore's restated capital by default, making both technologies
full-scope. It is skipped only where the capital figure is already full-scope
itself (solar under its default IEA basis); it still applies under
``solar_basis="ecoinvent"``, since that basis is capital-only too.

Sources
-------
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100. Activities are the
wind, offshore    GB per-kWh generation datasets and the capital "unit"
                  exchanges they draw on.
embodied carbon   IEA PVPS Task 12, "Environmental Life Cycle Assessment of
solar             Electricity from PV systems - 2023 data update", Stucki M.,
                  Goetz M., de Wild-Scholten M. & Frischknecht R., May 2024.
load factor,      DESNZ/Arup 2024 Cost of Electricity reports, via
lifetime          ``tech_costs.py``. See SOURCES.md.

Run:  python optimisation/renewables.py
