children.module_doc:
Generation step-up transformers — embodied carbon per MW connected.
=============================================================================

A wind turbine generates at **690 V**, which is *low* voltage — below the 1 kV
boundary ecoinvent itself draws, the same band as a household supply. The data
centre draws at *medium* voltage, 1–24 kV, because that is the level
``market for electricity, medium voltage`` describes and the level the Zhang
foreground is authored against. Something has to bridge those two, and it is
not optional: 100 MW at 690 V is **83,674 A**, which is not a cable. Stepped to
20 kV the same power is 2,887 A, which is.

So every turbine carries its own transformer at the foot of its tower. **One
per turbine, not one per farm** — a 100 MW farm has fifty of them. That is what
this module charges, per MW of ``cap_wind``.

The inventory is not here
-------------------------
It is a foreground activity, built by ``optimiser_lca/stepup_transformers.py``
alongside the hydrogen tank and for the same reason — ecoinvent cannot supply
the asset, so it is assembled from a published bill of materials. This module
only scores that activity and amortises it. To change what a transformer is
made of, edit that module and rebuild; to change how long it lasts, edit
``TX_ASSET_LIFE_YEARS`` in ``dc_config.py``. Both are stated once and read here.

    database  TRANSFORMER_DB
    code      wind_turbine_stepup_per_mw
    unit      1 MW of wind connected
    source    Leng et al. (2026), Processes 14(7) 1045, Supplementary Table S1

Why this is a gap and not a double count
----------------------------------------
Checked exchange by exchange against ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos:

* ``wind turbine construction, 2MW, onshore`` lists its own parts in its
  comment — "Rotor, Nacelle, Electronics, Tower, Foundation" — and no
  transformer is among them. Its only electrical item is 438.7 kg of
  ``electronics, for control units``: a control cabinet, an order of magnitude
  short of the 3–5 t a 2 MW turbine transformer weighs. Its stated component
  masses (rotor 37 t, nacelle 61 t, tower 165 t) account for the materials
  without leaving room for one, and it says outright that it excludes the grid
  connection.
* ``wind turbine network connection construction, 2MW, onshore`` is 1,398.7 m³
  of excavation, 1,375.7 kg of HDPE and 253.8 kg of copper — cable and trench.

Why ecoinvent cannot supply the asset
-------------------------------------
It has **four** transformer activities, which are two products with a market
and a production each, and both are electronics. ecoinvent's own comments say
so: "a typical high voltage use transformer **in electronic modules** has an
average weight of **280 g** … used in the information and communication
technology", and 30 g for the low-voltage one. Their compositions match — the
high-voltage one is 0.50 kg ferrite, 0.31 kg epoxy and 0.51 kg injection
moulding per kg, against 5 g of steel. There is no ``substation`` activity, no
``switchgear`` activity, and no power transformer at any rating.

Until this rewrite, wind scaled that 280 g component up by a factor of 205,000
to stand for a 57 t substation unit. Rebuilding a real transformer's bill of
materials on the same database gives 177.3 t CO2e against 306.2 t on that
dataset, and the manufacturer declares 147.4 t, so the old basis ran about
**2x** high in a known direction. Nobody who has looked at this used ecoinvent's
transformer: Leng built theirs from materials, Teffera built theirs from
materials, and Vestas scaled a real ABB EPD.

Why it scales exactly
---------------------
Sizing needs no power factor. Leng states the transformer content of a 100 MW
farm directly, and ``cap_wind`` is in MW of exactly that kind, so the ratio is
read off rather than derived. One unit per turbine means **30 MW and 1,000 MW
carry the same figure per MW**.

The plant-rated basis this replaces did not scale. Specific mass falls with
rating — 2,566 kg/MVA at 2.2 MVA, 1,434 at 40, 715 at 100, all measured — so a
single flat number taken from one farm size was out by up to 14 % across a
tenfold range of build.

Independently checked
---------------------
Teffera et al. (2021) Table 5, three Ethiopian farms totalling 324 MW, reported
per kWh rather than in tonnes. Converted onto this study's basis their
turbine-level transformers are 228–333 kg CO2e/MW/year depending on which of
their two capacity factors the inventory is built on, which they do not state.
Leng sits inside that band. Two teams, two countries, two reporting formats.

What is counted, and what is not
--------------------------------
**No grid-export transformer charged to generation.** Leng's farm also has a
100 MVA unit stepping up to 110 kV, and this module does not charge it to wind.
This study's generation is behind the meter: there is nothing to export into,
and the one transformation between the site and the outside world is the grid
intake, which ``cap_grid`` pays for through ``grid_connection.py``. Charging it
here would bill the site for a voltage change it does not make. That same
unit's bill is what ``grid_connection.py`` now scores for the grid intake
(``registry.TX_GRID``, built alongside the step-ups), so ecoinvent's 280 g
transformer is left only on the legacy solar basis below.

**No step between the collection network and the data centre.** Both sit in the
medium-voltage band, so the chain closes. ``stepup_transformers.TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV`` states
that as a number rather than leaving it as the phrase "the same bus", and
``check()`` refuses a value outside the band. Leng's units are wound for 35 kV,
above the band; a 20 kV unit of the same rating carries less insulation and is
lighter, so taking their mass errs **high** — the safe direction.

**No switchgear, protection or civils.** Absent here and absent from the grid
intake in ``grid_connection.py``, so it is a level shift rather than a bias. Teffera puts
MV plus HV switchgear at 0.61 t/MW against a plant transformer's 1.08 t/MW.
Registered in DATA_GAPS.md.

**No manufacturing energy, because Leng publish none.** Their Table S1 is a
materials bill; no factory electricity appears for either transformer (checked
21 Oct 2026). Their published totals sit above this rebuild because they score
on ecoinvent 3.11 with RoW steel proxies, not because a flow was dropped. The
solar unit's IEA PVPS bill does carry process energy (~6 % of it), so wind
errs low relative to solar by about that margin; stated rather than glossed.
**Civils** are in since 21 Oct: Leng's box-transformer pads on the wind units
and the IEA PVPS transformer station building on the solar units.

**Solar is on the same footing as wind.** ``solar_pv`` reads its own foreground
activity, ``solar_inverter_stepup_per_mwp``, built from IEA PVPS Task 12's
T12-33:2026 LCI report: the oil-immersed 2.5 MVA units in a utility PV plant's
inverter stations, four of them on the report's own 10 MWp reference plant. Two
things make this better than the wind side rather than merely equal to it. The
unit is wound **20 / 0.4 kV**, which is ``stepup_transformers.TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV`` and the
inverter's LV terminals exactly — so no voltage adjustment is applied, where
Leng's 35 kV units have to be taken as erring high. And the count is **read off**
Table 50 rather than derived, which retires the two ASSUMED constants the old
solar path needed (``SOLAR_DC_AC_RATIO``, ``POWER_FACTOR``).

The old basis — one invented plant-rated unit on ecoinvent's 280 g electronics
dataset, scaled by a 40 MVA EPD's specific mass, with no per-inverter-station
transformers at all — survives only as ``SOLAR_BASIS = "legacy"``, to reproduce
pre-2026 runs. It carried two errors that partly cancelled: the electronics
dataset runs high for a given mass, while a 40 MVA specific mass under-counts a
2.5 MVA unit by ~1.6x.

**No cost term.** DESNZ/Arup's capex is plant-plus-connection-to-the-point-of-
connection, so a £/MW transformer charge would double count. Carbon gains a term
and cost does not; the asymmetry is deliberate and is in ASSUMPTIONS.md.

**Losses are not charged here.** Two manufacturer EPDs put a transformer's
life-cycle GWP at ~99 % use phase, and that is not this module's to charge: the
lost kWh is generated by plant the LP has already sized. Its home is an
efficiency on the availability constraints, which is not implemented, and which
remains the largest open item in this chain — grid import carries its
delivery losses (3.38 % at high voltage, ``optimiser_lca.grid.DELIVERY``)
while on-site generation carries none.

Sources
-------
wind inventory    Leng, H. et al. (2026), "Life Cycle Assessment of an Onshore
                  Wind Farm: Carbon Emission Evaluation and Mitigation Pathway
                  Design", *Processes* 14(7), 1045, Supplementary Table S1.
                  Transcribed into dc_config.TX_LENG_BOX_KG and built
                  into the foreground by optimiser_lca/stepup_transformers.py.
cross-check       Teffera, B. et al. (2021), "Life cycle assessment of wind
                  farms in Ethiopia", *Int J LCA* 26:76-96, Table 5.
turbine voltage   690 V, stated for all four turbine models in Teffera Table 2
                  and the industry de facto standard. TRANSCRIBED.
voltage bands     ecoinvent 3.9.1 ``market for electricity, medium voltage``
                  [GB] comment: high >24 kV, medium 1-24 kV, low <1 kV.
asset life        35 years, this study's own generation life. See renewables.py.
solar (legacy)    Hitachi Energy S.p.A. EPD, 40 MVA (Monselice), EPDItaly rev.
                  3, 2022 — 57,380 kg / 40 MVA — on ``market for transformer,
                  high voltage use``. Known ~2x high; see DATA_GAPS.md.

Run:  python optimisation/transformers.py

    unit      1 MW of wind connected
    source    Leng et al. (2026), Processes 14(7) 1045, Supplementary Table S1

Why this is a gap and not a double count
----------------------------------------
Checked exchange by exchange against ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos:

* ``wind turbine construction, 2MW, onshore`` lists its own parts in its
  comment — "Rotor, Nacelle, Electronics, Tower, Foundation" — and no
  transformer is among them. Its only electrical item is 438.7 kg of
  ``electronics, for control units``: a control cabinet, an order of magnitude
  short of the 3–5 t a 2 MW turbine transformer weighs. Its stated component
  masses (rotor 37 t, nacelle 61 t, tower 165 t) account for the materials
  without leaving room for one, and it says outright that it excludes the grid
  connection.
* ``wind turbine network connection construction, 2MW, onshore`` is 1,398.7 m³
  of excavation, 1,375.7 kg of HDPE and 253.8 kg of copper — cable and trench.

Why ecoinvent cannot supply the asset
-------------------------------------
It has **four** transformer activities, which are two products with a market
and a production each, and both are electronics. ecoinvent's own comments say
so: "a typical high voltage use transformer **in electronic modules** has an
average weight of **280 g** … used in the information and communication
technology", and 30 g for the low-voltage one. Their compositions match — the
high-voltage one is 0.50 kg ferrite, 0.31 kg epoxy and 0.51 kg injection
moulding per kg, against 5 g of steel. There is no ``substation`` activity, no
``switchgear`` activity, and no power transformer at any rating.

Until this rewrite, wind scaled that 280 g component up by a factor of 205,000
to stand for a 57 t substation unit. Rebuilding a real transformer's bill of
materials on the same database gives 177.3 t CO2e against 306.2 t on that
dataset, and the manufacturer declares 147.4 t, so the old basis ran about
**2x** high in a known direction. Nobody who has looked at this used ecoinvent's
transformer: Leng built theirs from materials, Teffera built theirs from
materials, and Vestas scaled a real ABB EPD.

Why it scales exactly
---------------------
Sizing needs no power factor. Leng states the transformer content of a 100 MW
farm directly, and ``cap_wind`` is in MW of exactly that kind, so the ratio is
read off rather than derived. One unit per turbine means **30 MW and 1,000 MW
carry the same figure per MW**.

The plant-rated basis this replaces did not scale. Specific mass falls with
rating — 2,566 kg/MVA at 2.2 MVA, 1,434 at 40, 715 at 100, all measured — so a
single flat number taken from one farm size was out by up to 14 % across a
tenfold range of build.

Independently checked
---------------------
Teffera et al. (2021) Table 5, three Ethiopian farms totalling 324 MW, reported
per kWh rather than in tonnes. Converted onto this study's basis their
turbine-level transformers are 228–333 kg CO2e/MW/year depending on which of
their two capacity factors the inventory is built on, which they do not state.
Leng sits inside that band. Two teams, two countries, two reporting formats.

What is counted, and what is not
--------------------------------
**No grid-export transformer charged to generation.** Leng's farm also has a
100 MVA unit stepping up to 110 kV, and this module does not charge it to wind.
This study's generation is behind the meter: there is nothing to export into,
and the one transformation between the site and the outside world is the grid
intake, which ``cap_grid`` pays for through ``grid_connection.py``. Charging it
here would bill the site for a voltage change it does not make. That same
unit's bill is what ``grid_connection.py`` now scores for the grid intake
(``registry.TX_GRID``, built alongside the step-ups), so ecoinvent's 280 g
transformer is left only on the legacy solar basis below.

**No step between the collection network and the data centre.** Both sit in the
medium-voltage band, so the chain closes. ``stepup_transformers.TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV`` states
that as a number rather than leaving it as the phrase "the same bus", and
``check()`` refuses a value outside the band. Leng's units are wound for 35 kV,
above the band; a 20 kV unit of the same rating carries less insulation and is
lighter, so taking their mass errs **high** — the safe direction.

**No switchgear, protection or civils.** Absent here and absent from the grid
intake in ``grid_connection.py``, so it is a level shift rather than a bias. Teffera puts
MV plus HV switchgear at 0.61 t/MW against a plant transformer's 1.08 t/MW.
Registered in DATA_GAPS.md.

**No manufacturing energy, because Leng publish none.** Their Table S1 is a
materials bill; no factory electricity appears for either transformer (checked
21 Oct 2026). Their published totals sit above this rebuild because they score
on ecoinvent 3.11 with RoW steel proxies, not because a flow was dropped. The
solar unit's IEA PVPS bill does carry process energy (~6 % of it), so wind
errs low relative to solar by about that margin; stated rather than glossed.
**Civils** are in since 21 Oct: Leng's box-transformer pads on the wind units
and the IEA PVPS transformer station building on the solar units.

**Solar is on the same footing as wind.** ``solar_pv`` reads its own foreground
activity, ``solar_inverter_stepup_per_mwp``, built from IEA PVPS Task 12's
T12-33:2026 LCI report: the oil-immersed 2.5 MVA units in a utility PV plant's
inverter stations, four of them on the report's own 10 MWp reference plant. Two
things make this better than the wind side rather than merely equal to it. The
unit is wound **20 / 0.4 kV**, which is ``stepup_transformers.TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV`` and the
inverter's LV terminals exactly — so no voltage adjustment is applied, where
Leng's 35 kV units have to be taken as erring high. And the count is **read off**
Table 50 rather than derived, which retires the two ASSUMED constants the old
solar path needed (``SOLAR_DC_AC_RATIO``, ``POWER_FACTOR``).

The old basis — one invented plant-rated unit on ecoinvent's 280 g electronics
dataset, scaled by a 40 MVA EPD's specific mass, with no per-inverter-station
transformers at all — survives only as ``SOLAR_BASIS = "legacy"``, to reproduce
pre-2026 runs. It carried two errors that partly cancelled: the electronics
dataset runs high for a given mass, while a 40 MVA specific mass under-counts a
2.5 MVA unit by ~1.6x.

**No cost term.** DESNZ/Arup's capex is plant-plus-connection-to-the-point-of-
connection, so a £/MW transformer charge would double count. Carbon gains a term
and cost does not; the asymmetry is deliberate and is in ASSUMPTIONS.md.

**Losses are not charged here.** Two manufacturer EPDs put a transformer's
life-cycle GWP at ~99 % use phase, and that is not this module's to charge: the
lost kWh is generated by plant the LP has already sized. Its home is an
efficiency on the availability constraints, which is not implemented, and which
remains the largest open item in this chain — grid import carries its
delivery losses (3.38 % at high voltage, ``optimiser_lca.grid.DELIVERY``)
while on-site generation carries none.

                  Wind Farm: Carbon Emission Evaluation and Mitigation Pathway
                  Design", *Processes* 14(7), 1045, Supplementary Table S1.
                  Transcribed into dc_config.TX_LENG_BOX_KG and built
                  into the foreground by optimiser_lca/stepup_transformers.py.
cross-check       Teffera, B. et al. (2021), "Life cycle assessment of wind
                  farms in Ethiopia", *Int J LCA* 26:76-96, Table 5.
turbine voltage   690 V, stated for all four turbine models in Teffera Table 2
                  and the industry de facto standard. TRANSCRIBED.
voltage bands     ecoinvent 3.9.1 ``market for electricity, medium voltage``
                  [GB] comment: high >24 kV, medium 1-24 kV, low <1 kV.
asset life        35 years, this study's own generation life. See renewables.py.
solar (legacy)    Hitachi Energy S.p.A. EPD, 40 MVA (Monselice), EPDItaly rev.
                  3, 2022 — 57,380 kg / 40 MVA — on ``market for transformer,
                  high voltage use``. Known ~2x high; see DATA_GAPS.md.

unit's bill is what ``grid_connection.py`` now scores for the grid intake
(``registry.TX_GRID``, built alongside the step-ups), so ecoinvent's 280 g
transformer is left only on the legacy solar basis below.

**No step between the collection network and the data centre.** Both sit in the
medium-voltage band, so the chain closes. ``stepup_transformers.TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV`` states
that as a number rather than leaving it as the phrase "the same bus", and
``check()`` refuses a value outside the band. Leng's units are wound for 35 kV,
above the band; a 20 kV unit of the same rating carries less insulation and is
lighter, so taking their mass errs **high** — the safe direction.

**No switchgear, protection or civils.** Absent here and absent from the grid
intake in ``grid_connection.py``, so it is a level shift rather than a bias. Teffera puts
MV plus HV switchgear at 0.61 t/MW against a plant transformer's 1.08 t/MW.
Registered in DATA_GAPS.md.

**No manufacturing energy, because Leng publish none.** Their Table S1 is a
materials bill; no factory electricity appears for either transformer (checked
21 Oct 2026). Their published totals sit above this rebuild because they score
on ecoinvent 3.11 with RoW steel proxies, not because a flow was dropped. The
solar unit's IEA PVPS bill does carry process energy (~6 % of it), so wind
errs low relative to solar by about that margin; stated rather than glossed.
**Civils** are in since 21 Oct: Leng's box-transformer pads on the wind units
and the IEA PVPS transformer station building on the solar units.

**Solar is on the same footing as wind.** ``solar_pv`` reads its own foreground
activity, ``solar_inverter_stepup_per_mwp``, built from IEA PVPS Task 12's
T12-33:2026 LCI report: the oil-immersed 2.5 MVA units in a utility PV plant's
inverter stations, four of them on the report's own 10 MWp reference plant. Two
things make this better than the wind side rather than merely equal to it. The
unit is wound **20 / 0.4 kV**, which is ``stepup_transformers.TX_SITE_COLLECTION_KV`` and the
inverter's LV terminals exactly — so no voltage adjustment is applied, where
Leng's 35 kV units have to be taken as erring high. And the count is **read off**
Table 50 rather than derived, which retires the two ASSUMED constants the old
solar path needed (``SOLAR_DC_AC_RATIO``, ``POWER_FACTOR``).

The old basis — one invented plant-rated unit on ecoinvent's 280 g electronics
dataset, scaled by a 40 MVA EPD's specific mass, with no per-inverter-station
transformers at all — survives only as ``SOLAR_BASIS = "legacy"``, to reproduce
pre-2026 runs. It carried two errors that partly cancelled: the electronics
dataset runs high for a given mass, while a 40 MVA specific mass under-counts a
2.5 MVA unit by ~1.6x.

**No cost term.** DESNZ/Arup's capex is plant-plus-connection-to-the-point-of-
connection, so a £/MW transformer charge would double count. Carbon gains a term
and cost does not; the asymmetry is deliberate and is in ASSUMPTIONS.md.

**Losses are not charged here.** Two manufacturer EPDs put a transformer's
life-cycle GWP at ~99 % use phase, and that is not this module's to charge: the
lost kWh is generated by plant the LP has already sized. Its home is an
efficiency on the availability constraints, which is not implemented, and which
remains the largest open item in this chain — grid import carries its
delivery losses (3.38 % at high voltage, ``optimiser_lca.grid.DELIVERY``)
while on-site generation carries none.

Sources
-------
wind inventory    Leng, H. et al. (2026), "Life Cycle Assessment of an Onshore
                  Wind Farm: Carbon Emission Evaluation and Mitigation Pathway
                  Design", *Processes* 14(7), 1045, Supplementary Table S1.
                  Transcribed into dc_config.TX_LENG_BOX_KG and built
                  into the foreground by optimiser_lca/stepup_transformers.py.
cross-check       Teffera, B. et al. (2021), "Life cycle assessment of wind
                  farms in Ethiopia", *Int J LCA* 26:76-96, Table 5.
turbine voltage   690 V, stated for all four turbine models in Teffera Table 2
                  and the industry de facto standard. TRANSCRIBED.
voltage bands     ecoinvent 3.9.1 ``market for electricity, medium voltage``
                  [GB] comment: high >24 kV, medium 1-24 kV, low <1 kV.
asset life        35 years, this study's own generation life. See renewables.py.
solar (legacy)    Hitachi Energy S.p.A. EPD, 40 MVA (Monselice), EPDItaly rev.
                  3, 2022 — 57,380 kg / 40 MVA — on ``market for transformer,
                  high voltage use``. Known ~2x high; see DATA_GAPS.md.

children.module_doc:
Grid connection — embodied carbon per MW of connection.
=============================================================================

The one sized asset in ``dc_model`` that carried no carbon at all. Every other
capacity — wind, solar, battery power and energy, electrolyser, tank, fuel cell
— has an embodied coefficient; ``cap_grid`` had none, so a carbon-only solve
could not see the connection and had no reason to keep it small. On the 300 MW
Highland run that produced an 868 MW connection used for six hours a year, and
after the DUoS fix it produced a variable with a zero coefficient in *both*
objectives, whose reported size was whichever vertex the solver stopped at.

Why the cost side stays at zero, and why that is right
-----------------------------------------------------
It is tempting to read "£0/MW/year" as the same kind of hole. It is not. For a
transmission-connected **demand** site the use-of-system charge is the zonal
half-hourly demand tariff plus the TDR, and both are already modelled; NESO's
local substation tariffs are *generation* charges and do not apply. In a floored
TNUoS zone the zonal tariff really is £0.00/kW. What is missing on the cost side
is the **connection charge** for sole-use assets, which is bilateral under the
Connection Charging Methodology rather than a published £/MW tariff, so it
cannot be transcribed. That gap is registered in DATA_GAPS.md and is a different
gap from this one.

What is counted
---------------
The **materials** of the transformers that step the network down onto the
site — cradle-to-gate, the same boundary as the wind step-ups — charged per MW
of ``cap_grid``, and, since 22 Oct 2026, the **switchyard's civils** per MW of
connection (``registry.TX_GRID_CIVILS``: Leng et al. 2026 Table S3's outdoor
venue, decision D2 in SOURCE_DIFF.md). The line that reaches the site is scored
and reported but not charged per MW (see ``decompose``). Switchgear and
protection have no source and sit on the cut-off register, where they fail the
1 % test against this small denominator and are carried as estimates on the
coefficient (``optimiser_lca/exclusions.py``, ``dc_inputs.build_tech``); the
transformer's manufacturing energy likewise. Losses are the LP's; end-of-life
is out everywhere.

The inventory is not here
-------------------------
The transformer is a foreground activity, ``TRANSFORMER_DB`` /
``registry.TX_GRID``, built by ``optimiser_lca/stepup_transformers.py`` from
Leng et al. (2026) Supplementary Table S1 alongside the wind step-ups: the
Gaoyou farm's grid-end main transformer, **XZ11-100000/110**, one 100 MVA
unit at 71,458.6 kg = **714.6 kg/MVA**, per 1 MVA of rating. This module only
scores it, sizes it per MW and amortises it.

It replaces ecoinvent 3.9.1's ``market for transformer, high voltage use``,
which by its own comment is a ~280 g electronic component "used in the
information and communication technology" — scored per kg and scaled by a
300 t / 240 MVA mass DERIVED from a GB 400 kV supergrid transformer that had no
citation. That gave 333.5 kg CO2e/MW/year; the dataset ran ~2x high per kg of
real transformer when the wind side was rebuilt the same way.

The voltage judgement
---------------------
Leng's unit is wound for **110 kV**. That fits a GB **132 kV** EHV/DNO
connection, which is the common case for a ~100 MW data centre. For a site
connected to the transmission system at **275 or 400 kV** it errs **LOW**:
supergrid transformers carry more insulation and are heavier per MVA. It is
used for every site as the default, whatever ``transmission_connected`` says,
and the direction of the error is registered in DATA_GAPS.md.

Sources
-------
transformer         Leng, H. et al. (2026), *Processes* 14(7), 1045,
                    Supplementary Table S1, main transformer XZ11-100000/110:
                    100 MVA, 71,458.6 kg. TRANSCRIBED into
                    ``stepup_transformers.TX_LENG_MAIN_KG``; materials on
                    ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos via ``TX_MATERIAL_PROCESSES``.
line                ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, ``market for transmission network,
                    electricity, high voltage`` [GLO], per km. TRANSCRIBED.
redundancy          2 transformers for N-1. ASSUMED.
power factor        1.0, MW -> MVA. ASSUMED: a data centre's load is corrected
                    close to unity; a lower one would scale this up as 1/pf.
line length         ASSUMED, and site-specific in reality. Deliberately short:
                    a data centre sited for its connection is near a substation.
asset life          40 years. ASSUMED, and typical for transmission plant —
                    longer than any generation asset in this study.

Run:  python optimisation/grid_connection.py

children.module_doc:
Lithium-ion battery storage — cost and embodied carbon.
=============================================================================

Costs come from **Modo Energy**, which is the source NESO itself uses: the FES
2025 Economics Methodology report states its Li-ion CAPEX is "a combination of
Modo survey data with CAPEX data from the National Renewable Energy
Laboratory". Modo's model assumptions are published openly at
docs.modoenergy.com, already in **real 2025 GBP** — the same basis as every
other cost in this study, so no deflation or FX is needed.

Embodied carbon comes from ecoinvent 3.9.1. Cost and carbon are deliberately
kept on the same two-part structure — a **power** term (£/kW, kg CO2e/kW) and
an **energy** term (£/kWh, kg CO2e/kWh) — so the optimiser can size power and
duration independently instead of being locked to a 4-hour product.

Sources
-------
cost, technical   Modo Energy, "BESS Cost and Technical Assumptions",
                  docs.modoenergy.com/pages/jan-2026/uk-europe/model-assumptions/
                  (July 2026). ~£400/kW for a 1-hour system today falling to
                  ~£200/kW by 2040; each additional hour of duration adds
                  £100/kW in 2025. 15-year asset life, ~67 % capacity
                  remaining after 10,000 cycles (~12-15 years), 1-2 cycles per
                  day, WACC 5.0 % real. Real 2025 GBP.

cost spread       Modo Energy BESS CapEx Survey 2024 (30 market participants,
                  2.8 GW at 1.9 h average): average £580k/MW, two-hour median
                  £650k/MW, 68 % of projects between £400k/MW and £700k/MW.

round-trip eff.   88 %, Modo's standard assumption. Not stated on the model
                  assumptions page itself, so it is the least firmly sourced
                  number here.

embodied carbon   energy term: the ``battery foreground`` built by
                  ``optimiser_lca/bess.py`` — Jasper et al. (2026) Energy
                  Advances 5:550, liquid-cooled LFP container, around the Voß
                  et al. (2025) Energy Environ. Sci. 18:8104 LFP cell, on
                  ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos. Power term: ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos
                  500 kW inverter. IPCC 2021 GWP100.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/battery.py

children.module_doc:
Electrolysers — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

The Gerloff 2021 foreground (``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py``; called Hermesmann's
here until 22 Oct 2026) supplies electrolysis as a **per-kg-H2** activity
with the capital good already amortised over a lifetime output that Gerloff
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape for an optimiser, for exactly the reasons set out in
``renewables.py``:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW must not depend on how much hydrogen they happen to make.
2. **Gerloff's implied utilisation is not this study's.** All three
   technologies amortise their capital over **160 GWh of lifetime electricity
   throughput at 1 MW** — 160,000 full-load hours. Spread over a 25-year plant
   life that is a **73 % capacity factor**. An optimiser that builds an
   electrolyser to chase surplus wind at 20 % CF and charges its capital per kg
   produced would understate that machine's embodied carbon **by a factor of
   3.5**.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the ``unit``-denominated
capital exchange from the per-kg activity, scores it, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. What remains — water, heat, electrolyte — stays per kg, because
those genuinely do scale with output.

Nothing is invented. ``check_reconstruction()`` asserts that capital-per-MW
re-amortised at Gerloff's own throughput, plus the per-kg remainder,
reproduces ``lca_helpers.run_non_electricity_lca()`` exactly.

The 1 MW rating
---------------
Only PEM states its rating in the foreground ("1 unit (1 MW)"). AE and SOEC do
not, so the rating is **derived and cross-checked** rather than assumed: each
technology's lifetime hydrogen output times its own specific energy comes to
160 GWh to within 0.2 %, despite specific energies ranging from 42.3 to
54.0 kWh/kg. Three independent inventories agreeing to 0.2 % on a quantity none
of them states is not a coincidence — it is one shared 1 MW / 160 GWh capital
basis. ``check_rating()`` enforces the agreement, so if the foreground is ever
rebuilt on a different basis this module fails loudly instead of scaling
everything by a silent factor.

Stacks
------
Gerloff's unit carries **three stacks** over its 20-year life (§2.1.3; the
module carries the stack's rows x3 since 22 Oct 2026, as the SI's stack
manufacturing energy always was). The capital good is still one activity per
unit, amortised here on calendar life: a duty-driven stack count, as
``fuel_cell.py`` does for the fuel cell, would need the stack rows split out
as their own activity — possible from the SI's Stack/BoP labels, not done.
For an electrolyser run harder than Gerloff's 160,000 full-load hours this
understates the stack burden. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Sources
-------
inventories       Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage 43, 102759: alkaline / PEM / SOEC.
                  Built into ``hydrogen foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.
plant lifetime    25 years — NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal, the same figure
                  ``price_outputs/electrolyser_costs_clean.csv`` carries.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run:  python optimisation/electrolysers.py

children.module_doc:
Hydrogen storage — embodied carbon per kg of capacity.
=============================================================================

The one asset in the hydrogen chain that was already the right shape. ecoinvent
3.9.1 has no hydrogen vessel, so ``optimiser_lca/h2_tank.py`` builds one the
way Gandiglio et al. (2022) do — as a mass of steel and nothing else — with a
reference product of **one kilogram of storage capacity**. That is already a
capacity basis, so unlike the electrolyser and the fuel cell there is nothing to
decompose: this module reads it, amortises it, and offers the second design the
config defines but does not build.

What it adds over reading the activity directly:

1. **Both tank designs**, not just the one ``h2_tank.TANK_DESIGN``
   currently selects, so the optimiser can run 28 bar against 200 bar as a
   sensitivity without a foreground rebuild. The as-built design is
   cross-checked against Brightway; the other is scored from its own steel
   process at its own steel intensity.
2. **The charging parasitic**, which belongs to storage and not to the
   electrolyser: compression from the electrolyser's delivery pressure to the
   tank's. Zero for the 28 bar design, because the electrolyser already leaves
   at ~30 bar.
3. **Standing loss**, which is *not* in the inventory and is not modelled here
   either — see below.

Why steel mass alone is defensible, and where it is not
------------------------------------------------------
Gandiglio's inventory is one line: 15,652 kg of chromium steel 18/8 for a
21.6 m3, 28 bar vessel. Missing are foundations, the enclosure, valves and
instrumentation, and end-of-life. The notebook says so, and so does this module.
Against that, steel is the overwhelming majority of a pressure vessel's embodied
carbon, so the figure is a defensible lower bound rather than a guess.

Standing loss is deliberately zero and needs a source
-----------------------------------------------------
There is **no boil-off** from compressed gas at ambient temperature — that is a
liquid-hydrogen phenomenon, and this is a steel bottle at 28 bar. The real
losses are permeation through the wall, which is negligible for steel at this
pressure, and fitting and valve leakage, which is a maintenance-quality
question rather than a physical constant. ``LEAKAGE_FRAC_PER_HOUR`` is exposed
for the optimiser and **defaults to zero with no source**, which is the honest
position but not a verified one. It was thought to decide the seasonal
hydrogen-versus-battery contest; swept over 0-0.1 %/day on 14 Oct (an ASSUMED
range, through ``build_tech(tank_leakage_per_hour=...)``) it moves cost and
carbon by under 0.1 % and does not change which store dominates. Registered,
with the band, in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

If it is ever set non-zero, the leaked hydrogen should also be charged as a
greenhouse gas in its own right — H2 is an indirect GHG — from DESNZ / Warwick
et al. 2022, *Atmospheric implications of increased hydrogen use*.

Sources
-------
inventory         Gandiglio, M., Marocco, P., Bianco, I., Lovera, D.,
                  Blengini, G.A., Santarelli, M. (2022), "Life cycle assessment
                  of a renewable energy system with hydrogen-battery storage
                  for a remote off-grid community", Int. J. Hydrogen Energy 47.
                  Table 3 — the as-built 21.6 m3 vessel at Ginostra.
type I cylinder   ~1 wt% gravimetric capacity, a typical industrial stationary
                  bottle. DERIVED, not transcribed — see optimiser_lca/h2_tank.py.
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.
vessel lifetime   25 years, the paper's own plant life. The tank is never
                  replaced within it.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

PEM fuel cell — embodied carbon split into capital, wear and maintenance.
=============================================================================

``pemfc_op_1kwh_h2`` charges **everything per kWh delivered**: the stack over
30,000 operating hours, the balance of plant over 80,000, and a service every
8,000. For an attributional study of a fuel cell
that runs continuously, that is correct and elegant.

For an optimiser it is a trap, and a worse one than the electrolyser's. The
configuration ``grid_h2`` most wants to build is a fuel cell **installed at full
data-centre rating and run a few hundred hours a year** — backup, not baseload.
Charged per kWh delivered, that machine arrives with almost **no** embodied
burden at all, because it delivers almost no kWh. The steel, the platinum and
the graphite are real whether or not the thing ever runs.

So this module splits the inventory three ways:

| term | scales with | why |
|---|---|---|
| **balance of plant** | whichever runs out first: 20 calendar years, or 80,000 operating hours | a physical system that both ages and wears |
| **stack** | whichever runs out first: 10 calendar years, or 30,000 operating hours | you must buy one to have a fuel cell; you buy another every 30,000 hours of running |
| **maintenance** | MWh delivered | a service (air filter, coolant) every 8,000 operating hours |

Neither replaceable component is simply "capital" or "throughput". Each is

    replacements per MW per year = max( 1 / calendar_life_years ,
                                        full_load_hours_per_year / duty_life_hours )

which looks non-linear but is a maximum of two linear functions, so an LP
expresses it exactly: put ``units ≥ cap_fc / calendar_life`` and
``units ≥ throughput_MWh / duty_life`` on a free variable and let the objective
push it down onto whichever binds. ``REPLACEMENT_LP_NOTE`` carries the
formulation to the model layer so it cannot be lost in translation.

This matters at **both** ends. Charge the balance of plant on calendar life
alone and a fuel cell run flat out gets 20 years out of an 80,000-hour machine —
under-charged by 2.2x. Charge it on duty alone and a backup machine gets 400
years out of it. ``check_full_duty()`` asserts that at 8,760 h/yr the rule
reproduces the foreground's own per-kWh figure exactly, which is the case where
the two conventions must agree.

Hydrogen is deliberately **excluded** from every coefficient here. In the
optimiser the LP supplies hydrogen explicitly, from an electrolyser or a
purchase, each with its own burden; leaving the inventory's own hydrogen input
in would count the fuel twice. ``h2_kg_per_MWh`` is reported separately as the
consumption rate the LP needs.

Sources
-------
stack             Babatunde, S. et al. (2024), "Environmental Impact Assessment
                  of a 1 kW Proton-Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell", Table S1.
                  Built into ``fuel cell foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
balance of plant  Usai et al. 2021 SI Table 1 process loops (80 kW H2 PEM
                  system, per kW net) + ecoinvent 500 kW inverter + the
                  battery's 20 ft container at one per MW. Built as
                  ``pemfc_bop_stationary_1kw`` by optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.py.
                  Replaced ecoinvent's 2 kW natural-gas micro-CHP on 14 Oct.
maintenance       an air filter and a coolant change every 8,000 h (ASSUMED
                  interval), Usai's amounts. Replaced ecoinvent's reformer-
                  catalyst service event.
stack duty life   30,000 h — stationary H2 stacks refurbished at 24-30k h
                  (Nedstack); Bionaz et al. 2022 use 40k.
system duty life  80,000 h — DOE's 100 kW-3 MW stationary class, and
                  ecoinvent's own system life. Was 60,000, the residential class.
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.

**BoP calendar life: 20 years.** Nedstack give 20 y for the balance of plant
of their 120 kW CHP unit (10 y for their mobile unit); DOE's backup-power target
is a 15-year system life. Sweep 15-25. Was 25 y, ASSUMED to match the
electrolyser.

**Stack calendar life: 10 years.** The Clean Hydrogen Partnership's stationary
PEMFC KPIs are set on a 10-year system life, and Nedstack's mobile unit is
10 y; Gandiglio et al. 2022 replace their 50 kW Engie-EPS unit every 5. PEM
membranes age at open circuit, so this is the life that binds for a backup
stack that sits idle. Sweep 5 / 10 / 15. It was a 25-year placeholder.

Neither calendar life is a manufacturer warranty on a MW-class H2 unit, and
none was found; both stay flagged ``*_IS_ASSUMED`` for that reason.

Both calendar lives are read from the constants below on every call, never from
the decomposition cache, so editing one takes effect without a Brightway rerun.

children.module_doc:
Grid and price series for a region and window — built in Python, on demand.
=============================================================================

The optimiser needs two half-hourly series for every run: grid carbon for the
site's Carbon Intensity region, and the GB wholesale price. ``profiles.py``
reads them from ``custom_grid_lca_outputs/`` and ``price_outputs/``; when a
window is missing, ``sites.ensure_grid_series`` calls this module to make it.

This replaces the notebook route (``1.dashboard_lca_adaptive`` → ``3.1`` →
``5.prices``, run through nbconvert after patching the config file on disk).
The science is unchanged — it is the same API calls, the same fuel-to-ecoinvent
mapping and the same closed-form score — but it now takes the region and dates
as arguments, so nothing on disk is edited to ask for a build.

Grid carbon, per half-hour
--------------------------
1. The Carbon Intensity API's regional endpoint gives the generation mix
   (% gas, wind, nuclear, imports, ...) for each half-hour. Its own
   ``intensity`` figure is kept as ``carbon_intensity`` for reference only:
   it counts direct combustion, not life cycle.
2. Elexon's FUELHH gives every interconnector's flow for the same half-hours.
   The region's imports are split across exporting countries from those flows,
   weighted by how much of each link reaches the region
   (``optimiser_lca.grid.IMPORT_ATTRIBUTION``, fitted by
   ``fit_import_attribution``). Recorded per row as ``imp_<CC>``.
3. Each fuel maps to one activity, named by its exact identity in
   ``optimiser_lca.grid.SOURCES`` and resolved by exact match — never by search
   ranking — then scored once per process for GWP100. Those per-kWh scores are
   life cycle: plant construction, fuel supply chain and combustion.
   Everything LCA about the series is in that one module.
4. ``generation_kgco2e_per_kwh`` = Σ share × score, per kWh generated, and
   ``custom_electricity_score`` = that delivered at high voltage (losses plus
   network). The LP reads the generation column and delivers it at the site's
   own voltage (``dc_inputs.build_series``).

Every file records what scored it
---------------------------------
``grid_sources_id()`` is a short hash of ``optimiser_lca.grid.basis()`` —
sources, method, weights, import attribution and delivery terms. Each grid CSV
carries it in a ``grid_sources`` column, with the basis and the scored sources
in a ``.sources.json`` beside it, and ``profiles`` ignores a series scored on
any other basis. Changing any of it therefore makes every series stale rather
than silently mixing bases; ``rescore()`` (``--rescore`` on the command line)
re-scores the files already on disk from the fuel mix each one recorded. The
first rescore of a file written before the import split fetches its window's
interconnector flows; after that it needs no API calls.

Output file names match what notebook 3.1 wrote, so every series already on
disk still reads.

Every series is UTC
--------------------
Grid, price (Elexon ``startTime``) and weather (Renewables.ninja) are all
stored as naive UTC timestamps, and a requested window is read as UTC. The
grid series used to be London local time, which put intraday carbon an hour
out of step with price and weather for seven months of the year. Files are
marked with a ``clock`` column; ``profiles.py`` ignores grid files without it,
so a series in the old basis is rebuilt rather than silently used. Anything
defined on the UK clock (DUoS time bands) converts from UTC itself.

Run:  python -m optimisation.grid_build 13 2025-06-02 2025-06-09
      python -m optimisation.grid_build --rescore
      python -m optimisation.grid_build --fit-imports

children.module_doc:
Hydrogen purchase price by colour.
=============================================================================

Hydrogen is **bought**, not self-produced: every colour is a delivered £/kg
that the data centre pays. These are plant-gate prices plus one leg of
delivery: the compression that puts the hydrogen on a road trailer, which the
seller pays for and the buyer therefore does too. Road *haulage* itself remains
out of scope — ``ASSUMPTIONS.md`` excludes it on the grounds that production is
co-located with use, which is true of the hydrogen this study makes and not of
the hydrogen it buys. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Each colour is tied to the Brightway activity that supplies its *emissions*,
so a price and its LCA can never drift apart.

Sources, and how solid each one is
----------------------------------
green (PEM / Alkaline)  TRANSCRIBED. NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal,
                        "Levelised cost of green hydrogen modelling, 2025 to
                        2050" (resource cc2dad0c). A full sensitivity cube:
                        tech x scenario x build year x capacity factor x
                        electricity price x discount rate.

blue (ATR + CCS)        TRANSCRIBED. Same NESO dataset family, "Levelised
                        cost of blue hydrogen modelling, 2025 to 2050"
                        (resource 3f3b1bf0). Includes its own fuel, CO2 T&S
                        and emissions cost components.

children.module_doc:
Electrolysers — embodied carbon per MW installed.
=============================================================================

The Gerloff 2021 foreground (``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py``; called Hermesmann's
here until 22 Oct 2026) supplies electrolysis as a **per-kg-H2** activity
with the capital good already amortised over a lifetime output that Gerloff
chose. That is the right shape for an attributional study of a fixed plant. It
is the wrong shape for an optimiser, for exactly the reasons set out in
``renewables.py``:

1. **Capacity is a decision variable.** The optimiser sizes MW; the burden of
   building those MW must not depend on how much hydrogen they happen to make.
2. **Gerloff's implied utilisation is not this study's.** All three
   technologies amortise their capital over **160 GWh of lifetime electricity
   throughput at 1 MW** — 160,000 full-load hours. Spread over a 25-year plant
   life that is a **73 % capacity factor**. An optimiser that builds an
   electrolyser to chase surplus wind at 20 % CF and charges its capital per kg
   produced would understate that machine's embodied carbon **by a factor of
   3.5**.

So this module strips the capital back out: it reads the ``unit``-denominated
capital exchange from the per-kg activity, scores it, and reports **kg CO2e per
MW installed**. What remains — water, heat, electrolyte — stays per kg, because
those genuinely do scale with output.

Nothing is invented. ``check_reconstruction()`` asserts that capital-per-MW
re-amortised at Gerloff's own throughput, plus the per-kg remainder,
reproduces ``lca_helpers.run_non_electricity_lca()`` exactly.

The 1 MW rating
---------------
Only PEM states its rating in the foreground ("1 unit (1 MW)"). AE and SOEC do
not, so the rating is **derived and cross-checked** rather than assumed: each
technology's lifetime hydrogen output times its own specific energy comes to
160 GWh to within 0.2 %, despite specific energies ranging from 42.3 to
54.0 kWh/kg. Three independent inventories agreeing to 0.2 % on a quantity none
of them states is not a coincidence — it is one shared 1 MW / 160 GWh capital
basis. ``check_rating()`` enforces the agreement, so if the foreground is ever
rebuilt on a different basis this module fails loudly instead of scaling
everything by a silent factor.

Stacks
------
Gerloff's unit carries **three stacks** over its 20-year life (§2.1.3; the
module carries the stack's rows x3 since 22 Oct 2026, as the SI's stack
manufacturing energy always was). The capital good is still one activity per
unit, amortised here on calendar life: a duty-driven stack count, as
``fuel_cell.py`` does for the fuel cell, would need the stack rows split out
as their own activity — possible from the SI's Stack/BoP labels, not done.
For an electrolyser run harder than Gerloff's 160,000 full-load hours this
understates the stack burden. Registered in ``DATA_GAPS.md``.

Sources
-------
inventories       Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage 43, 102759: alkaline / PEM / SOEC.
                  Built into ``hydrogen foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/hydrogen.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.
plant lifetime    25 years — NESO Green Hydrogen Data Portal, the same figure
                  ``price_outputs/electrolyser_costs_clean.csv`` carries.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

children.module_doc:
PEM fuel cell — embodied carbon split into capital, wear and maintenance.
=============================================================================

``pemfc_op_1kwh_h2`` charges **everything per kWh delivered**: the stack over
30,000 operating hours, the balance of plant over 80,000, and a service every
8,000. For an attributional study of a fuel cell
that runs continuously, that is correct and elegant.

For an optimiser it is a trap, and a worse one than the electrolyser's. The
configuration ``grid_h2`` most wants to build is a fuel cell **installed at full
data-centre rating and run a few hundred hours a year** — backup, not baseload.
Charged per kWh delivered, that machine arrives with almost **no** embodied
burden at all, because it delivers almost no kWh. The steel, the platinum and
the graphite are real whether or not the thing ever runs.

So this module splits the inventory three ways:

| term | scales with | why |
|---|---|---|
| **balance of plant** | whichever runs out first: 20 calendar years, or 80,000 operating hours | a physical system that both ages and wears |
| **stack** | whichever runs out first: 10 calendar years, or 30,000 operating hours | you must buy one to have a fuel cell; you buy another every 30,000 hours of running |
| **maintenance** | MWh delivered | a service (air filter, coolant) every 8,000 operating hours |

Neither replaceable component is simply "capital" or "throughput". Each is

    replacements per MW per year = max( 1 / calendar_life_years ,
                                        full_load_hours_per_year / duty_life_hours )

which looks non-linear but is a maximum of two linear functions, so an LP
expresses it exactly: put ``units ≥ cap_fc / calendar_life`` and
``units ≥ throughput_MWh / duty_life`` on a free variable and let the objective
push it down onto whichever binds. ``REPLACEMENT_LP_NOTE`` carries the
formulation to the model layer so it cannot be lost in translation.

This matters at **both** ends. Charge the balance of plant on calendar life
alone and a fuel cell run flat out gets 20 years out of an 80,000-hour machine —
under-charged by 2.2x. Charge it on duty alone and a backup machine gets 400
years out of it. ``check_full_duty()`` asserts that at 8,760 h/yr the rule
reproduces the foreground's own per-kWh figure exactly, which is the case where
the two conventions must agree.

Hydrogen is deliberately **excluded** from every coefficient here. In the
optimiser the LP supplies hydrogen explicitly, from an electrolyser or a
purchase, each with its own burden; leaving the inventory's own hydrogen input
in would count the fuel twice. ``h2_kg_per_MWh`` is reported separately as the
consumption rate the LP needs.

Sources
-------
stack             Babatunde, S. et al. (2024), "Environmental Impact Assessment
                  of a 1 kW Proton-Exchange Membrane Fuel Cell", Table S1.
                  Built into ``fuel cell foreground`` by
                  ``optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.py`` (python -m optimiser_lca.build).
balance of plant  Usai et al. 2021 SI Table 1 process loops (80 kW H2 PEM
                  system, per kW net) + ecoinvent 500 kW inverter + the
                  battery's 20 ft container at one per MW. Built as
                  ``pemfc_bop_stationary_1kw`` by optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.py.
                  Replaced ecoinvent's 2 kW natural-gas micro-CHP on 14 Oct.
maintenance       an air filter and a coolant change every 8,000 h (ASSUMED
                  interval), Usai's amounts. Replaced ecoinvent's reformer-
                  catalyst service event.
stack duty life   30,000 h — stationary H2 stacks refurbished at 24-30k h
                  (Nedstack); Bionaz et al. 2022 use 40k.
system duty life  80,000 h — DOE's 100 kW-3 MW stationary class, and
                  ecoinvent's own system life. Was 60,000, the residential class.
embodied carbon   ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos, IPCC 2021 GWP100.

**BoP calendar life: 20 years.** Nedstack give 20 y for the balance of plant
of their 120 kW CHP unit (10 y for their mobile unit); DOE's backup-power target
is a 15-year system life. Sweep 15-25. Was 25 y, ASSUMED to match the
electrolyser.

**Stack calendar life: 10 years.** The Clean Hydrogen Partnership's stationary
PEMFC KPIs are set on a 10-year system life, and Nedstack's mobile unit is
10 y; Gandiglio et al. 2022 replace their 50 kW Engie-EPS unit every 5. PEM
membranes age at open circuit, so this is the life that binds for a backup
stack that sits idle. Sweep 5 / 10 / 15. It was a 25-year placeholder.

Neither calendar life is a manufacturer warranty on a MW-class H2 unit, and
none was found; both stay flagged ``*_IS_ASSUMED`` for that reason.

Both calendar lives are read from the constants below on every call, never from
the decomposition cache, so editing one takes effect without a Brightway rerun.

Run:  python optimisation/fuel_cell.py

children.module_doc:
The data centre powering LP — size and dispatch, solved together.
=============================================================================

Give it a data centre size, a site, a window and a power option; it returns the
cheapest or the cleanest set of kit that keeps that data centre running every
half-hour of the window, and the dispatch that goes with it.

Why a linear program
--------------------
``sizing.py`` searches four dimensions with differential evolution over a
merit-order dispatch. That works for its question — cheapest build for a *fixed*
electrolyser. This problem has **nine** sizing dimensions and an inter-seasonal
hydrogen store, and at ~17,000 half-hourly steps per evaluation a population
search would take hours per configuration and still not find the global optimum.

Both objectives are linear in the same decision variables. That is not luck: it
is what ``baseline_grid.py``'s ``fixed + Σ kWh × EF`` decomposition established,
and what the capacity-shaped coefficients in ``electrolysers.py``,
``fuel_cell.py`` and ``h2_storage.py`` preserve. So the sizing and the dispatch
can be solved *jointly and exactly*, and the Pareto front between cost and
carbon is exact rather than sampled.

Solving them jointly is the point. A tank's value comes from filling in March
and draining in November, so its size cannot be chosen before its dispatch is
known. A merit-order rule — like the one in ``4.3.wind_h2_storage_system.ipynb``
— has no foresight and systematically mis-sizes the store.

One node, and what that means
-----------------------------
Constraint (1) is a copper plate at the campus. There is deliberately no
"route renewables to the data centre" variable separate from "route renewables
to the electrolyser": the allocation is what the LP *solves for* when it picks
``p_ely[t]`` against ``demand[t]``, and generation not consumed is curtailed
because (2) is an inequality. Adding routing variables would double the model
and change nothing. It does mean no internal network, no transmission limits and
no curtailment priority within the site.

Perfect foresight is an optimistic bound
----------------------------------------
The LP sees every half-hour at once, so it will electrolyse in March surplus
*because* it knows a November lull is coming. No operator has that forecast.
This is a legitimate way to answer **"what should I build?"** and an illegitimate
way to answer **"what will I achieve?"**. Every result carries
``perfect_foresight=True`` so the distinction survives into the write-up.

Linearisations, stated
----------------------
* **No unit commitment.** Minimum load on the electrolyser and the fuel cell is
  genuinely a binary constraint. The LP will run an electrolyser at 1 % of
  rating, which is physically wrong and economically near-irrelevant since full
  capital is charged either way. Revisit only if a result looks wrong.
* **Replacement counts** for the fuel cell stack and BoP use the convex
  ``max(calendar, duty)`` rule from ``fuel_cell.REPLACEMENT_LP_NOTE``, expressed
  exactly as two ``>=`` constraints on a free variable the objective minimises.
* **Storage is cyclic.** ``soc.roll(t=1)`` wraps the last step into the first, so
  the store cannot free-ride on ending the year empty.
* **Surplus-only is a window constraint**, not a per-step one — the per-step form
  is infeasible rather than binding whenever generation falls short. See
  ``apply_strategy``. One consequence, expected rather than a bug: in the
  islanded rows ``flexible`` and ``free`` land close together, because with no
  grid and no battery the only alternatives to serving demand from renewables
  are unserved load or a lossy round trip through the tank. The real contrast
  there is ``baseload`` against the rest.

Run:  python optimisation/dc_model.py

Baseline 1 — data centre on the GB grid.
=============================================================================

The Zhang et al. data centre is authored against ``market for electricity,
medium voltage [US-SERC]``. This replaces that with the half-hourly GB grid
mix built by ``grid_build.py`` from the Carbon Intensity API, and prices the
same electricity at the Elexon half-hourly wholesale price it also fetches.

The data centre is assumed to run flat at 100%. That is not a new assumption:
the foreground's own 1.60e9 kWh over 25 years is 7,306 kW continuous, which is
where the old ``dashboard_config.SYS_DC_DEMAND_MW = 7.31`` came from.

Emissions are computed as ``fixed + sum_t(kWh_t * EF_t)`` rather than by
re-solving the LCI per slice. That decomposition is exact — validated against
a full Brightway swap to within 1e-4 % — and it is what lets an optimiser
treat the LCA as linear coefficients instead of calling Brightway in its
inner loop.

Every number in this module is listed in ``SOURCES.md`` alongside its
source and provenance grade (transcribed / derived / assumed).

Run from the project root with the ``brightway`` environment:

    python optimisation/baseline_grid.py

children.module_doc:
Transformer conversion losses — the energy each voltage step costs.
=============================================================================

The LP's node balance used to treat a kWh at a generator's terminals as a kWh
at the data centre, while every kWh imported already paid its delivery losses
down to high voltage (``optimiser_lca.grid.DELIVERY``, ×1.0338). That flattered
on-site generation against import, one way only. ``transformers.py`` and
``grid_connection.py`` charge the transformers' *capital*; this module charges
their *losses*, which two manufacturer EPDs put at ~99 % of a transformer's
life-cycle GWP. The lost kWh is not given a carbon coefficient: it has to be
generated or imported, by plant and connections the LP already sizes and
charges, so it enters as energy and its carbon follows.

Three steps, each a transformer the study already inventories:

* **wind** — one turbine step-up per turbine, Leng et al. (2026)'s 2.2 MVA unit,
  50 per 100 MW (1.1 MVA per MW);
* **solar** — IEA PVPS T12-33:2026's 2.5 MVA inverter-station unit, 4 per 10 MWp
  (1.0 MVA per MWp);
* **grid intake** — Leng's 100 MVA main transformer, two per MW of connection
  for N-1 (``grid_connection.TRANSFORMER_REDUNDANCY``), each carrying half;
* **battery** and **fuel cell** (added 15 Oct) — the containerised LV → 20 kV
  unit each container carries: Jasper et al. 2026's 1,600 kW CSS, and one per
  ``FC_KW_PER_CONTAINER`` of fuel cell, one MVA per MW of inverter rating.
  Their loading is a solve outcome, so like the intake they take an ASSUMED
  energy-weighted loading. The fuel cell's unit stays energised on standby
  (black-start readiness), so its no-load loss is drawn every hour whether or
  not it runs — the one place these losses are not negligible for the asset.

Loss figures are the GB legal maxima, retained Commission Regulation (EU)
No 548/2014 Annex I, Tier 2 (from 1 July 2021), read on legislation.gov.uk on
14 Oct 2026. A real unit is at or below them, so these err high — but only
by the margin a design beats the floor of the regulation.

How the losses enter a linear model
-----------------------------------
A transformer of rating S carrying power p loses ``Po + Pk (p/S)²``.

* **No-load loss** ``Po`` is drawn whenever the unit is energised, which is
  always: a demand on the node of ``Po/S`` MW per MVA installed, so it scales
  with capacity, not output.
* **Load loss** is quadratic. It is linearised as ``Pk/S · x_eff · p``, where
  ``x_eff = Σx² / Σx`` is the energy-weighted loading. That is exact in energy
  terms when the unit carries its availability profile; ``dc_model`` computes
  it from the window's own capacity factors, so it follows the site and the
  resampling. Curtailment lowers the true loading, so this errs slightly high.
  The grid intake's loading is a solve outcome, so it takes an ASSUMED
  ``x_eff`` instead.

Out of scope: inverter and PCS losses (inside the battery's round-trip
efficiency and the fuel cell's net efficiency), and the data centre's own
distribution, which the PUE carries.

=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.
children.module_doc:
Utility-scale PV plant — Smith et al. (NREL 2024), fixed tilt, rescored on apos.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
The solar generation coefficient, rebuilt. It replaces a basis that priced a
solar farm using the footprint of a 3 kWp domestic roof: IEA PVPS Task 12's
2023 data update, 35.8 g CO₂e/kWh — a good number for the system it describes
("1 kWh AC … produced with a 3 kWp PV system, rooftop mounted"), but
``cap_solar`` is a utility-scale MWp, so the study was charging solar for roof
rails and a domestic string inverter and no fence, no plant-scale cabling, no
land. It was also the one coefficient not scored on ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos.

    Smith, B.L., Sekar, A., Mirletz, H., Heath, G. & Margolis, R. (2024), "An
    Updated Life Cycle Assessment of Utility-Scale Solar Photovoltaic Systems
    Installed in the United States", NREL/TP-7A40-87372, Appendix A.

**Why a rebuild and not a citation.** Smith publishes on ecoinvent cut-off. A
cut-off result cannot be relabelled as APOS, because the two differ exactly
where recycled content matters — for a PV plant, the aluminium, steel and
copper. So his *inventory* is taken and rescored here, and his results are
never transcribed; that makes the answer 3.9.1 apos by construction, the way
every other foreground here is. His process names are ecoinvent-native and
resolve directly, 93 % with no decision at all.

**Functional unit: 1 MWp DC of fixed-tilt plant** (``upv_fixed_tilt_plant_per_mwp``,
capital only), with 30 years of O&M as its own activity and the GB fleet's kWh
as a third; Smith's tables are activities per m² of module or per unit, as
printed, and the plant draws on them.

**The chain** — eleven nested unit processes, each consuming the one above:
A1 silica sand (per 9.25e4 t) → A2 metallurgical silicon (+3.58 kg direct
fossil CO₂) → A3 polysilicon (72 kWh HV, China grid) → A4 Czochralski ingot →
A5 wafer (m²) → A7 PERC cell (m², + CF₄ and C₂F₆, GWP 7,380 and 12,400; A6
trimethylaluminum feeds it) → A8 PERC module (frame, glass, EVA) ; A10
inverter (2.7 MWac unit) ; A12 electrical BOS (m²) ; A13 fence (m²).

**Where the rows are.** Every Smith table this study uses is written out
below as one ``Activity``, row for row, with the amount as printed and the
flow named as Smith names it — so the inventory reads here, not in a PDF or a
data file. The transcription it was checked against is
``optimisation/data/smith-nrel-2024-life-cycle-inventory.md`` (all 23 tables,
including the end-of-life ones this study excludes). Nineteen zero-GWP
biosphere rows whose ecoinvent v2 names differ from 3.9.1's were left out
until 22 Oct 2026 and are now in under their 3.9.1 names (the flows table says
which; a sourced in-boundary row is in whatever its size). Tables A14
(installation) and A15 (O&M) are not activities of their own: the parts kept
enter the plant and O&M activities as the parameters below.

**The four substitutions**:

1. **Fixed tilt for the tracker.** Smith's system is single-axis tracked; GB
   utility-scale is fixed tilt. Table A9 is dropped and IEA PVPS T12-33:2026
   ``Z-PV-239`` — a pile-driven steel table at 20° — put in its place. That
   makes the mounting *heavier* (9.730 vs 9.618 kg/m² of structure) and
   removes the motor, Li-ion cell and control electronics.
2. **No transformer.** ``stepup_transformers`` charges solar's step-up from
   IEA PVPS at 20/0.4 kV. Smith's A11 is unusable anyway at 19,796 kg/MVA,
   ~9× the measured specific mass at that rating.
3. **Inverter count from the stated ILR.** Smith's Table 3 says DC/AC 1.34;
   his Table A14 uses 4.30E-05 inverters/m², which at this module implies
   1.75. The two are inconsistent in the source; the stated design value is
   used, and ``check()`` refuses an implausible band.
4. **O&M keeps the replacement fraction, not the count.** A15 charges 30 % of
   the installed inverters over 30 years (Mason's 10 %/decade). The fraction
   transfers to our own count where his absolute number would not.

**Scope.** Included: manufacturing, mounting, electrical BOS, fence,
inverters, installation energy, land occupation (A14, zero GWP), 30 years of
O&M (rescaled to the study's life by ``renewables.py``). Excluded, each with
its direction: end-of-life (as everywhere in this study); delivery to site
(A14's transport rows — the sea leg alone is 201 t·km/m² for the import chain,
so this understates by ~1.5 %; outside the boundary because the site is not
known); the step-up transformer, charged elsewhere. Supply chain:
SE Asia import case — China national grid for the silicon chain, Thailand for
cell and module.

**How it is verified.** 290 of 290 scientific-notation values in Appendix A
appear in the transcription; 251 rows association-checked against the PDF,
249 clean (the 2 flagged are zero-GWP flows). Of 79 biosphere rows, exactly
four carry a non-zero GWP100 factor — the silicon CO₂ and the two fluorinated
cell gases — and all four are in. A8 lands at 684 kg CO₂e/kWdc; Smith states
his average-import module sits above the 630 kg CO₂e/kW EPEAT threshold, and
it does (``tests/test_coefficients.py``).

**Biosphere compartments.** Smith's biosphere rows name a substance, not a
compartment. The original build matched each by name to the *first* flow of
that name in the biosphere database — an accident of iteration order, which
has since changed (re-running that match today lands on different
compartments). The compartments the original build actually used are pinned
in the ``flows`` table below so the inventory is reproducible. The four
GWP-carrying flows (fossil CO₂ to air, CF₄, C₂F₆) are in sensible
compartments; the zero-GWP rest are arbitrary (cyanide to air, fluoride to
soil, waste heat to forestry soil) and must be fixed before any non-GWP
category is used.

children.module_doc:
GB grid electricity, 2025 annual mean, delivered at high voltage.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
**Functional unit: 1 kWh of electricity delivered at high voltage**, on the
grid this study scores everywhere else (``optimiser_lca.grid``), as a
foreground activity, so that an inventory which takes GB grid power (the
hydrogen routes) links to it instead of ecoinvent's 2018 GB market. Every grid
kWh in the study is then on one basis.

Composition: the 2025 time-mean of NESO's GB-wide generation mix (Carbon
Intensity API region 18, built by ``grid_build.build_grid(18, ...)``),
each fuel on its ``grid.SOURCES`` activity, wind split by
``grid.WIND_GROUP_WEIGHTS``, imports by the national interconnector flows
recorded in the series. Shares are kept exactly as the series averages them
(they sum to 0.99974, as the API's own percentages do), so the activity scores
to the series mean.

Delivery: ``grid.DELIVERY["high"]`` — every source amount grossed up by the
high-voltage losses, plus the GB high-voltage market's own non-electricity
exchanges (HVDC lines, N2O from corona discharge, ozone) per kWh of
throughput, which is what ``grid.derive_delivery`` measures as the network
term. A seller of fossil hydrogen is an industrial plant at transmission
voltage, as Hermesmann's comment on the SMR plant says.

Checked: ``check_against_series()`` re-derives the shares from the CSV;
``optimiser_lca.validate`` scores the activity against the series mean.

children.module_doc:
Hydrogen production — Hermesmann & Müller 2022 (fossil routes), Gerloff 2021
(electrolysers), six routes.
=============================================================================

Source and scope
----------------
* SMR, SMR-CCS, CCS and MP-E: Hermesmann, M. & Müller, T.E. (2022), "Green,
  Turquoise, Blue, or Grey? Environmentally friendly Hydrogen Production in
  Transforming Energy Systems", Prog. Energy Combust. Sci. 90, 100996 —
  Tables 2–3 (inventories per kg H2) and §3.2.3 (CCS). Transcribed through the
  study's own SimaPro project (SMR.XLSX, smr ccs.XLSX, ccs.XLSX); checked row
  by row against the paper on 21–22 Oct 2026.
* AE, PEM and SOEC units and operation: Gerloff, N. (2021), J. Energy Storage
  43, 102759 — SI Figures 1–5 (the 1 MW bills, every row labelled BoP or
  Stack) and Tables 3–6 (manufacturing energy, lifetime hydrogen, operating
  data). Transcribed through the same SimaPro project; checked row by row
  against the SI on 22 Oct 2026.

**Functional units.** ``smr``, ``smr_ccs``, ``mp_e`` and the three ``*_op``
activities: **1 kg of hydrogen** at the production site (Hermesmann's FU is at
30 bar). ``ccs``: treatment of **1 kg of captured CO2**. ``ae_unit``,
``pem_unit``, ``soec_unit``: **one 1 MW electrolyser over Gerloff's 20-year
life**, which each operation activity draws on at 1 unit per lifetime hydrogen
output (3.09, 2.96 and 3.78 million kg; all three are 160 GWh of electricity
at 1 MW — ``electrolysers.py`` re-amortises per MW installed).

**Boundary.** Cradle to gate at the production site. Out: end-of-life
(Gerloff Table 4's disposal processes), delivery to site (Gerloff's second
250 km lorry leg), and every by-product credit — Hermesmann's excess
electricity (SMR 1.10 kWh, SMR-CCS 0.05 kWh per kg) and MP-E's 3.00 kg of solid
carbon are not credited; the whole burden sits on the hydrogen (attributional,
no system expansion, ASSUMPTIONS.md §5; user decision 21 Oct 2026). In: the
first 250 km leg (materials to assembly), three stacks per unit life (Gerloff
§2.1.2–2.1.3: the stack is "replaced 3 times", and SI Table 3's stack energy is
already ×3), manufacturing energy, foundations.

**Substitutions, each stated once where it applies.** Electricity: the three
units are manufactured in Germany, as Gerloff (§2: "Germany (DE) has been chosen
provided that the opportunity for it existed"), so SI Table 3's manufacturing
electricity is on ecoinvent's German LV market for AE, PEM and SOEC alike (PEM and
SOEC were on GB LV until 26 Oct 2026, as the user's UK exports had them). The
operation activities' electricity (GB LV) is stripped out by ``electrolysers.py``
and charged by the LP on the study's own GB grid. Iridium: Gerloff's 0.8 kg of
anode iridium has no 3.9.1 dataset; platinum stands in for it (SOURCE_DIFF S3).
SOEC heat: on Mehmeti et al. 2018's natural-gas boiler, the source of the
5.24 kWh, rather than Gerloff's coal-heavy "other than natural gas" heat (see
``heat_ng_boiler``). CCS well drilling: Hermesmann's "15.4 kg diesel per kg
CO2" read as per tonne and burned (SOURCE_DIFF S4). LSM layer: Gerloff name
La2O3 and SrCO3 with no amount (#11); ASSUMED amounts from the layer's
geometry stand in until the sheet is held.

**Carbon balance (DERIVED, this module's addition).** Every carbon atom in the
gas an SMR plant takes leaves as CO2. ecoinvent's GB high-pressure gas carries
0.7410 kg fossil C per kg at 0.7350 kg/m3, i.e. 1.9956 kg CO2 per m3; the
paper's IEAGHG-based figures (9.00 kg on 4.85 m3) imply a leaner gas. The gap
is charged as CO2: all of it to air for SMR (0.679 kg); for SMR-CCS, which is
post-combustion flue-gas capture at 90 % (Hermesmann §4.1.1, Fig. 9), 90 % of
the gap to the capture train and 10 % to air. The paper's own SMR-CCS numbers
close on that reading: 9.00 × 5.33/4.85 = 9.89 kg, 0.99 emitted (printed),
8.90 captured. The export's 8.01 kg captured (= 9.00 − 0.99) was a slip and was
replaced on 22 Oct 2026.
