children.name: Fuel cell stack calendar life
children.section: Open — public source identified, not yet pulled
cells: DOE stationary and backup-power fuel cell targets; Clean Hydrogen Partnership SRIA stationary KPIs; backup-PEMFC manufacturer design lives

`fuel_cell.STACK_CALENDAR_LIFETIME_YEARS` = **10 y since 14 Oct** (was a 25-y placeholder), still flagged ASSUMED. Indicative sources: the Clean Hydrogen Partnership's stationary PEMFC KPIs are set on a 10-y system life; Nedstack's mobile unit 10 y; Gandiglio et al. 2022 replace a 50 kW Engie-EPS unit every 5 y. PEM membranes age at open circuit, so this binds for an idle backup stack — sweep 5 / 10 / 15 and report the band. **It moves cost as well as carbon**: at backup duty the stack line is £30.9k/MW-yr at 10 y against £12.3k at 25 y, and 9.7 against 3.9 t CO₂e/MW-yr.

children.name: DUoS for EHV-connected sites
children.section: Open — public source identified, not yet pulled
cells: LPN Annex 2 EHV charges are *site specific* — one row per named site — so they cannot be generalised into a study input. `network_charges.py` uses the HV Site Specific family instead, which overstates DUoS somewhat for a large EHV-connected data centre

children.name: NESO electrolyser capex has no published range
children.section: Open — public source identified, not yet pulled
cells: NESO publishes one capex per technology per build year; its Low/Central/High labels vary the LCOH scenario, not the capital cost. So AE and PEM capex are fixed across a cost-case sweep while every assumed input around them moves, understating the spread on on-site electrolysis results

children.name: CO2 transport & storage
children.section: Open — public source identified, not yet pulled
cells: FES: **£450/tCO2 in 2025**, falling to **£200/tCO2** long term; opex 5 % of capex

**Already inside blue's price** — NESO's ATR+CCS LCOH carries a £0.62/kg T&S line and EHO implies ~£0.74/kg — so adding FES on top would double count (+£3.60/kg at SMR-CCS's 8.01 kg CO2/kg). If FES is wanted it must *replace* the embedded rate, and the £450 may be capital (~£55/t levelised). Separately, grey's central price carries 2024 ETS (~£32/t), not FES CP2 (£78.96/t). Audit §3.6.

children.name: Battery fixed opex
children.section: Open — public source identified, not yet pulled
cells: BEIS 2022 *Benefits of Long Duration Electricity Storage*
Public PDF, and what FES itself routes to. The one battery input with no source today: Modo do not publish it, so a flagged 2 %-of-capex proxy is in use.

children.name: Battery component lives (Jasper 20 y / 15 y)
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: Jasper et al. 2026 §2.4.6 run the container system **20 years**: the container, transformer, cables, controller and air cooling last it; the liquid cooling, the inverter (PCS) and the cells last **15 years** and are counted ×1.33 ("a theoretical replacement factor is calculated by dividing the operating time by the expected service life"). The model charges everything over Modo's 15-year asset life, because `audit.py` requires each asset's carbon life to equal its cost life, and the cost annuity runs over Modo's 15 years. Taking Jasper's lives would lower `gwp_batt_e` by roughly 1–4 % and the container transformer by 25 %. **Kept at 15 y (user, 26 Oct 2026)** until the cost side can move to a 20-year system with mid-life replacements.

children.name: Hydrogen loading compressor capex
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: The compression **carbon** term is complete; the **cost** term is electricity only, at `PRODUCER_ELEC_GBP_PER_MWH`. No public per-kg figure for a hydrogen loading compressor was found, so the seller's compressor capital is in neither objective. The cost side is therefore a floor and a residual bias toward buying remains — smaller than before, and now in one place rather than two

children.name: Battery standing loss
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: Self-discharge plus auxiliary/HVAC load, `battery.STANDING_LOSS_PER_HOUR`. Zero and **assumed**, now stated in the module rather than supplied by a caller's `getattr` default against a constant that had never been defined — the model ran a loss-free battery and nothing said so. Not negligible in principle: auxiliary load moves system RTE by 2–4 points seasonally and bites hardest on a lightly cycled battery, which is what the minimum-carbon builds hold (below 1 % of capacity for 5,540 of 8,675 hours on the 300 MW Highland run). Modo's 88 % is a round-trip figure and carries no standing term, so a value cannot be taken from it. This and the tank's leakage are the same parameter on opposite sides of the hydrogen-versus-battery seasonal contest, and both are still zero by default. **Bounded by sweep, 14 Oct** — battery 0 / 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5 %/day × tank 0 / 0.01 / 0.1 %/day, both objectives, `optimisation_outputs/storage_loss_sweep.csv`. Overridable as `build_tech(batt_standing_loss_per_hour=…)`, a fraction **per hour** (`dc_model`'s keep factor is `1 − loss × dt`, so it is resolution-independent): %/day ÷ 2,400. Reference case: North Norfolk, 100 MW IT at PUE 1.5, 2025, hourly, **islanded**, with wind, solar, battery, PEM electrolyser, tank and fuel cell all available (`res_h2` with the battery unlocked) — the one architecture where the two stores actually compete; every stored grid-connected run builds no electrolyser or tank at all. Across the whole grid: **min cost** £132.02–132.30m (+0.21 %), 62,542–62,665 t CO₂e (−0.04 to +0.16 %), battery 2,048–2,069 MWh, tank 187–192 t, electrolyser 5.6–5.7 MW, fuel cell 35.7–36.4 MW; **min carbon** £166.67–166.85m (+0.11 %), 53,624–53,641 t (+0.03 %), battery 217–221 MWh, tank 167.3 t, electrolyser 80.2–80.4 MW, fuel cell 119.5–119.8 MW. **No flip at any point**: the battery delivers 87 % of stored output at min cost and hydrogen 61–66 % at min carbon. It is small because both builds keep the battery nearly empty — it averages ~9 % of capacity at min cost and ~7 % at min carbon — and the model charges the loss on *stored* energy. That is the judgement to check: HVAC/BMS auxiliary load really scales with *installed* capacity, so charged that way the top of the band is ~3.75 GWh/yr at min cost, ~0.3 % of the 1.31 TWh demand — still no flip. The result is now bounded at these orders of magnitude, not open; one site, one year, perfect foresight, and taken while the grid-connection transformer rebuild was in flight (that term is zero here, islanded). Candidate sources for a value: BEIS 2022, or a BESS auxiliary-load study.

children.name: Alkaline delivery pressure
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: `electrolysers.DELIVERY_PRESSURE_BAR` is sourced for PEM (30 bar, the commercialised class) and SOEC (atmospheric), but **assumed** at 30 bar for alkaline, which is deployed both ways and whose source inventory does not state which. If the AE inventory is atmospheric, its compression parasitic is understated by ~2.1 kWh/kg, the same error SOEC carried.

children.name: Electrolyser consumables cost
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: Found by `audit.py`. Water and heat are charged in carbon (`variable_kgco2e_per_kg`) and not in cost, because no price for either is sourced here. Material and one-directional: SOEC draws **18.864 MJ (5.24 kWh) of external heat and 0.65 m³ of water per kg H₂**, against PEM's 0.28 kWh and 0.10 m³. SOEC's electricity advantage over PEM is 21.7 %; on **total energy** it is 12.4 %. The model therefore selects SOEC partly on heat it does not pay for. *Availability* is closed (14 Oct): since the heat became a gas boiler (Mehmeti 2018) it is bought fuel, not the data centre's ~40 °C waste heat, and the electric-boiler scenario buys power. What remains is the cost.

children.name: Transmission connection capital cost
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: Since DUoS was made conditional on the connection tier, a transmission-connected site in a floored TNUoS zone has a per-MW connection cost of exactly **£0/MW/year** — TNUoS locational is £0.00 in Northern and Southern Scotland and DUoS does not apply. That is right as a *tariff*, and wrong as a *cost*: the connection assets (bays, transformers, cable, substation works) are charged under the Connection Charging Methodology, which no module reads. The `tech_costs.py` DESNZ/Arup figures are generator-side and are not a substitute. Consequence: `cap_grid` has a zero coefficient in both objectives, so `dc_pareto` now pins it with a lexicographic second stage rather than relying on the solver returning the smallest basic value. A sourced £/MW connection cost would remove the need for that.

children.name: The dispatch profile and the amortisation load factor disagree by ~20 %
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: Found while wiring in the utility-scale basis. Embodied carbon is amortised over DESNZ/Arup's **net** load factor of 12.2 %, but the LP dispatches solar from a Renewables.ninja profile whose full-year 2025 mean capacity factor at the study's 20° tilt is **13.5 % (London), 14.3 % (North Norfolk), 14.5 % (Exeter) and 11.4 % (Inverness)** — re-fetched 14 Oct; the 13.96–15.15 % quoted here before were the old 35° series. So the per-kWh figures quoted in SOURCES.md (22.0 g CO₂e/kWh) are an *amortisation basis*, not the intensity the model effectively applies, which is nearer 19–20 g in the south and ~24 g at Inverness. Not obviously an error — DESNZ's is a net figure carrying availability, soiling, degradation and curtailment, while Renewables.ninja gives a resource-based figure with a flat 10 % system loss, so they measure different things — but nothing in the repo said so, and the capacity charge is the LP's primitive while the per-kWh number is only a derived diagnostic. Related: **array geometry was an undocumented function default**. `profiles.fetch_solar_cf` hard-coded tilt 35°, azimuth 180°, 10 % loss and no tracking in its signature; `dc_inputs.build_series` never passed them, so the data centre model silently took 35° and could not override it, and its docstring called that "a conventional GB utility-scale choice" when GB practice is 20–25°. Now `cfg.PV_TILT_DEG` = 20°, matching the mounting structure whose embodied carbon is charged, and threaded through.

children.name: DUoS regional coverage
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: Only London Power Networks HV Site Specific is transcribed, so any distribution-connected site outside LPN is priced on London tariffs. Material for distribution-scale runs; no longer affects transmission-connected ones.

children.name: TDR band boundaries
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: The bands are percentiles of the GB site population (40th/70th/85th on agreed capacity for distribution, 40th/70th/93rd on gross consumption for transmission — CUSC 14.15.137 via CMP389), re-derived each price control and not published as an MW lookup. The EHV kVA boundaries in `network_charges.EHV_BAND_KVA` come from secondary summaries and **need verification against DCUSA Schedule 32**; the T-Demand consumption boundaries are unpublished, so only the top band is used and only far above any plausible 93rd percentile.

children.name: Transmission-vs-distribution threshold
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: No code sets an MW boundary — it is a network-design outcome. `network_charges.TRANSMISSION_MW_ASSUMED` is an assumed 100 MW, and every caller can override it with `transmission_connected=`. It swings the TDR band between £270,752 and £4,670,801/year, so it is the most consequential assumption in the charging stack.

children.name: Bought green H₂ supply mix
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: `h2_prices.GREEN_H2_GRID_SHARE` = **0.5**, the fraction bought from grid-connected rather than behind-the-meter electrolysers. **ASSUMED, and the weakest input in the bought-hydrogen stack.** No GB breakdown of green hydrogen production by connection type is published, and at the current size of the GB electrolyser fleet any such split would be dominated by a handful of projects. It moves the coefficient across 0.976–1.107 kg CO₂e/kg (1.469 on the low-voltage delivery basis used until 13 Oct) and the price across £4.93–8.33/kg, so it should be swept rather than trusted — `build_tech(green_h2_grid_share=...)` exists for that.

children.name: Behind-the-meter capacity factor in the green price
children.section: Open — no public source
cells: EHO UK 2024 gives directly-connected and grid electrolysis near-identical CAPEX (€2.771 vs €2.761/kg), i.e. **the same utilisation for both**, when a behind-the-meter electrolyser is limited to its generator's 24–38 % load factor. CAPEX is 49 % of the behind-the-meter total; rescaling it alone gives £5.69/kg at CF 0.38, £6.54 at 0.30, £7.55 at 0.24 against grid-connected's £8.33. So £4.93/kg and strictly matched dedicated wind are probably not both available, and the 50:50 default's price is correspondingly optimistic. Related: the LCA's capital amortises at an implied CF of 0.732 and NESO's green cube central case at 0.50 — three different utilisation assumptions in one commodity.

children.name: UK government PV embodied carbon
children.section: Checked and confirmed absent
cells: POSTnote 383 *Carbon Footprint of Electricity Generation* (June **2011**); DESNZ GHG Conversion Factors; DESNZ/Arup Cost of Electricity reports; UK Solar Roadmap (June 2025) / Solar Taskforce

**Nothing usable.** The POSTnote predates every modern c-Si inventory; the conversion factors are operational only and carry no capital goods for generation assets; the cost reports carry no inventories; the Roadmap is deployment and planning policy. Same pattern as the hydrogen chain: **the UK publishes costs and tariffs, not inventories.** Solar therefore uses IEA PVPS Task 12 — see `SOURCES.md`

children.name: A UK wind LCA factor
children.section: Checked and confirmed absent
cells: DESNZ GHG Conversion Factors; DESNZ/Arup Cost of Electricity; DUKES; POSTnotes 383 and 268; RenewableUK; the Carbon Trust

**Nothing usable.** No GB fleet-average or per-technology wind carbon intensity is published anywhere in the UK evidence base as an *inventory*: the conversion factors are operational and carry no capital goods, and the rest publish costs, capacities and load factors. Same pattern as the hydrogen chain and solar — **the UK publishes costs and tariffs, not inventories.** Bought green H₂ therefore uses this study's own ecoinvent turbine activity, with IEA 2025's harmonised median as the documented alternative — see `SOURCES.md`

children.name: A hydrogen carbon intensity from UK or EU regulation
children.section: Checked and confirmed absent
cells: UK Low Carbon Hydrogen Standard; EU RED II / RFNBO delegated acts (Regulation 2023/1185)

**Structurally incapable of supplying one.** Both exclude capital goods and therefore set renewable electricity to 0.0 g CO₂e/kWh — they zero-rate precisely the term an attributional coefficient has to estimate. The UK's published default for wind/solar electrolysis, 0.0048 kg CO₂e/kg, is an accounting artefact of that exclusion. They give **ceilings** only: LCHS 2.400 kg CO₂e/kg, RFNBO 3.384. Recorded as bounds in `h2_prices.LCHS_CEILING_KGCO2E_PER_KG`, never as values

children.name: A power transformer in ecoinvent
children.section: Checked and confirmed absent
cells: Every activity in ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos matching `transformer`, `substation`, `switchgear` or `switch cabinet`

**Nothing usable.** Four transformer activities exist, being two products with a market and a production each, and both are electronic components — ecoinvent's own comments give their average weights as **280 g** and **30 g** and describe them as used "in the information and communication technology". Zero substation, switchgear or switch-cabinet activities. The largest single use of the high-voltage one anywhere in the database applies **12.8 t** of a 280 g component to a solar thermal plant, so the mis-scaling is widespread rather than particular to this study. Power transformers must therefore be assembled from a bill of materials — which is what Leng, Teffera and Vestas each did independently

children.name: A newer ecoinvent PV dataset
children.section: Checked and confirmed absent
cells: ecoinvent 3.10.1 apos, present in the `hypt` Brightway project on this machine

**No improvement.** `photovoltaic plant construction, 570kWp, multi-Si, on open ground` has all six technosphere exchanges byte-identical to 3.9.1. Only the background differs, and mixing versions would break the "3.9.1 apos throughout" consistency claim. GB has three PV activities in either version; the other two are 3 kWp slanted-roof of the same vintage

children.name: H2 storage capex (FES)
children.section: Not applicable
cells: FES models **salt caverns** only (DNV-GL 2019). This study uses a ~10 t steel vessel, already inventoried from Gandiglio et al. 2022.

children.name: H2 transmission/distribution
children.section: Not applicable
cells: Out of scope under co-location.

children.name: Hydrogen refuelling stations
children.section: Not applicable
cells: Not relevant to a data centre.

children.name: Fuel cell capex, and a per-replacement stack cost.
children.note: One job, not two — a £/replacement figure fixes the duty-versus-calendar asymmetry at the same time. Until then the cost axis of *every* hydrogen architecture is a ~4× range with a known-direction bias, and cost-optimal builds over-run the fuel cell for free. `h2_capex.py`, `fuel_cell.py`, `DATA_GAPS.md`. BoP duty reached cost on 12 Oct (plan §1 step 1); step 2 — discount the stack the same way and put fixed opex on full system capex — is part of this job, since it moves every backup fuel cell (+12 % central).

children.name: SOEC capex/opex.
children.note: Currently PEM × 1.2/1.5/2.0 with no source at all. Try NESO Green Hydrogen Portal, then IEA. Carbon-only SOEC runs are a defensible partial result meanwhile — cost-optimal SOEC is not.

children.name: Electrolyser consumables cost.
children.note: SOEC's 5.24 kWh/kg external heat and 0.65 m³/kg water are charged in carbon and free in cost, so the cost objective prefers SOEC partly for a reason that does not exist (except in the electric-boiler scenarios, where the heat is bought power). The heat is a gas boiler (Mehmeti 2018, `SOURCES.md`), so a gas tariff ÷ boiler efficiency prices it. Availability is no longer a question: bought fuel, not the data centre's waste heat (closed on the carbon side 14 Oct).

children.name: Tank cost and tank carbon describe different vessels.
children.note: Default `gandiglio_28bar` is 313 kg stainless/kg H₂ in carbon, but costed at the €500–1,040/kg high-pressure range — ~3–10× low on its own shell mass. Price it from `steel_kg_per_kg_h2` (Capital Equipment Cost Database). Needs a decision on the default design. Plan §3 item 1, §6.3.

children.name: The import price carries no levies.
children.note: RO/FiT/CfD/CM/AAHEDC ≈ £54/MWh plus CCL — about +50 % on the grid-only bill, and it flatters import against every on-site asset. `ELECTRICITY_DELIVERED_UPLIFT` cannot reach the LP (`profiles.py` never reads `price_timeslices`). Audit §3.5.

children.name: Connection tier and band follow the cap, not the connection built
children.note: (19 Oct, supervisor point 4). Replace the assumed 100 MW threshold with GB's voltage rule (ENWL ES216, 240 MVA in England and Wales; 132 kV in Scotland), and bound `cap_grid` below by its band's floor. Moves the London headline. Sequenced in `docs/CONNECTION_TIER_PLAN.md`.

children.name: CO₂ transport & storage: replace, don't add.
children.note: Blue's price already carries T&S — NESO's ATR+CCS LCOH has a £0.62/kg T&S line, EHO implies ~£0.74/kg — so adding FES's £450/tCO₂ on top would double count (+£3.60/kg). If FES is wanted, swap it for the embedded rate (and check whether the £450 is capital, ~£55/t levelised). `h2_prices.py:81` already reads CP1/CP2 of that workbook. Also: grey's central price carries 2024 ETS (~£32/t), not FES CP2 (£78.96/t). Audit §3.6.

children.name: Sweep the fuel cell calendar lives.
children.note: Stack 5 / 10 / 15 y (central 10 since 14 Oct), BoP 15 / 20 / 25 y (central 20). Both indicative, not MW-class H₂ warranties; the stack's binds at backup duty and carries ~80 % of a backup unit's fuel-cell carbon. Both move cost too. Plan §2.

children.name: MW of fuel cell per container
children.note: — 1 MW assumed in `optimiser_lca/fuel_cell.FC_KW_PER_CONTAINER`; sweep 0.5–2. 3.7 of the BoP's 44 t/MW.

children.name: Battery fixed opex from BEIS 2022
children.note: *Benefits of Long Duration Electricity Storage*. Public PDF, and what FES itself routes to. Replaces the 2 %-of-capex proxy — the one battery input with no source.

children.name: Check Marocco et al. 2020 (Energy Convers. Manag. 211:112768) for a tank cost.
children.note: Gandiglio 2022 has none (read 22 Oct 2026: LCA only, and it points to Marocco for the economics of the same Ginostra system), so Marocco is the one source that would match the vessel actually modelled. Not held.

children.name: Report the two big assumed scalars as bands, not points.
children.note: `green_h2_grid_share` and `transmission_connected` both already have override hooks on `build_tech()`. No sourcing — just run the sweep and publish the range. The T/D threshold alone swings TDR £270k–£4.67m/year.

children.name: Read NESO's variable opex.
children.note: `electrolyser_costs_clean.csv` carries `variable_opex_GBP_per_kWh_H2_HHV` — stack replacement and water, PEM £0.12/kg — and `h2_capex.electrolyser_costs()` drops it. Audit §3.3.

children.name: One price base and one discount-rate policy.
children.note: DESNZ is 2023 real and never rebased (~6 % low against Modo/EHO 2025); DOE $ and tank € are converted at the exchange rate only; the 6 % on H₂ assets has no source, and the Green Book 3.5 % marked closed in `DATA_GAPS.md` is used nowhere. Audit §4.

children.name: Battery: the £100/kWh is not on the cited Modo page
children.note: (re-checked 30 Sep — it gives only "~£400/kW (1h)"), yet it sets 66–75 % of battery capex. Also bound duration: an islanded solve builds 42 h of Li-ion. Audit §3.2.

children.name: Generation cost scope.
children.note: DESNZ opex includes the *generator's* TNUoS/DUoS (+11.6 % on onshore) for plant behind our meter, and excludes land and business rates (~21 % of `cost_wind`). Audit §3.1.

children.name: Network charge shape.
children.note: DUoS uses the "No Residual" class (a data centre is Band 1–4) and an unverified Nov–Feb red band (historic LPN is all-year 11–14 and 16–19: £6.96 vs £2.05/MWh); TDR is banded on the connection ceiling while DUoS bills `cap_grid`; TNUoS HH is a Triad charge, not a capacity one. Audit §3.5.

children.name: Tank heel.
children.note: `cap_tank` drains to zero; a 1–5 bar minimum for the FC feed makes both objectives 4–22 % low per usable kg. Audit §3.3.

gap73.name: Battery standing loss
cells: Self-discharge plus auxiliary/HVAC load, `battery.STANDING_LOSS_PER_HOUR`. Zero and **assumed**, now stated in the module rather than supplied by a caller's `getattr` default against a constant that had never been defined — the model ran a loss-free battery and nothing said so. Not negligible in principle: auxiliary load moves system RTE by 2–4 points seasonally and bites hardest on a lightly cycled battery, which is what the minimum-carbon builds hold (below 1 % of capacity for 5,540 of 8,675 hours on the 300 MW Highland run). Modo's 88 % is a round-trip figure and carries no standing term, so a value cannot be taken from it. This and the tank's leakage are the same parameter on opposite sides of the hydrogen-versus-battery seasonal contest, and both are still zero by default. **Bounded by sweep, 14 Oct** — battery 0 / 0.1 / 0.25 / 0.5 %/day × tank 0 / 0.01 / 0.1 %/day, both objectives, `optimisation_outputs/storage_loss_sweep.csv`. Overridable as `build_tech(batt_standing_loss_per_hour=…)`, a fraction **per hour** (`dc_model`'s keep factor is `1 − loss × dt`, so it is resolution-independent): %/day ÷ 2,400. Reference case: North Norfolk, 100 MW IT at PUE 1.5, 2025, hourly, **islanded**, with wind, solar, battery, PEM electrolyser, tank and fuel cell all available (`res_h2` with the battery unlocked) — the one architecture where the two stores actually compete; every stored grid-connected run builds no electrolyser or tank at all. Across the whole grid: **min cost** £132.02–132.30m (+0.21 %), 62,542–62,665 t CO₂e (−0.04 to +0.16 %), battery 2,048–2,069 MWh, tank 187–192 t, electrolyser 5.6–5.7 MW, fuel cell 35.7–36.4 MW; **min carbon** £166.67–166.85m (+0.11 %), 53,624–53,641 t (+0.03 %), battery 217–221 MWh, tank 167.3 t, electrolyser 80.2–80.4 MW, fuel cell 119.5–119.8 MW. **No flip at any point**: the battery delivers 87 % of stored output at min cost and hydrogen 61–66 % at min carbon. It is small because both builds keep the battery nearly empty — it averages ~9 % of capacity at min cost and ~7 % at min carbon — and the model charges the loss on *stored* energy. That is the judgement to check: HVAC/BMS auxiliary load really scales with *installed* capacity, so charged that way the top of the band is ~3.75 GWh/yr at min cost, ~0.3 % of the 1.31 TWh demand — still no flip. The result is now bounded at these orders of magnitude, not open; one site, one year, perfect foresight, and taken while the grid-connection transformer rebuild was in flight (that term is zero here, islanded). What remains is the cost.

gap76.name: Transmission connection capital cost
cells: Since DUoS was made conditional on the connection tier, a transmission-connected site in a floored TNUoS zone has a per-MW connection cost of exactly **£0/MW/year** — TNUoS locational is £0.00 in Northern and Southern Scotland and DUoS does not apply. That is right as a *tariff*, and wrong as a *cost*: the connection assets (bays, transformers, cable, substation works) are charged under the Connection Charging Methodology, which no module reads. The `tech_costs.py` DESNZ/Arup figures are generator-side and are not a substitute. Consequence: `cap_grid` has a zero coefficient in both objectives, so `dc_pareto` now pins it with a lexicographic second stage rather than relying on the solver returning the smallest basic value. A sourced £/MW connection cost would remove the need for that.

gap77.name: The dispatch profile and the amortisation load factor disagree by ~20 %
cells: Found while wiring in the utility-scale basis. Embodied carbon is amortised over DESNZ/Arup's **net** load factor of 12.2 %, but the LP dispatches solar from a Renewables.ninja profile whose full-year 2025 mean capacity factor at the study's 20° tilt is **13.5 % (London), 14.3 % (North Norfolk), 14.5 % (Exeter) and 11.4 % (Inverness)** — re-fetched 14 Oct; the 13.96–15.15 % quoted here before were the old 35° series. So the per-kWh figures quoted in SOURCES.md (22.0 g CO₂e/kWh) are an *amortisation basis*, not the intensity the model effectively applies, which is nearer 19–20 g in the south and ~24 g at Inverness. Not obviously an error — DESNZ's is a net figure carrying availability, soiling, degradation and curtailment, while Renewables.ninja gives a resource-based figure with a flat 10 % system loss, so they measure different things — but nothing in the repo said so, and the capacity charge is the LP's primitive while the per-kWh number is only a derived diagnostic. Related: **array geometry was an undocumented function default**. `profiles.fetch_solar_cf` hard-coded tilt 35°, azimuth 180°, 10 % loss and no tracking in its signature; `dc_inputs.build_series` never passed them, so the data centre model silently took 35° and could not override it, and its docstring called that "a conventional GB utility-scale choice" when GB practice is 20–25°. Now `cfg.PV_TILT_DEG` = 20°, matching the mounting structure whose embodied carbon is charged, and threaded through.

gap78.name: DUoS regional coverage
cells: Only London Power Networks HV Site Specific is transcribed, so any distribution-connected site outside LPN is priced on London tariffs. Material for distribution-scale runs; no longer affects transmission-connected ones.

gap79.name: TDR band boundaries
cells: The bands are percentiles of the GB site population (40th/70th/85th on agreed capacity for distribution, 40th/70th/93rd on gross consumption for transmission — CUSC 14.15.137 via CMP389), re-derived each price control and not published as an MW lookup. The EHV kVA boundaries in `network_charges.EHV_BAND_KVA` come from secondary summaries and **need verification against DCUSA Schedule 32**; the T-Demand consumption boundaries are unpublished, so only the top band is used and only far above any plausible 93rd percentile.

gap80.name: Transmission-vs-distribution threshold
cells: No code sets an MW boundary — it is a network-design outcome. `network_charges.TRANSMISSION_MW_ASSUMED` is an assumed 100 MW, and every caller can override it with `transmission_connected=`. It swings the TDR band between £270,752 and £4,670,801/year, so it is the most consequential assumption in the charging stack.

gap81.name: Bought green H₂ supply mix
cells: `h2_prices.GREEN_H2_GRID_SHARE` = **0.5**, the fraction bought from grid-connected rather than behind-the-meter electrolysers. **ASSUMED, and the weakest input in the bought-hydrogen stack.** No GB breakdown of green hydrogen production by connection type is published, and at the current size of the GB electrolyser fleet any such split would be dominated by a handful of projects. It moves the coefficient across 0.976–1.107 kg CO₂e/kg (1.469 on the low-voltage delivery basis used until 13 Oct) and the price across £4.93–8.33/kg, so it should be swept rather than trusted — `build_tech(green_h2_grid_share=...)` exists for that.

gap82.name: Behind-the-meter capacity factor in the green price
cells: EHO UK 2024 gives directly-connected and grid electrolysis near-identical CAPEX (€2.771 vs €2.761/kg), i.e. **the same utilisation for both**, when a behind-the-meter electrolyser is limited to its generator's 24–38 % load factor. CAPEX is 49 % of the behind-the-meter total; rescaling it alone gives £5.69/kg at CF 0.38, £6.54 at 0.30, £7.55 at 0.24 against grid-connected's £8.33. So £4.93/kg and strictly matched dedicated wind are probably not both available, and the 50:50 default's price is correspondingly optimistic. Related: the LCA's capital amortises at an implied CF of 0.732 and NESO's green cube central case at 0.50 — three different utilisation assumptions in one commodity.

gap83.name: UK government PV embodied carbon
cells: POSTnote 383 *Carbon Footprint of Electricity Generation* (June **2011**); DESNZ GHG Conversion Factors; DESNZ/Arup Cost of Electricity reports; UK Solar Roadmap (June 2025) / Solar Taskforce

**Nothing usable.** The POSTnote predates every modern c-Si inventory; the conversion factors are operational only and carry no capital goods for generation assets; the cost reports carry no inventories; the Roadmap is deployment and planning policy. Same pattern as the hydrogen chain: **the UK publishes costs and tariffs, not inventories.** Solar therefore uses IEA PVPS Task 12 — see `SOURCES.md`

gap84.name: A UK wind LCA factor
cells: DESNZ GHG Conversion Factors; DESNZ/Arup Cost of Electricity; DUKES; POSTnotes 383 and 268; RenewableUK; the Carbon Trust

**Nothing usable.** No GB fleet-average or per-technology wind carbon intensity is published anywhere in the UK evidence base as an *inventory*: the conversion factors are operational and carry no capital goods, and the rest publish costs, capacities and load factors. Same pattern as the hydrogen chain and solar — **the UK publishes costs and tariffs, not inventories.** Bought green H₂ therefore uses this study's own ecoinvent turbine activity, with IEA 2025's harmonised median as the documented alternative — see `SOURCES.md`

gap85.name: A hydrogen carbon intensity from UK or EU regulation
cells: UK Low Carbon Hydrogen Standard; EU RED II / RFNBO delegated acts (Regulation 2023/1185)

**Structurally incapable of supplying one.** Both exclude capital goods and therefore set renewable electricity to 0.0 g CO₂e/kWh — they zero-rate precisely the term an attributional coefficient has to estimate. The UK's published default for wind/solar electrolysis, 0.0048 kg CO₂e/kg, is an accounting artefact of that exclusion. They give **ceilings** only: LCHS 2.400 kg CO₂e/kg, RFNBO 3.384. Recorded as bounds in `h2_prices.LCHS_CEILING_KGCO2E_PER_KG`, never as values

gap86.name: A power transformer in ecoinvent
cells: Every activity in ecoinvent 3.9.1 apos matching `transformer`, `substation`, `switchgear` or `switch cabinet`

**Nothing usable.** Four transformer activities exist, being two products with a market and a production each, and both are electronic components — ecoinvent's own comments give their average weights as **280 g** and **30 g** and describe them as used "in the information and communication technology". Zero substation, switchgear or switch-cabinet activities. The largest single use of the high-voltage one anywhere in the database applies **12.8 t** of a 280 g component to a solar thermal plant, so the mis-scaling is widespread rather than particular to this study. Power transformers must therefore be assembled from a bill of materials — which is what Leng, Teffera and Vestas each did independently

gap87.name: A newer ecoinvent PV dataset
cells: ecoinvent 3.10.1 apos, present in the `hypt` Brightway project on this machine

**No improvement.** `photovoltaic plant construction, 570kWp, multi-Si, on open ground` has all six technosphere exchanges byte-identical to 3.9.1. Only the background differs, and mixing versions would break the "3.9.1 apos throughout" consistency claim. GB has three PV activities in either version; the other two are 3 kWp slanted-roof of the same vintage

cells: FES models **salt caverns** only (DNV-GL 2019). This study uses a ~10 t steel vessel, already inventoried from Gandiglio et al. 2022.
